charities.blurb: Australia's national charity dedicated to protecting ocean wildlife.

name: American Alligator
range: Freshwater wetlands of the southeastern United States, from North Carolina to Texas
tagline: The swamp giant whose bellow makes the water dance
lede: A broad-snouted relic of the swamps, the American alligator roars so deeply that droplets leap from the water around it. Hunted to the edge a century ago, it has come back so strongly that it now turns up on golf courses across the American South.
home:
American alligators live in the freshwater wetlands of the southeastern United States, from the Lowcountry of South Carolina south to the Everglades and west to South Texas, with populations in North Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Louisiana, Alabama, Mississippi, Arkansas, Oklahoma and Texas. They use swamps, rivers, ponds, lakes, marshy prairies and canals, and females and juveniles also turn up in seasonal wetlands.

They can wander into brackish water, but the salt glands on their tongues don't work, so they tolerate salt far less well than the American crocodile. They cope with cold far better, though: no other crocodilian lives so far from the equator. When the surface freezes, an alligator pokes its snout up through the ice to breathe and can stay like that for several days.
anatomy:
Adult males are usually 3.4 to 4.8 metres long and can weigh up to 450 kg, while females reach 2.6 to 3.35 metres. Alligators are olive, brown, grey or black above, among the darkest of all crocodilians, with cream undersides.

Their U-shaped snout is broader than a crocodile's, and when the jaws close, the upper jaw covers the lower teeth, hiding the fourth tooth that stays visible in crocodiles. An alligator has 74 to 80 teeth and replaces them roughly once a year.

Its bite was once the strongest ever measured in a laboratory, at up to 13,172 newtons, yet the muscles that open the jaws are so weak that a captured animal's mouth can be held shut with tape. In water it swims with side-to-side sweeps of its tail, helped by webbed hind feet, and it can shift its lungs within its body to dive, rise and roll.
life:
Alligators are apex predators that take fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals and even other alligators, while hatchlings mostly eat invertebrates. Their teeth grip but cannot slice, so they swallow stones and let a gizzard grind their food.

They have also been seen eating wild grapes, elderberries and citrus fruit, and groups have been watched herding fish towards a bank, taking turns at pushing and catching. They are noisy reptiles. Adults growl, hiss and cough at rivals, and both sexes bellow in deep, intermittent roars.

In the breeding season, males produce infrasound so powerful that the surface over their backs sprinkles upwards, a display known as the water dance. Bellowing choruses are often felt more than heard, and can be set off by tubas, sonic booms and large aircraft.
family:
Breeding begins in spring. The female builds a mound of plants, sticks, leaves and mud near the water and lays 20 to 50 white eggs about the size of a goose egg.

The rotting vegetation keeps them warm, and the temperature decides the hatchlings' sex: warmer nests on levees produce males, cooler marsh nests produce females. She guards the nest for the 65-day incubation, digs the young out when she hears them yelp, and carries them to the water in her mouth.

Hatchlings are striped with yellow bands for camouflage and stay in pods near their mother, who may protect them for a year or longer. Males mature at about 11.6 years and females at about 15.8, and alligators typically live to 50, possibly beyond 70.
remarkable:
Alligators are among the first reptiles recorded using tools. In Florida and Louisiana they have been seen balancing sticks on their heads in the nesting season, apparently luring birds that come looking for building material.

A later experiment failed to show that they do this more often near bird colonies, so the purpose of the trick is still debated.
outlook:
From the 19th to the mid-20th century, alligators were hunted and poached so heavily that their survival was in doubt. Alabama banned hunting them in 1938, and in 1967 the species was listed as endangered.

With federal and state protection it recovered so well that it was taken off the endangered list in 1987, and it is now rated Least Concern. Trade in alligators is still regulated, partly so that skins of threatened crocodilians can't be passed off as alligator.
people:
The name comes from the Spanish el lagarto, 'the lizard'. Fatal attacks on people are rare but do happen as homes spread into low-lying land: Florida has documented 257 attacks since 1948, an estimated 23 of them deadly. Alligator farming is a growing industry in Georgia, Florida, Texas and Louisiana, which together produce some 45,000 hides a year.

Alligator wrestling, first practised by the Miccosukee and Seminole peoples to catch food, became a tourist show from the late 1880s. The alligator is the state reptile of Florida, Louisiana and Mississippi, and the University of Florida's teams have been the Gators since 1911, after a printer put an alligator emblem on a batch of football pennants.
relatives:
The American alligator is one of only two living alligators; the other is the much smaller Chinese alligator. Together they form the subfamily Alligatorinae, the sister group of the caimans.

It was first described in 1801 by the French zoologist François Marie Daudin, and Georges Cuvier created the genus Alligator for it in 1807. Fossils identical to the modern species appear throughout the Pleistocene, though how far back its lineage stretches is still debated.
didYouKnow: American alligators bellow in B flat, at a frequency of about 58 Hz.

quiz.prompt: What decides whether an alligator hatchling is male or female?
choices: The amount of salt in the water around the nest site
quiz.explanation: Warmer nests produce males and cooler nests produce females.

quiz.prompt: How can you tell an alligator from a crocodile when its mouth is shut?
choices: Its snout is narrow and pointed
Its tail is shorter than its body
Its eyes are set on the sides of its head like a lizard's
quiz.explanation: In an alligator the upper jaw covers the lower teeth, hiding the fourth tooth.

quiz.prompt: Why was the alligator taken off the US endangered list in 1987?
choices: It was reclassified as a lizard
Its range was found to extend far into Mexico and Cuba
quiz.explanation: Protection allowed numbers to recover so well that it was no longer considered endangered.

charities.name: The Nature Conservancy
charities.blurb: Protects wetlands and other natural lands across the United States and beyond.

name: Arapaima
range: Amazon and Tocantins–Araguaia river basins of South America
tagline: A giant armoured fish that must gulp air to survive
lede: Every 5 to 15 minutes, a shadow rises through a murky Amazon lake and gulps air with a loud smack. The arapaima is one of the largest freshwater fish on Earth, a living relic clad in armour-like scales, and its need to breathe at the surface very nearly cost it everything.
home:
The arapaima is native to the basins of the Amazon and the Tocantins–Araguaia rivers, and is known from Brazil and Peru, with small populations also recorded in Ecuador, Colombia and Guyana. Its life follows the flood.

When the rivers rise, it moves into the flooded forest, where prey is plentiful for adults and young alike. As the water falls, it retreats to lower forest and then to lakes, where it may be cut off until the next high water. It has also spread far beyond its home.

Introduced to the Madre de Dios region of Peru for fish farming in 1976, it escaped when ponds overflowed and reached Bolivian rivers within about a decade. It has been taken to East Asia too, and is farmed in Thailand and Malaysia and found in Java and Sumatra.
anatomy:
Arapaima commonly reach 2 metres, with reports of exceptional fish up to 4.5 metres, and adults may weigh 200 kg. The body is streamlined, with the dorsal and anal fins set far back towards the tail. It is mostly grey to grey-green, but mature males develop red colouring over as much as 70% of the body, a sign of age that may help attract mates.

Its scales are a natural armour, with a hard mineralised outer layer over a tough, flexible inner layer of collagen, and they help protect it from piranhas. Each is typically 5 to 7 centimetres across and can reach 10 centimetres. To breathe, it uses a modified swim bladder lined with lung-like tissue.

Young fish switch from water-breathing to air-breathing just 8 to 9 days after hatching, and their gills change shape as they do.
life:
The arapaima is a specialised carnivore that eats mainly fish, including several families of catfish, along with invertebrates. Young fish favour insects and fish larvae. It will also take birds, mammals, fruits and seeds from the water's surface, and its growth swings with the seasons as food comes and goes.

It grows remarkably fast, putting on about 10 kg in its first year. Growth slows once it matures at around 5 years old, when it is about 1.65 metres long. In the high-water season, lakes hold dense gatherings of arapaima, which find safety, food and partners there.
family:
Spawning happens in lakes and river channels between August and March, when the water is low. Pairs use their mouths to dig a nest in the bottom and lay small, separate batches of eggs, usually fewer than 500 at a time, which spreads the risk in an unpredictable environment. If breeding fails, a pair may try again.

The male does most of the parenting, guarding the young for three to six months. Both parents have a gland on the head that releases a secretion of around 400 substances, including hormones and proteins, which helps them communicate with their offspring and also nourishes the newly hatched fry. In captivity arapaima live 15 to 20 years; their lifespan in the wild is unknown.
remarkable:
The arapaima is caught in what has been called the biodiversity conservation paradox. In its native rivers it has declined and vanished from some areas, while escaped farm fish are spreading as an invader elsewhere.

In Bolivia its arrival has been linked to falling numbers of native fish, and the Beni River has few natural barriers to stop it moving further.
outlook:
Overfishing hit the arapaima hard, made worse because a fish that must surface regularly is easy to harpoon. Habitat loss and broken migration routes have left some populations isolated and inbred. The IUCN lists it as Data Deficient because too little is known about its numbers, and its trade has been controlled under CITES since 1975.

There is good news too. Brazil banned arapaima fishing from 1996 to 1999, then allowed it only in designated areas under careful management, and stocks there rose from 2,500 in 1999 to over 170,000 in 2017. Illegal fishing remains a problem, making up about 77% of the harvest in the lower Amazon.
people:
The fish goes by several names. In Brazil it is the pirarucu, from an Indigenous word for 'red fish', which may refer to the red flecks near its tail or the reddish-orange colour of its meat. In Bolivia and Peru it is called paiche.

It is an important traditional food for communities around the Amazon, and fishing and fish farming provide many jobs in the region. Its big, tough scales are commonly used as nail files, and young fish are sold into the ornamental trade in Europe, North America, South America and Asia.
relatives:
The arapaima belongs to an ancient group of carnivorous bony-tongued fishes. For a long time it was thought to be the only species in its genus, but others, such as Arapaima leptosoma and Arapaima agassizii, have since been recognised.

Because specimens are rare and several type specimens have been lost, how many species there really are remains unclear. A fossil of an arapaima, or something very like one, about 13 million years old has been found in the Villavieja Formation of Colombia.
didYouKnow: In arapaima only the left ovary or left testis develops, sitting close to the swim bladder.

quiz.prompt: Why does an arapaima have to come to the surface?
choices: To warm itself in the sun
To scrape parasites off its scales on floating plants
quiz.explanation: It relies on a lung-like swim bladder and must gulp air every 5 to 15 minutes.

quiz.prompt: Which parent mainly guards arapaima young?
choices: Both equally, taking turns every few hours
quiz.explanation: Males provide most of the parental care, guarding the young for three to six months.

quiz.prompt: What does the Brazilian name 'pirarucu' mean?
choices: Fish that no hunter catches twice
quiz.explanation: It comes from an Indigenous word for 'red fish'.

charities.name: WWF
charities.blurb: Works across the Amazon to protect rivers, forests and freshwater wildlife.

charities.name: Wildlife Conservation Society
charities.blurb: Protects wildlife and wild places in the Amazon and around the world.

name: Domestic Silk Moth
range: Domesticated in China and now reared worldwide; unknown in the wild
tagline: The flightless moth behind 5,000 years of silk
lede: For at least 5,000 years, people have raised a small white moth for the thread its caterpillar spins. The domestic silk moth has been shaped so thoroughly by that partnership that it can no longer fly, has lost its colour, and exists nowhere in the wild.
home:
The domestic silk moth lives only in human care. It was domesticated from the wild silk moth, Bombyx mandarina, which ranges from northern India through northern China, Korea and Japan to the far east of Russia, and the domestic form derives from Chinese rather than Japanese or Korean stock.

Today it is reared wherever silk is made, and breeds fall into three types by how often they produce a brood. Univoltine moths, mainly in and around Europe, have a single brood a year, and their eggs must pass the winter before hatching.

Bivoltine varieties of East Asia breed faster, helped by warmer climates. Polyvoltine moths, found only in the tropics, can run through up to eight generations a year, with eggs hatching in 9 to 12 days.
anatomy:
The adult moth has a wingspan of 3 to 5 centimetres and a white, hairy body. Females are 2 to 3 times bulkier than males because they carry so many eggs. Like all adult moths in its family, it has reduced mouthparts and never feeds.

Its wings are too small for its heavy body, so although some moths can briefly lift off, none can manage sustained flight. The caterpillar, the silkworm, spins its cocoon from raw silk made in its salivary glands.

A single cocoon is one thread between 300 and about 900 metres long, with fine, lustrous fibres about 10 micrometres across. The silkworm's genome, published in 2008, holds at least 3,000 genes found in no other genome, including sucrase genes apparently acquired from bacteria that let it cope with toxic mulberry leaves.
life:
Silkworms are fussy eaters, feeding almost entirely on mulberry leaves and preferring white mulberry, whose scent compound cis-jasmone attracts them. Researchers have since developed artificial diets, and some strains have been bred to eat other foods. A silkworm passes through five stages, moulting four times, and turns slightly yellow with tight skin just before it starts to spin.

Centuries of breeding have made the domestic moth bigger, faster-growing and better at digesting its food, and tolerant of handling and crowding. It has also lost any fear of predators. Because males cannot fly off to find females, as wild Bombyx males do, people have to bring the sexes together.
family:
Eggs take about 14 days to hatch and are kept in incubators to help them along. After its last larval stage, the silkworm seals itself in its cocoon, where the final moult into a pupa takes place in safety. If it survives, the moth releases enzymes that dissolve a hole in the cocoon so it can climb out.

Those enzymes break the long thread into short lengths, so in conventional silk farming the cocoons are put in boiling water before the moth can emerge. The heat kills the pupa and loosens the silk for unwinding. Damaged cocoons are still used as stuffing for duvets and jackets.
remarkable:
The silk moth is a working laboratory animal as well as a farm animal.

Scientists have engineered silkworms that make spider silk, used them to discover antibiotics such as lysocin E, and built a pavilion at the MIT Media Lab with the help of 6,500 of them. Hundreds of strains are kept, and over 400 inherited mutations have been described.
outlook:
As a domesticated insect, the silk moth has no conservation status and depends entirely on people. Its main threats are diseases in rearing houses: the fungus Beauveria bassiana, which strikes in cold, humid conditions; a virus that causes grasserie; pébrine, caused by a microsporidian parasite; and flacherie, which matters greatly in India.

Silk farming has also drawn criticism from animal welfare campaigners. Mahatma Gandhi opposed it on the principle of ahimsa, not harming any living thing, and that idea led to Ahimsa silk, made from the cocoons of wild and semi-wild moths that have been allowed to emerge.
people:
The oldest archaeological evidence of silk moth domestication comes from the Yangshao culture of northern China. Carp were raised in ponds on early silk farms and fed silkworm larvae and droppings, so fish farming and silk farming went hand in hand. Silk making spread from China to India, Korea, Nepal and Japan, and then to the West.

China guarded the secret closely; one story tells of a princess who smuggled silkworms in her hair when she married a prince of Khotan. Silk is under 0.2% of world fibre production but enormously valuable, and it takes over 100 kg of mulberry leaves to make 1 kg of raw silk.

China produces 70% of it. The pupae are eaten as beondegi in Korea, roasted by street vendors in China and fried with chilli in Assam, and in a Vietnamese folk tale silkworms began as the soul of a young woman who wished to go on helping people.
relatives:
Bombyx mori belongs to the family Bombycidae. Its closest relative is the wild silk moth, Bombyx mandarina, with which it can still breed and sometimes produce hybrids; whether it can cross with other Bombyx species is unknown.

Only a few moths have been exploited for fabric, mainly Bombyx and the Antheraea moths of the family Saturniidae. Its genetics hold a quirk too: in females, paired chromosomes are held together during egg formation without any crossing over between them.
didYouKnow: Teachers in the United States, China, South Africa, Iran and other countries raise silk moths in classrooms so pupils can watch an insect's whole life cycle.

quiz.prompt: Why can't the domestic silk moth fly?
choices: Its wings are glued shut by silk
Breeders clip its wings so it cannot escape the farm
quiz.explanation: Its wings are too small to carry its big, heavy body in sustained flight.

quiz.prompt: What do silkworms almost exclusively eat?
choices: Fallen fruit and the sap of young trees
quiz.explanation: Silkworms feed almost entirely on mulberry, preferring white mulberry.

name: American Bison
range: Prairies, plains and parklands of North America, mainly in parks and reserves
tagline: North America's heaviest land animal, back from the brink
lede: Before the 1870s, perhaps 60 million bison thundered across North America. Within a few years almost all were gone, slaughtered in one of the most deliberate wildlife massacres in history. Today the shaggy giant is the national mammal of the United States, and its slow return is one of conservation's great comebacks.
home:
Around 11,000 years ago, bison roamed a vast belt of grassland from Alaska to the Gulf of Mexico and east almost to the Atlantic coast. Today they live in river valleys, prairies and plains, on open and semi-open grassland, sagebrush and scrub, and in hilly country where slopes are gentle.

Some herds go much higher: Yellowstone bison are often found above 2,400 metres, and in Yukon they summer on alpine plateaus above the treeline. After many reintroductions, bison roam free again in parts of the United States, Canada and Mexico. Wood bison sent from Alberta have even been established in Yakutia, Russia, since 2006.
anatomy:
Bison are North America's heaviest land animals. Males can reach 3.5 metres from head to rump, plus a tail of up to 95 centimetres, and stand around 2 metres at the shoulder. The heaviest wild bull on record weighed 1,270 kg, while females are much smaller, typically 360 to 640 kg.

The head and forequarters are massive, topped by a hump, and both sexes carry short, curved horns up to 60 centimetres long. The dark brown winter coat is long and shaggy, replaced in summer by a lighter one.

There are two forms: the plains bison, smaller with a rounded hump, and the larger wood bison, with a taller, square hump. Calves are paler than adults for their first 2 months, and white bison, though extremely rare, do exist.
life:
Bison are mostly grazers, eating grasses and sedges and turning to sagebrush in hard times, and they drink or eat snow every day. Herds migrate, sometimes uphill and downhill with the seasons; in Wyoming's Hayden Valley they average about 3 km a day in summer.

In autumn they rub their horns on aromatic trees such as cedar and pine, perhaps to coat themselves in scents that deter insects, and they roll in dusty or muddy hollows called wallows, which boost plant and animal variety on the prairie. Their size protects them from most predators, but wolves hunt weak cows and calves, especially in late winter.

When wolves attack in the open, cows with young calves lead the escape while bulls guard the rear. Bison look sluggish but can run at 65 to 70 km/h.
family:
Females and their young live in maternal herds, while young males leave at about three years old to live alone or in bachelor groups. During the summer rut, a dominant bull 'tends' a cow, following her, chasing off rivals and even blocking her view of other males with his body. Bulls take no part in raising calves.

After a pregnancy of 285 days, a cow gives birth to a single reddish-brown calf, which nurses for at least 7 or 8 months and sometimes until the next calf arrives. Cows can breed at three years old. Calves born early in the season tend to grow larger and more dominant. Bison live around 15 years in the wild and up to 25 in captivity.
remarkable:
Bison may have helped draw the map of North America. Their seasonal trails, beaten hard by countless hoofs following ridges and watersheds, became paths for Indigenous hunters and warriors, then routes for explorers and pioneers.

Several east–west buffalo traces, such as the one through the Cumberland Gap, were later followed by railways.
outlook:
By 1889 the species had been reduced to just 541 animals. Every modern plains bison descends from about 100 survivors in six herds, five kept by private ranchers and one by the New York Zoological Park, plus a wild herd of 25 in Yellowstone.

Careful protection raised numbers from 325 in 1884 to about 500,000 in 2017, though most live in commercial herds and only about 15,000 are considered truly wild and free-ranging. Genetics are a lingering problem. Ranchers once crossed bison with cattle, and many herds still carry a little cattle DNA, so perhaps only 12,000 to 15,000 pure bison remain.
people:
For the Indigenous peoples of the Great Plains, the bison provided food, clothing, shelter and tools, with more than 150 uses for its parts, and it remains a sacred animal. Its destruction was pursued partly to break those nations, and the Crow chief Plenty Coups said that when the buffalo went away, the hearts of his people fell to the ground.

Today the Inter Tribal Bison Council, formed in 1990, brings together 56 tribes restoring herds on tribal lands. In American English, 'buffalo' and 'bison' are both correct, though in British English buffalo means the African or water buffalo. The bison appears on the Manitoba flag and the famous buffalo nickel, and was named the US national mammal in 2016.
relatives:
There are two living bison, the American and the European. The American is slightly heavier, with shorter legs and a hairier body; it grazes more and browses less, and it fights by charging rather than locking horns.

Genetic studies show that the closest living relatives of bison are yaks. Bison first appeared in Asia about 2.6 million years ago and reached North America from Siberia across Beringia between 195,000 and 135,000 years ago. The modern species is thought to have evolved from the extinct Bison antiquus.
didYouKnow: Between 1980 and 1999, bison injured more than three times as many people in Yellowstone National Park as bears did.

name: Crown-of-thorns Starfish
range: Coral reefs of the Indo-Pacific, from the Red Sea to Central America
tagline: A spiny, many-armed starfish that eats coral reefs
lede: Bristling with venomous spines and up to 21 arms, the crown-of-thorns starfish crawls over coral and digests it alive. On a healthy reef it is just another resident, but in plague years its numbers explode and whole stretches of reef are stripped white.
home:
The crown-of-thorns starfish has a vast Indo-Pacific range. It lives wherever there are coral reefs or hard coral communities, from the Red Sea and the coast of East Africa across the Indian Ocean and the Pacific to the west coast of Central America, and is perhaps most common around Australia.

Young starfish settle on coralline algae and live hidden among dead coral rubble and other concealed surfaces. For their first two years they stay out of sight, coming out at night to feed, and solitary adults usually remain secretive too. Often the only clue to one is a fresh white feeding scar on nearby coral.
anatomy:
Adults are usually 25 to 35 centimetres across, making this one of the largest starfish in the world. Although it starts life with the five-fold symmetry typical of starfish, it ends up with many arms.

Its colour depends on diet and region: purple, purple-blue, reddish grey, brown with red-tipped spines, or green with yellow tips. The upper surface is covered with stiff, very sharp spines 4 to 5 centimetres long, which give it its crown-like look.

Beneath them the body is soft and membranous; taken out of water, it collapses and leaks fluid, recovering its shape if put back alive. Two rows of tube feet run to the tip of each arm, letting it grip and bend around the complex shapes of coral. Unusually, it has true image-forming vision.
life:
This starfish is a coral predator. It climbs onto a living colony, presses close to the surface, and pushes its stomach out through its mouth over an area almost as wide as itself. Digestive enzymes liquefy the coral tissue, which it absorbs, leaving a white skeleton that algae soon cover.

One starfish can consume up to 6 square metres of living coral a year. It prefers branching and table corals such as Acropora and avoids rounder corals such as Porites, and small crabs living among branching corals can fend it off.

Its spines are a strong defence, and its tissues carry saponins, bitter, detergent-like chemicals. Fish that try juveniles often mouth them and spit them out. About 11 species have been reported eating healthy adults, including triggerfish, pufferfish, the painted shrimp and the giant Triton's trumpet snail.
family:
In early to midsummer, starfish gather high on the reef and release eggs and sperm together, apparently prompted by a spawning pheromone. Large females are astonishingly fertile: one 40 centimetres across can produce 47 to 53 million eggs. The larvae swim and filter-feed on tiny green algae for around 11 days or more before settling, usually on coralline algae, and turning into five-armed starfish less than 1 millimetre wide.

The young eat coralline algae at first, then switch to coral and grow fast, maturing at about 20 centimetres across by the end of their second year. In aquariums, most died of old age between 5 and 7.5 years.
remarkable: At low densities, crown-of-thorns starfish may actually help reefs. Because they pick and choose what they eat, they stop fast-growing corals from swamping slower-growing kinds, and some ecologists think they play a real part in keeping reefs diverse. The trouble comes only when their numbers soar.
outlook:
The species itself is not at risk; the worry is the reefs it eats. Outbreaks, with densities of 140 to 1,000 starfish per hectare, were confirmed at 21 reef locations from the Red Sea to French Polynesia between the 1960s and 1980s.

Suggested causes include overfishing of predators such as tritons and the humphead wrasse, nutrient run-off from land, and warmer seas helping larvae. After an outbreak, bare skeletons are overgrown by algae, branching corals may collapse into rubble, and fish that depend on coral lose out. People fight back with divers who inject the starfish with sodium bisulfate, bile salts or household vinegar.

In 2018 volunteer divers culled 47,000 of them on the Swains Reefs of the Great Barrier Reef, and a robot called COTSBot has been built to hunt them.
people:
The starfish is named after the crown of thorns in the Bible, which its spiny back resembles. Those spines cannot inject anything, but when one pierces skin it leaves saponin-laden tissue in the wound, causing sharp pain for hours, bleeding, nausea and swelling that can last a week or more.

Brittle spine tips can snap off and may have to be removed surgically. Alarm about the starfish began when high numbers were found around Green Island, off Cairns, in the early 1960s. Some popular books claimed the whole Great Barrier Reef was dying, and fierce disagreements among scientists over the cause became known as the 'starfish wars'.
relatives:
Georg Eberhard Rumphius first described the species in 1705 from Ambon in Indonesia, and Linnaeus named it formally in 1767 in honour of Janus Plancus. Its family, Acanthasteridae, appears to be derived from the starfish family Oreasteridae, and its sibling species is Acanthaster brevispinus, a less specialised starfish of soft seabeds.

Genetic work suggests that what was called A. planci is really a complex of four species: one each in the northern Indian Ocean, the southern Indian Ocean, the Pacific and the Red Sea. The Pacific form has been named Acanthaster solaris.
didYouKnow: A polyp-like cnidarian of the genus Paracorynactis has been seen swallowing whole a crown-of-thorns starfish up to 34 centimetres across.

quiz.explanation: It spreads its stomach over the coral and digests the living tissue.

name: Black Mamba
range: Savannas, woodlands and rocky hills of sub-Saharan Africa
tagline: Africa's longest venomous snake, with an inky-black mouth
lede: The black mamba is not black. It is grey, olive or brown, and earns its name from the inside of its mouth, which it flashes wide open when cornered. Long, fast and armed with venom that can kill within hours, it is the most feared snake in Africa, yet it would almost always rather flee.
home:
Black mambas live across a wide sweep of sub-Saharan Africa, from Burkina Faso and Cameroon east to Ethiopia, Eritrea and Somalia and south to South Africa, Namibia and Angola. Records from Senegal in the 1950s have never been confirmed. They favour fairly dry country such as light woodland, scrub, rocky outcrops and semi-arid savanna, but also live in moist savanna and lowland forest.

They are rarely found above 1,000 metres, though they have been recorded at 1,800 metres in Kenya. A mamba shelters in termite mounds, old burrows, rock crevices and tree cracks, and often keeps a permanent lair that it returns to again and again.
anatomy:
This is a long, slender snake with a coffin-shaped head and a slight brow ridge. Adults usually measure 2 to 3 metres, and some have reached 4.3 to 4.5 metres, making it the longest venomous snake in Africa and second in the world only to the king cobra. Despite that length it is light: one study of seven snakes found an average weight of 1.03 kg.

Its colour ranges from olive and yellowish-brown to khaki and gunmetal, sometimes with a purplish sheen, over a greyish-white belly. Young snakes are paler and darken with age. The inside of the mouth is dark bluish-grey to nearly black. Its fangs, up to 6.5 millimetres long, sit at the front of the upper jaw.
life:
Black mambas are active by day and live both on the ground and in trees. In South Africa they bask from about 7 to 10 in the morning and again from 2 to 4 in the afternoon, often at the same spot.

They hunt mostly small warm-blooded animals such as birds, especially fledglings, rodents, squirrels and hyraxes, and occasionally other snakes. A mamba bites and lets go, waiting for its prey to be paralysed before swallowing it, and can digest a meal in 8 to 10 hours. They are skittish and seldom let people come closer than about 40 metres.

A threatened mamba usually slips away into a hole or brush. Cornered, it gapes, spreads a narrow hood and hisses, and any sudden movement may trigger a burst of rapid strikes. Its speed is often exaggerated, but it can reach 16 km/h over short distances.
family:
The breeding season runs from September to February. Rival males wrestle, twining their bodies together and pushing with their necks to force each other down, a contest sometimes mistaken for courtship. Mating itself can last more than two hours.

The female lays a clutch of 6 to 17 long, oval eggs. Hatchlings are already 40 to 60 centimetres long and dangerous from the start, and they grow fast, reaching 2 metres within their first year. Black mambas have been recorded living 11 years and may live longer.
remarkable: The black mamba's venom contains mambalgins, toxins that block certain pain-sensing channels in the nervous system and have a painkilling effect. Researchers are interested in them as possible new analgesics, so one of the world's most dreaded venoms might one day help relieve pain.
outlook:
The black mamba is rated Least Concern by the IUCN, thanks to its huge range and no documented decline.

Its main natural enemies are birds of prey, especially brown snake eagles, which kill adults up to at least 2.7 metres long; tawny and martial eagles, mongooses, honey badgers and Nile crocodiles also take them. Mongooses and honey badgers have some resistance to its venom. Young mambas fall prey to Cape file snakes, southern ground hornbills, marsh owls and hooded vultures.
people:
The venom is mostly neurotoxic. Symptoms such as a metallic taste and drooping eyelids can appear within 10 minutes, a bite can cause collapse within 45 minutes, and without antivenom, death from respiratory failure usually follows in 7 to 15 hours. In a South African survey from 1957 to 1979, 21 of 75 people confirmed as bitten by black mambas died.

After a mamba-specific antivenom was introduced in 1962, deaths fell sharply. Most bites happen in the breeding season, when the snakes are most irritable. The word mamba comes from the Zulu imamba. In Tanzania the Ngindo name ndemalunyayo means 'grass-cutter', and in some languages its name means 'dassie catcher', after the rock hyraxes it sometimes hunts.
relatives:
Albert Günther formally described the black mamba in 1864 from a specimen collected by John Kirk on David Livingstone's Second Zambezi expedition, still kept at the Natural History Museum in London. It belongs to the family Elapidae.

Its genus name, Dendroaspis, means 'tree asp', and polylepis means 'many scales'. For 50 years it was lumped together with the eastern green mamba, until the two were split again in 1946. A 2016 genetic study showed they are each other's closest relatives, with Jameson's mamba more distant.
didYouKnow: Unlike many venomous snakes, the black mamba usually causes little swelling at the bite, and the first sign may be just a tingling sensation.

choices: The black termite mounds where it lays its eggs
quiz.explanation: The inside of its mouth is dark bluish-grey to nearly black; its body is not.

choices: The reticulated python, which is also more venomous
quiz.explanation: The black mamba is the second-longest venomous snake, after the king cobra.

choices: Climbs a tree and waits to drop onto the intruder
quiz.explanation: It seldom lets people closer than about 40 metres and usually retreats into cover.

name: Andean Cock-of-the-rock
range: Andean cloud forests from Venezuela to Bolivia
tagline: Peru's blazing national bird, a dancer of the cloud forest
lede: Deep in the misty ravines of the Andes, flame-orange males with crests like feathered discs gather to show off before watching females. The Andean cock-of-the-rock stages one of the most extravagant performances in South America's forests, and it is the national bird of Peru.
home:
The Andean cock-of-the-rock lives in the cloud forests of the Andes, across a range of about 260,000 square kilometres in Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia. It keeps mostly to ravines and forested streams in the mountains, between 500 and 2,400 metres up, usually in the lower and middle levels of the forest, though it climbs higher into fruiting trees and sometimes crosses clearings.

It has four subspecies. R. p. aequatorialis is the most widespread, from eastern Colombia and western Venezuela through eastern Ecuador to eastern Peru.

The nominate form lives only in the Andes of central Peru, sanguinolentus in western Colombia and north-western Ecuador, and saturatus in south-eastern Peru and western Bolivia. Despite its colours the bird is shy and easily missed, often glimpsed only as it bursts from cover or speeds down a valley.
anatomy:
This is a large perching bird, about 32 centimetres long and weighing around 265 grams, with the heaviest males reaching 300 grams. Males and females look very different. The male is brilliant scarlet or orange, with a large disc-shaped crest, a black tail and wings, and pale grey feathers over the shoulders.

The female is far drabber, a darker, browner bird with a smaller crest. The male's bill is yellowish, while the female's is dark with a small yellow tip. Eye colour varies with sex and subspecies, from red, orange, yellow or bluish-white in males to whitish, reddish or brown in females.
life:
Cocks-of-the-rock eat mainly fruit, especially from the laurel, custard-apple and coffee families, along with insects, and lizards and frogs have also been recorded in their diet. Oddly, they seem to pass over high-protein fruits in favour of others. They are among the many birds known to follow swarms of army ants.

A foraging bird that is disturbed, or one in flight, gives a loud, questioning 'tank?'. Their showy habits draw attention, and predators are attracted to the display grounds by the noisy, conspicuous males. Hawk-eagles, forest-falcons, hawks and owls hunt them, as do jaguars, mountain lions, ocelots and boa constrictors.
family:
Males are polygamous and play no part in nesting. Instead they gather at communal display grounds called leks, where they pair off for 'confrontation displays', facing each other while bowing, jumping and flapping their wings, snapping their bills and giving squawks and grunts.

When a female approaches, the show becomes a frenzy of colour and very strange sounds. The males are easily disturbed, so all this is hard to watch. Breeding times vary: in Colombia it usually runs from February to July, in Ecuador from July to February. The female does the rest alone.

She builds a cup-shaped nest of mud, plant matter and her own saliva, plastered to a rock face or cave entrance in a forest ravine. She usually lays two white eggs and incubates them for about 25 to 28 days, then raises the chicks by herself.
remarkable:
The display grounds change the forest around them. Seeds swallowed by the birds are dropped around leks and nests, where they sprout and grow, so the variety of these plants rises there and falls in the surrounding forest.

Even abandoned nests get a second life: a white-capped dipper was found laying its eggs in an old cock-of-the-rock nest.
outlook: No one knows how many Andean cocks-of-the-rock there are, or whether their numbers are rising or falling. The species is patchily distributed and its forest is being destroyed, but its range is large enough that the IUCN rates it as Least Concern.
people:
The Andean cock-of-the-rock is the national bird of Peru, and in Quechua it is called tunki. Both young and adult birds have occasionally been kept as pets.

Its scientific name describes where it nests. Rupicola comes from the Latin rupes, 'rock' or 'cliff', and cola, 'inhabiting', after its habit of nesting on rock walls, while peruvianus means 'of Peru'. Older books spell it peruviana, but because Latin names ending in -cola were masculine or neuter, peruvianus is the form now used.
relatives:
The species was first described by the English ornithologist John Latham in 1790. It is one of only two species in the genus Rupicola; the other is the Guianan cock-of-the-rock, its closest relative.

Both belong to the Cotingidae, the cotingas, a family of tropical forest birds that mostly eat fruit. Cotingas are suboscines, a branch of the perching birds separate from the songbirds proper.
didYouKnow: One study found that males display at the same level of light in the morning as in the afternoon, suggesting brightness sets their schedule.

quiz.prompt: Who builds the Andean cock-of-the-rock's nest?
choices: Several males working as a team at the lek
quiz.explanation: The female builds the nest, incubates the eggs and raises the young on her own.

quiz.explanation: It comes from Latin words meaning 'rock' and 'inhabiting', after its rock-wall nests.

name: Atlantic Bluefin Tuna
range: North Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea
tagline: A warm-blooded giant that crosses oceans to spawn
lede: The Atlantic bluefin tuna is built like a torpedo and can weigh more than half a tonne. It roams the whole width of an ocean, dives into the dark below 1,000 metres and runs its body several degrees warmer than the water around it. After decades of overfishing pushed it towards collapse, it has become one of the great comeback stories of the sea.
home:
Atlantic bluefins live on both sides of the Atlantic and throughout the Mediterranean Sea, although they have disappeared from the Black Sea. They forage across vast distances, from warm southern waters to the cold, food-rich seas of the far North Atlantic.

There are two main breeding populations. The eastern stock spawns in the western Mediterranean, especially around the Balearic Islands, while the western stock spawns in the Gulf of Mexico, and a third spawning area may exist in the Slope Sea off the northeastern United States.

Satellite tags show that most fish, however far they wander, return to the area where they were born to breed. Their distribution also shifts north and south as the climate of the North Atlantic warms and cools, which explains the recent rise in sightings around Britain.
anatomy:
The bluefin has a robust, diamond-shaped body, a conical head and a fairly large mouth. It is dark blue above and grey below, with a golden shimmer along its flanks and bright yellow finlets near the tail.

Its pectoral fins are relatively short, and a small 'pineal window' in the head is thought to help it navigate its huge range. Fully grown adults average 2 to 2.5 metres long and weigh about 225 to 250 kg. The largest one caught under game-fishing rules, off Prince Edward Island in Canada, weighed 679 kg and measured 3.84 metres.

Its power comes from massive muscles linked by a pair of tendons to a crescent-shaped tail. The body stays stiff while only the tail flicks, which makes each stroke very efficient, and its blood carries unusually high levels of haemoglobin to keep those muscles supplied with oxygen.
life:
Bluefins hunt small schooling fish such as sardines, herring, mackerel and eels, along with squid and crustaceans. They travel and feed in schools sorted by size, and bursts of speed from their white muscle let them run down fast prey.

The species carries more than 70 kinds of parasite, none known to harm it. Once grown, an Atlantic bluefin has very few enemies: only the largest billfishes, toothed whales and some open-ocean sharks can tackle an adult.
family:
Bluefins gather in great numbers to spawn, and over several days a female releases her eggs into the open water, where males fertilise them. A big female can shed up to 40 million eggs at a time. The eggs hatch in about two days, and within a week the larvae are tiny fish that already eat one another.

Only about 40% survive their first week, and roughly 0.1% their first year, which is why adults time their spawning to particular places and phases of the moon. In the Gulf of Mexico spawning runs from mid-April to mid-June, in water of 24 to 29 °C, while in the Mediterranean it happens from June to August. Eastern fish are thought to mature a year or two earlier than western ones.

Most bluefins in one survey were under 15 years old, but the very largest may live to 50.
remarkable:
All tunas are warm-blooded to some degree, but the bluefin is the best at it of any fish. A heat-exchanging network of blood vessels called a rete mirabile passes warmth from blood leaving its core muscles to cold blood arriving from the gills, so the heat stays inside its body instead of leaking into the sea.

This is what lets the bluefin hunt in the chilly North Atlantic, where few other large predatory fish can keep up.
outlook:
Demand for its meat drove severe overfishing. In 2009 the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas reported that stocks had fallen by 72% in the eastern Atlantic and 82% in the western Atlantic over 40 years.

A proposal to ban international trade in the species was voted down in 2010, and Greenpeace placed it on its seafood red list that year. Stricter quotas and better enforcement have since paid off. In 2021 the IUCN moved the species from Endangered to Least Concern, and by 2026 it was being described as back from the brink, helped by its huge egg output, favourable ocean conditions and recovering prey.

Some regional stocks, including the western fish that spawn in the Gulf of Mexico, remain depleted, and the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill struck that spawning ground at its busiest season.
people:
People have eaten bluefin for an extraordinarily long time: its bones turn up in Middle Palaeolithic layers of Gorham's Cave in Gibraltar. Around the Mediterranean, elaborate mazes of nets known as tonnara in Italy and almadraba in Spain trapped spawning tuna for more than a thousand years.

In Britain it was long called the tunny, and the word 'tuna', from the Spanish atún, caught on in California in the early 1900s. Today about 80% of the Atlantic and Pacific bluefin caught are eaten in Japan, where it is prized for sushi and sashimi.

One Atlantic bluefin caught off the eastern United States sold for US$247,000 at Tokyo's Tsukiji market in 2008. Canadian fishermen began fattening wild-caught young tuna in pens in the 1970s, and such ranching now takes place across the Mediterranean.
relatives:
Carl Linnaeus described the species in 1758 as Scomber thynnus. It belongs to the mackerel family, Scombridae, and its closest relative is the Pacific bluefin tuna.

The southern bluefin looks similar but is actually closer to the yellowfin and bigeye tunas; the resemblance arose through convergent evolution. Alongside marlins and swordfish, the Atlantic bluefin ranks among the largest of the spiny-finned fishes.
didYouKnow: In 1934, off Liverpool in Nova Scotia, six anglers taking turns battled a single bluefin for 62 hours, the longest recorded fight between people and a tuna.

quiz.prompt: Where does the western stock of Atlantic bluefin spawn?
choices: In the cold waters off Prince Edward Island
quiz.explanation: Western fish spawn in the Gulf of Mexico; eastern fish spawn in the western Mediterranean.

quiz.prompt: How does the bluefin keep its core muscles warm?
choices: A heat-exchanging web of blood vessels
Eating oily prey that releases heat as it digests
quiz.explanation: A rete mirabile passes heat from outgoing to incoming blood so it isn't lost to the sea.

quiz.prompt: Roughly what share of caught bluefin is eaten in Japan?
choices: Almost none, since most is canned for Europe
quiz.explanation: About 80% of Atlantic and Pacific bluefin caught are consumed in Japan.

name: Seven-spot Ladybird
range: Europe, most of Asia and North Africa; introduced to North America
tagline: The aphid hunter in a scarlet, seven-spotted coat
lede: Seven black spots on scarlet wing cases make this one of the most recognisable insects on Earth. Behind the cheerful colours is a tireless predator of aphids, so useful to farmers that it has been carried across continents to guard their crops.
home:
The seven-spot ladybird is native to the Palearctic, ranging across Europe, including Britain and European Russia, most of Asia from the Middle East to China, Japan, the Koreas, India and Pakistan, and North Africa. It thrives wherever the climate is temperate, plants are plentiful and aphids gather.

It turns up in forests, grasslands, farmland, marshes, parks and gardens, on everything from herbs and crops to trees and shrubs, from sea level up to about 1,500 metres. It has also been introduced to South Africa and North America, where it is now found across the whole United States and southern Canada.
anatomy:
The adult is a small, oval, domed beetle 6.5 to 7.8 millimetres long and about 4 millimetres wide. Its hardened forewings, the elytra, are orange-red, with three black spots on each side and a seventh straddling the join just behind the head.

Two small white patches sit just in front of that central spot, and there are more white marks on the shield over its thorax. The size and position of the spots vary a little between individuals, and the colours double as a warning: the redder the wings and the bigger the spots, the more toxic the beetle tends to be.

The eggs are about 1 millimetre long, orange or yellow and spindle-shaped. Larvae look nothing like the adults: they are long, segmented and mostly dull black, growing from 1 to 2 millimetres at hatching to about 8 millimetres.
life:
Both adults and larvae feed on aphids, taking at least 24 different species. They find them by smell, homing in on the alarm signals aphids give off and on chemicals released by plants under aphid attack. Some aphids are best avoided: the lupin aphid absorbs toxins from its food plant that can stupefy the ladybird and stunt its growth.

When aphids run short, the beetles survive on pollen, nectar, thrips and whitefly, though they cannot breed on that diet. Adults have few enemies.

As well as their warning colours, they defend themselves by reflex bleeding, oozing a foul-tasting fluid laced with alkaloids from their leg joints. Birds, small mammals, spiders and other ladybirds still take some, and parasitic wasps lay their eggs inside them. In winter adults gather in clusters to hibernate, drawn together by a scent one of them releases, which also guarantees partners when spring comes.
family:
The seven-spot develops from egg through four larval stages and a pupa to the adult in about six weeks, and in good conditions it can fit in five generations a year.

Adults are ready to breed 10 to 14 days after emerging, and unmated females release a scent that draws in males. In summer, females lay clusters of about 10 to 30 eggs on leaves and stems, using smell to avoid spots where other seven-spots have already laid.

Over her life a female lays 250 to 500 eggs. Larvae hatch after about four days and start by eating their own eggshells and any infertile eggs nearby. There is no parental care. An adult can live for one to two years, depending on whether it survives the winter.
remarkable:
During the English heatwave of 1976, a warm spring had produced a glut of aphids, and then the drought shrivelled their food plants. Ladybirds that had multiplied on the feast took to the air in search of food, and an estimated 23.65 billion seven-spots piled up along the south and east coasts.

Healthy ones can fly 120 kilometres at a height of 1,000 metres, but these were too exhausted to cross the sea. Locals called it 'the year of the ladybird', and the thirsty beetles even bit people in an effort to take in moisture.
outlook:
The seven-spot ladybird has not been evaluated by the IUCN. It is common across much of its range, but in parts of Europe it is declining because of the harlequin ladybird from Asia, which resists disease better, competes for the same food and even eats seven-spots.

The harlequin reached the south coast of England in 2004. In North America the roles are reversed. There, the seven-spot is the newcomer, and together with the harlequin it is thought to have contributed to sharp declines in native ladybirds, including other members of its own genus.
people:
Legend says that medieval farmers prayed to the Virgin Mary to save their crops from pests, and red beetles arrived to eat them. The farmers called them 'The Beetle of Our Lady', which became 'ladybird' and 'ladybug', and the red wings were linked to the red cloak Mary wears in paintings. In Sweden the insect is called nyckelpiga, 'key helper', and in Spain mariquita, from Maria.

It is the national insect of Finland and the official insect of five US states: Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Delaware, Ohio and Tennessee. Repeated efforts were made between 1956 and 1971 to release it in North America to fight aphids, and breeding programmes around the world now mass-rear it for release on farmland.
relatives:
Carl Linnaeus named the species in 1758. Coccinella comes from the Latin coccineus, 'scarlet', and septempunctata simply means 'seven-spotted'. It is one of roughly 5,000 species in the ladybird family, Coccinellidae.

Its relatives include the invasive harlequin ladybird, which eats a broader range of food, and the nine-spotted ladybug, the state insect of New York.
didYouKnow: Despite deliberate releases, the seven-spot only became established in the United States in 1973, when a population turned up in New Jersey, apparently brought in by accident with waste from John F. Kennedy International Airport.

quiz.prompt: What is the seven-spot ladybird's 'reflex bleeding'?
choices: Oozing foul fluid from its leg joints
Flashing its hind wings to startle an attacker into fleeing
quiz.explanation: It releases a bitter, alkaloid-rich fluid from its leg joints to deter predators.

quiz.prompt: Roughly how many seven-spots swarmed England's coasts in 1976?
choices: Nearly a trillion, covering every beach in Britain
quiz.explanation: An estimated 23.65 billion piled up on the south and east coasts during the heatwave.

quiz.prompt: Which country has the seven-spot as its national insect?
quiz.explanation: It is the national insect of Finland.

name: Bat-eared Fox
range: Dry grasslands and savannas of eastern and southern Africa
tagline: A termite-eating fox that hunts with its huge ears
lede: Picture a small fox wearing ears far too big for its head, and you have the bat-eared fox. Instead of chasing rabbits or birds, it spends its time listening for termites underground, and it carries a mouthful of teeth unlike any other dog's.
home:
Bat-eared foxes live in the dry and semi-dry country of eastern and southern Africa, in two separate populations roughly 1,000 kilometres apart that were probably joined during the Pleistocene. One subspecies ranges from southern Sudan, Ethiopia and Somalia through Uganda and Kenya to southwestern Tanzania; the other runs from Angola, Namibia and Botswana through South Africa to the Cape, and east into Zimbabwe and Mozambique.

They favour short grassland, open acacia woodland and the drier parts of the savanna, especially bare ground where grazing antelope and other hoofed animals keep the grass short. They dig dens to escape heat and wind as well as to raise their young, rest in the shade of acacias, and duck into tall grass or thick shrubs when threatened. A home range covers 0.3 to 3.5 square kilometres.
anatomy:
This is a small canid, weighing 3 to 5.3 kg, with a head and body 46 to 66 centimetres long and a bushy tail of 23 to 34 centimetres.

Its ears measure 11 to 13 centimetres and help it shed heat as well as hear. The coat is tan with grey-tipped guard hairs, pale on the throat and belly, with dark legs and a black muzzle, face mask and tail tip; the insides of the ears are white. Unusually for a canid, females are generally larger than males.

Its teeth are small and blunt, with strong roots but little shearing edge, suited to crunching insects rather than slicing meat. It has 46 to 50 teeth in total, the highest number known in any land mammal that is not a marsupial, including more molars than any other placental mammal. A step-shaped bony ledge on the lower jaw anchors a muscle that lets it open and shut its mouth five times a second.
life:
The bat-eared fox is the only truly insect-eating member of the dog family, and harvester termites can make up 80 to 90% of its diet. It also eats other termites, ants, dung beetles, crickets, grasshoppers, millipedes, scorpions and spiders, along with occasional rodents, lizards, eggs, fruit and even desert truffles.

It refuses snouted harvester termites, probably because it cannot cope with their chemical defences. It hunts mainly by sound, walking slowly with its nose low and its ears tilted forward, and it will raid termite mounds that aardvarks have broken open.

Around the Serengeti it is active mostly at night, while in South Africa it switches to daytime foraging in winter. These are sociable animals that forage, play and rest together, groom each other at length and talk with their ears and tails; an arched tail signals excitement, aggression or play.
family:
Most pairs are monogamous, though some groups include one male and up to three related females. After a pregnancy of 60 to 70 days the female gives birth to one to six pups, born in the southern spring. She nurses them for 14 to 15 weeks, spending much of her time foraging to keep up her milk, but she does not carry food back to them.

The young leave their family at 5 to 6 months old and are mature at 8 to 9 months. Bat-eared foxes have lived up to 9 years in the wild and 14 to 17 years in captivity.
remarkable:
In most of the dog family the mother does the bulk of the childcare, but bat-eared foxes reverse the roles.

The father grooms the pups, huddles with them, guards the den, chaperones them on outings and carries them between dens. How much time a male spends at the den is directly linked to how many of his pups survive.
outlook:
The bat-eared fox is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN and by the South African National Biodiversity Institute, and parts of its range lie within protected areas. There are no major threats to the species, though hunting, drought and diseases such as canine distemper, parvovirus and rabies can cut numbers locally for a while.

Large carnivores, big birds of prey and rock pythons all take bat-eared foxes. Black-backed jackals are the main danger to pups, and adults gang up to mob them away from breeding areas.
people:
The 'bat' in its name probably refers to the Egyptian slit-faced bat, a common bat in the same region that also has very large ears. It goes by many other names, including big-eared fox, black-eared fox, Delalande's fox and motlosi.

By eating harvester termites, which are considered pests, the fox does farmers a favour. It has been hunted for its fur in Botswana, and it is kept in zoos in North America, South Africa, Europe and Asia.
relatives:
Its scientific name means 'big-eared ear-dog': Otocyon comes from the Greek for ear and dog, and megalotis from the Greek for large ear. First described as Canis megalotis because it resembles a jackal, it was later given its own genus, of which it is the only living member.

Genetically it is a sister to all other fox-like canids rather than a true fox, and it is similar in size to its close relatives the Cape fox and the raccoon dog. Its fossil record is thin. An extinct relative, now usually placed in the genus Prototocyon, is known from Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania, and the oldest fossils of the bat-eared fox itself, from Kenya, are about 300,000 years old.
didYouKnow: When termites are plentiful, feeding gatherings of up to 15 bat-eared foxes from different families can form without any fighting over food.

quiz.prompt: Which parent does most of the pup care in bat-eared foxes?
choices: Unrelated helpers from neighbouring family groups
quiz.explanation: Males groom, guard, huddle with and carry the pups.

quiz.prompt: How does a bat-eared fox mainly locate its prey?
choices: By feeling vibrations in the sand through its paws
quiz.explanation: It finds insects mainly by sound, walking slowly with its ears tilted forward.

quiz.prompt: What makes up most of the bat-eared fox's diet?
choices: Small birds and their eggs taken from ground nests
quiz.explanation: Harvester termites can make up 80 to 90% of what it eats.

name: Elkhorn Coral
range: Shallow reefs of Florida, the Bahamas and the Caribbean
tagline: The antler-shaped coral that built the Caribbean's reefs
lede: Elkhorn coral grows in thick, flattened branches that look like the antlers of an elk, forming thickets just below the surface of Caribbean seas. For thousands of years it was a foundation of the region's reefs. Within a single human lifetime, it has all but vanished from many of them.
home:
Elkhorn coral grows in clear, shallow water throughout the Bahamas, Florida and the Caribbean, reaching as far as the northern coast of Venezuela. Its northernmost outpost lies off Broward County in Florida, and today it survives in places such as the southern Florida coast and the Bay Islands of Honduras.

It lives between 1 and 5 metres deep, in rough, wave-washed water. That depth gives its partner algae plenty of sunlight, and the constant pounding of the surf actually helps it spread, by snapping off pieces that can grow into new colonies.
anatomy:
Each colony builds a hard skeleton of calcium carbonate in the shape of broad, branching antlers, dull brownish-yellow in colour. A large colony can stand more than 2 metres high and spread up to 13 metres wide, and its thick branches interlock into a dense lattice.

It is one of the fastest-growing corals. Colonies typically add 5 to 10 centimetres a year, healthy branches can lengthen by up to 13 centimetres, and a colony can reach full size in 10 to 12 years. Colonies can live for centuries, although growth slows sharply when they are stressed.
life:
Most of the coral's food comes from zooxanthellae, single-celled algae living inside its cells. They use sunlight to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugars and oxygen, which they share with their host in return for shelter. Because it relies so heavily on light, elkhorn coral suffers when the water turns cloudy. It can also hunt.

At night it reaches out with its tentacles to catch zooplankton, the tiny animals that sink to the depths by day and rise towards the surface after dark. Feeding at night saves energy, and during bleaching or long spells of murky water this filter feeding helps keep it alive.
family:
Each colony is a simultaneous hermaphrodite, producing both eggs and sperm, but it seldom fertilises itself: two genetically different parents are needed. Spawning happens once a year, for just a few nights after a full moon in July, August or September. The colonies release eggs and sperm into the water, and the larvae that result settle on hard surfaces to start new colonies. Success rates are low.

Most new colonies form another way. Storms, heavy waves or passing boats break off branches, which are carried elsewhere, take hold and grow. These new colonies are clones of their parent, and unlike spawning, this fragmentation can happen at any time of year.
remarkable:
Elkhorn coral evolved during the Pliocene, between about 5.2 and 2.58 million years ago, and its speed and its knack for spreading by fragments made it a chief architect of Caribbean reefs.

For the last 5,000 years it formed the southeastern reefs together with staghorn and star corals. Its growth rate even let reefs keep pace with rising sea levels, and since its decline no other coral has taken over that role.
outlook:
Elkhorn coral dominated the Caribbean in the early 1980s, but its numbers fell by around 97% between 1980 and 2006. Rising sea temperatures make it expel its algae and bleach, ocean acidification weakens its skeleton, and overfishing removes the fish that graze down smothering seaweed. Untreated sewage spreads white pox, a contagious disease whose lesions can grow by 10.5 square centimetres a day; one outbreak in 2005 wiped out 75% of Caribbean corals.

It was listed as threatened under the US Endangered Species Act in 2006, alongside staghorn coral, and kept at that level in 2014 partly over fears that a more severe listing would discourage restoration. After the marine heatwave of 2023, it is considered functionally extinct on Florida's Coral Reef.
people:
Elkhorn thickets are valuable to people as well as fish. Their tangled branches shelter young fish and protect them from predators, making reefs richer and more attractive to tourists. They also act as natural breakwaters, absorbing the energy of storm waves before they hit the shore and reducing damage to coastal homes.

In 2009 US recovery funding paid for a network of coral nurseries off southern Florida and the US Virgin Islands. New research suggests nursery-grown fragments can be planted on reefs after just two weeks instead of months or years, making restoration roughly 30 times cheaper.
relatives:
Elkhorn coral belongs to the genus Acropora, a large group of branching reef-building corals.

Its closest companion in the Caribbean is staghorn coral, which shares its habitat and many of its traits and is listed with it under US law. The two even interbreed, producing a hybrid known as Acropora prolifera.
didYouKnow: Only about half of all elkhorn coral colonies are genetically unique individuals, because so many are clones grown from broken fragments.

quiz.prompt: How do most new elkhorn coral colonies form?
choices: By releasing eggs at every full moon of the year
quiz.explanation: Fragmentation by storms, waves and boats is its most common way of reproducing.

quiz.prompt: Where does elkhorn coral get most of its food?
choices: Sunlight soaked up directly by its limestone skeleton
quiz.explanation: Zooxanthellae algae living in its cells photosynthesise and share their sugars.

quiz.prompt: By roughly how much did elkhorn coral decline between 1980 and 2006?
choices: Barely at all, though it moved into deeper water
quiz.explanation: Disease, warming, algae and human activity cut its numbers by about 97%.

name: Chinese Alligator
range: A few ponds and wetlands in southeastern Anhui, China
tagline: A shy, snail-eating alligator that may have inspired dragons
lede: Small, dark and armoured from snout to belly, the Chinese alligator spends half the year dormant in underground tunnels and the warm months crunching snails by night. Once it ranged as far as Japan; now it clings on in a handful of ponds, and it may have helped inspire the Chinese dragon.
home:
The Chinese alligator is found only in China. It once lived throughout the Yangtze river system, but by the late 1980s it was confined to small ponds in six counties of southeastern Anhui province, and it may survive in neighbouring Jiangsu and Zhejiang. The IUCN puts the area it occupies at about 5 square kilometres.

It is the only member of the alligator family living in the Eastern Hemisphere. It lives in freshwater wetlands and ponds where subtropical and temperate climates meet, at the foot of hills with grass and shrubs. Habitat loss has pushed some alligators higher than they would choose, into colder places where the soil is poor for digging.
anatomy:
This is one of the smallest crocodilians, 1.5 to 2.1 metres long and 36 to 45 kg as an adult, less than half the size of the American alligator. Females are about three-quarters the length of males. The largest reported male was 2.46 metres long and weighed 84 kg.

Adults are almost entirely black or dark grey. The snout is short, broad and slightly upturned, the head is sturdy, and a bony wall divides the nostrils. Unlike its American cousin it is armoured even on the belly, with up to 17 rows of scales, and it has bony plates on its upper eyelids. Its toes are not webbed, and its 72 to 76 teeth are dull, which suits a diet of shelled animals.
life:
From late October to mid-April it lies dormant in burrows dug with its head and front legs beside ponds. These tunnels are often 10 to 25 metres long, with several chambers, pools and entrances, and they never get colder than 10 °C.

In spring it basks, and through the summer it feeds at night and shelters by day, avoiding both heat and people. It is docile and does not normally attack humans. It eats whatever is available, mostly fish and invertebrates such as snails, mussels, clams, crustaceans and insects, plus rodents and waterbirds when it can.

In one 1985 study, snails made up 63% of its diet. It is a chatty reptile, hissing, whining and slapping its head on the water at close range and bellowing over long distances, always at low pitches under 500 hertz that carry well through dense vegetation.
family:
Mating peaks in mid-June. Both sexes gather at ponds for bellowing choruses that last about 10 minutes, and females mate only with males bigger than themselves. Many clutches have more than one father. In July or August the female piles rotting leaves into a nest 40 to 70 centimetres high, often on an island under thick cover, and lays usually 20 to 30 eggs at night.

At about 6 centimetres long and 45 grams, they are the smallest eggs of any crocodilian. The eggs incubate for about 70 days at around 25 to 26 °C, and the temperature decides whether each hatchling will be male or female.

In September the mother helps her young out and carries them to the water. Hatchlings are just 20 to 22 centimetres long, with pale speckles, and have only about two months to feed before their first winter, when they depend on their mother's protection. Females mature at 4 to 7 years, and the species can live beyond 50 years, reaching 70 in captivity.
remarkable:
The wild and captive fortunes of this alligator could hardly be more different. In 1998 the largest group left in the wild was 11 animals in a single farmland pond, and fewer than 130 survived in 2001.

Yet captive breeding, begun in the 1970s, had produced at least 20,000 Chinese alligators by 2016, about 15,000 of them at one breeding centre near Xuancheng in Anhui.
outlook:
The species is listed as Critically Endangered by the IUCN, and China has given it the highest level of legal protection since 1972. Its wetlands were drained for rice paddies and dams, and in the 1970s and 1980s people killed alligators as pests, out of fear or for meat thought to cure colds.

Floods, poisoned rats and a snail-killing chemical used on farms from 1958 took a toll too. Captive-bred alligators are now being returned to the wild, starting with six in 2007, and the wild population had grown to about 300 by 2017. With so few left, inbreeding remains a serious worry.
people:
The alligator appears in the Classic of Poetry, composed between the 11th and 7th centuries BCE. Marco Polo, the first outsider to write about it, saw it in the late 1200s and reported that it hid in caverns by day, hunted at night and was prized for its meat, skin and gall bladder. It was once called the muddy dragon.

Some writers think it inspired the Chinese dragon, a helpful water creature of royal power and good fortune. The gentle animal wakes as the rainy season begins and returns underground as rivers fall, and drums may once have imitated its bellows, linked to the dragon's power of summoning rain. Its burrows are less welcome to farmers, since they can damage dykes.
relatives:
The French naturalist Albert-Auguste Fauvel described it scientifically in 1879. It and the American alligator are the only living members of the genus Alligator, in the family Alligatoridae.

Its oldest known fossil, about 3 million years old, comes from Japan and shows it was once larger, at least 2 metres long, and Pleistocene fossils show it ranged from Shandong to the Taiwan Strait.
didYouKnow: Chinese alligators bellow most often in the early morning, between about 6 and 7 am.

quiz.prompt: Which food made up most of the Chinese alligator's diet in a 1985 study?
choices: Young turtles dug from riverbank nests
quiz.explanation: Snails made up 63% of its diet in that study.

quiz.prompt: What decides whether a Chinese alligator hatchling is male or female?
choices: Which of several males fathered that particular egg
quiz.explanation: Like many reptiles, it has temperature-dependent sex determination.

quiz.prompt: In which Chinese province do wild Chinese alligators mainly survive?
choices: Guangdong, near the mouth of the Pearl River
quiz.explanation: It is confined to small ponds in southeastern Anhui.

name: Arctic Tern
range: Breeds around the Arctic; winters at the edge of Antarctic ice
tagline: The pole-to-pole flyer with two summers a year
lede: The Arctic tern weighs about 100 grams, yet it makes the longest migration known in the animal kingdom, flying from the far north to the edge of Antarctica and back every year. By chasing the sun between hemispheres, it lives through two summers a year and sees more daylight than any other creature.
home:
Arctic terns breed right around the top of the world, in the Arctic and subarctic of Europe, Asia and North America, south to Brittany in France and Massachusetts in the United States. They nest in colonies on coasts and islands, and sometimes inland on tundra near water.

After breeding they head south and spend the southern summer at sea, reaching the northern edge of the Antarctic ice. They usually travel far enough offshore that they are rarely seen from land outside the nesting season.
anatomy:
This is a slim, medium-sized seabird, 33 to 36 centimetres long with a wingspan of 76 to 85 centimetres and a weight of 86 to 127 grams. Its long, narrow wings and deeply forked tail suit a life of endless flight.

In the breeding season it is grey above and pale grey below, with a black cap and nape, white cheeks and a dark red bill, legs and webbed feet. The tips of the pale grey upper wings are almost see-through. In winter the crown turns whiter and the bill darker. Young birds have black bills and legs and scaly-looking wings. It closely resembles the common tern but has a longer tail, a bill of one colour and a more nasal, rasping call.
life:
Arctic terns feed mostly on small fish, especially young shoaling species such as herring, cod, sand lances and capelin, along with crustaceans like amphipods, crabs and krill. They also take molluscs, marine worms and berries, and catch insects on the breeding grounds.

They snatch food from just below the surface or plunge-dive, and may swoop at other birds, including other terns, auks and grebes, to make them drop their catch. The migration is far longer than a straight line suggests.

Although the shortest distance between breeding and wintering grounds is 19,000 kilometres, the birds take winding routes that ride the prevailing winds. A 2010 tracking study found that terns from Greenland and Iceland flew 70,900 kilometres a year on average, and birds from the Netherlands about 48,700 kilometres, following the coasts of Europe and Africa.
family:
Arctic terns usually start breeding at three or four years old, mate for life and return to the same colony year after year. Courtship begins with a 'high flight', in which the female chases the male high into the sky, followed by 'fish flights' as he offers her fish.

The nest is just a scrape in the ground, where the pair raise one to three mottled eggs, usually two, taking turns to incubate them for 22 to 27 days. The downy chicks are up and exploring within a few days, are brooded for about ten days, and fly at 21 to 24 days old.

Parents bring them bigger fish than they eat themselves, and help them on the first journey south. Colonies are defended fiercely: Arctic terns dive at intruders, including people, and strike the head hard enough to draw blood. Many birds live 15 to 30 years, and the record is 31.
remarkable:
Between 2015 and 2017, a tern from the Farne Islands in northeast England wearing a tiny light-logging tag flew 96,000 kilometres in just 10 months. It went down the Atlantic, across the Indian Ocean and halfway over the South Pacific before returning along the Antarctic coast, a journey more than twice the circumference of the Earth.

Over a lifetime an Arctic tern may cover around 2.4 million kilometres, the same as flying to the Moon and back more than three times.
outlook:
With more than 2 million birds, over half of them in Europe, and a huge breeding range, the Arctic tern is listed as Least Concern, though its numbers are thought to be falling.

In the late 1800s, New England's colonies were reduced by hunting for feathers to decorate hats, and in western Greenland numbers have dropped sharply since 1950 because of continued exploitation. Food shortages are a growing problem. In Iceland the species was moved to Vulnerable in 2018 after sand eel stocks crashed. At colonies, herring gulls steal eggs and cats take chicks.
people:
The Arctic tern has appeared on stamps from Canada, Finland, Iceland, Cuba, the Faroe Islands, Åland and Alderney. A European fleet of polar-orbiting weather satellites is named EPS-Sterna in honour of its travels, and the bird once starred in a sketch on the comedy show Whose Line Is It Anyway?

Scots names such as pictarnie and tarrock are thought to imitate its call, and because Arctic and common terns are so hard to tell apart, the two share most of their folk names.
relatives:
The Arctic tern belongs to the gull and tern family, Laridae, and has no recognised subspecies. Its genus name, Sterna, comes from the Old English for tern, and paradisaea from the Late Latin for paradise.

Its closest look-alikes are the common tern, with which it often nests in mixed colonies, and the roseate tern, which is slightly paler and shorter-winged.
didYouKnow: A chick ringed on the Farne Islands in the summer of 1982 turned up in Melbourne, Australia, that October, just three months after leaving the nest.

quiz.prompt: Why does the Arctic tern see more daylight than any other creature?
choices: It follows summer between the poles
It roosts on floating ice that never sees darkness
quiz.explanation: Migrating between Arctic and Antarctic summers gives it two summers a year.

quiz.prompt: How many eggs does an Arctic tern usually lay?
choices: Six, laid one at a time over a fortnight
quiz.explanation: It lays one to three eggs, most often two.

quiz.prompt: What colour is the breeding adult's bill?
choices: Orange with a black tip, like a common tern's
quiz.explanation: Breeding adults have a dark red bill, legs and feet.
