name: Green Anaconda
range: Tropical South America east of the Andes, from Trinidad to Paraguay
tagline: The world's heaviest snake, waiting in the shallows
lede: The green anaconda is the heaviest snake on Earth, a giant constrictor that lurks almost unseen in the rivers and swamps of South America. Females dwarf the males, and a big one can outweigh a grown person. Its real size is impressive enough, yet the legends have grown even faster.
home:
Green anacondas live in South America east of the Andes, in countries including Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Brazil and the Guianas, from the island of Trinidad south to northern Paraguay. They favour tropical rainforest and especially shallow, slow-moving water: streams, rivers and flooded grasslands such as the llanos. They spend most of their time in the water, but also move through thick vegetation on land.

As of August 2023, 11 green anacondas had been verifiably seen in the wild in Florida, spread over more than 560 km. No breeding population is known there, but the state added the species to its list of prohibited non-native animals in 2021 and rates its risks as very high.
anatomy:
Mature females typically reach up to 5 metres, averaging about 4.6 metres, while males average about 3 metres, and adults usually weigh 30 to 80 kg. The longest reliably recorded reach about 6.3 metres.

Herpetologist Jesús Rivas, who examined more than 900 anacondas, found the biggest to be a 5.21-metre female weighing 97.5 kg. It is slightly shorter than the reticulated python but far bulkier: a 5.2-metre anaconda is as hefty as a 7.4-metre python. Its skin is olive green with black blotches, and orange-yellow stripes usually run along each side of its narrow head.

Its jaw bones are joined at the front by stretchy ligaments, so it can swallow prey wider than its own head, and an opening of the windpipe in its mouth lets it breathe while swallowing.
life:
Mostly active at night, the anaconda is a fast swimmer that floats underwater with only its eyes and nostrils, set high on its head, above the surface. When prey passes close, it strikes, wraps around it, suffocates it and swallows it whole. Digestion takes many days, during which the snake is sluggish. An apex predator, it takes almost anything it can overpower: fish, amphibians, birds, mammals and reptiles.

Prey is often 14 to 50% of its own weight, from capybaras and caimans to turtles, peccaries and deer, and the largest anacondas occasionally manage tapirs and even jaguars. Big prey can injure or kill it, a risk it may reduce by drowning its victim. Even adults are eaten by Orinoco crocodiles, black caimans and jaguars.
family:
Anacondas are solitary until the mating season in the rainy months, usually around April and May. Females leave pheromone trails, and many males may converge on one female from all directions. Up to 12 males can wrap around her in a breeding ball, wrestling in slow motion for 2 to 4 weeks and scratching her with small spurs.

After a gestation of 6 to 7 months, the female gives birth to live young, usually 20 to 40 but sometimes as many as 100, and may lose up to half her weight. The newborns, 70 to 80 cm long, get no parental care. Anacondas live about 10 years in the wild and 30 or more in captivity, where one reached 37 years and 317 days.
remarkable:
Female anacondas sometimes eat males. Most recorded cases of cannibalism involve a large female eating a smaller male, perhaps because she needs food to sustain her long pregnancy and he is simply nearby.

Females can also reproduce without males at all: in 2014, a green anaconda at West Midland Safari Park gave birth to 3 young by parthenogenesis.
outlook:
Green anacondas still occupy a vast area of South America, and the biggest live deep in remote parts of the Amazon. That remoteness also makes them hard to study. Transporting huge specimens is difficult, skins can stretch by more than 50% when tanned, and even trained scientists tend to overestimate a snake before it is measured.

Where they have escaped or been released, as in Florida, anacondas are a worry for native wildlife. Authorities there fear they could compete with native predators and eat animals such as white-tailed deer, American alligators, crocodiles and wading birds.
people:
The Guinness Book of World Records says this species may have been subject to the most extreme size exaggerations of any living animal. The naturalists Henry Walter Bates and Alfred Russel Wallace heard rumours of anacondas 9 to 12 metres long, but only saw snakes of about 6 metres. In Guyana in 1937, zoologist Alpheus Hyatt Verrill asked his team to guess the length of a coiled anaconda: guesses ran from 6.1 to 18.3 metres, and it measured 5.9 metres.

Horror films often show it as a man-eater, but there is no verified case of a green anaconda eating a person, possibly because the largest live far from people. The local Carib peoples called it akayima, 'the great snake', long before scientists described it, and other names include water boa and sucuri.
relatives:
The green anaconda belongs to the boa family, Boidae, and like all boas it is a non-venomous constrictor. It is the largest snake native to the Americas. Linnaeus first named it Boa murina in 1758, based on a description of a spotted American snake that lies in wait for mice, and in 1830 Johann Georg Wagler gave it its own genus, Eunectes.

The species name murinus means 'of mice'. Several proposals to split off new species or subspecies, most recently Eunectes akayima in 2024, are now treated as part of the green anaconda.
didYouKnow: The green anaconda's largest internal organ is its liver.

quiz.prompt: How do green anacondas produce their young?
choices: They give birth to live young
They lay eggs in a nest
They lay eggs inside termite mounds, which keep them warm
quiz.explanation: The species is ovoviviparous, and females give birth to live young.

quiz.prompt: Which sex is larger in green anacondas?
choices: Males, which grow up to twice the length of females
quiz.explanation: Females are generally much larger, averaging about 4.6 metres against about 3 metres for males.

quiz.prompt: What did the guesses in Verrill's 1937 test show?
choices: Coiled snakes always measure longer than they look
quiz.explanation: Guesses ranged up to 18.3 metres for a snake that measured 5.9 metres.

name: Electric Eel
range: Rivers and swamps of northern South America
tagline: A fish that stuns its prey with up to 860 volts
lede: Electric eels can deliver shocks of up to 860 volts, the strongest electricity made by any living thing. They hunt in murky water with poor eyesight, sensing the world through electric fields, and they must rise to the surface to gulp air. And despite the name, they are not eels at all.
home:
The 3 species of electric eel live in northern South America, with largely separate ranges. E. electricus lives in the north, on the Guiana Shield, and E. voltai in the south, from the Brazilian Shield northwards, both in upland waters.

E. varii lives in between, mostly in lowlands where streams, grasslands, ravines and ponds swell and shrink with the wet and dry seasons. All three live on muddy river bottoms and sometimes in swamps, favouring areas in deep shade.
anatomy:
Electric eels have long, stout bodies, rounded at the front and flatter towards the tail. E. electricus can reach 2 metres and 20 kg. The skin is smooth, thick and scaleless, brown to black with a yellow or red belly.

Males are larger than females. They swim by rippling a long fin that runs along the underside of the body, supported by more than 400 bony rays. They have small eyes and poor vision but can hear well. All the vital organs are packed into the front 20% of the body, kept apart from the electric organs.

They get most of their oxygen by gulping air about every 2 minutes and absorbing it through a frilled, blood-rich lining in the mouth, and they shed most of their carbon dioxide through the skin. With wet skin, they can survive on land for some hours.
life:
Electric eels are mostly nocturnal and mainly eat fish. E. voltai favours armoured catfish, and one was found with a caecilian, a legless amphibian with toxic skin, in its stomach. E. voltai sometimes hunts in packs, herding a shoal of tetras into a tight mass and then striking together.

E. varii also hunts fish, especially armoured catfish and cichlids. To find prey, an eel uses electroreceptors in patches across its body and a lateral line that senses water movements. A weak discharge of nearly 10 volts is thought to serve for electrolocation.

To stun prey, it fires high-voltage pulses as fast as 500 a second, each lasting about 2 milliseconds, and it can curl around its victim to concentrate the shock. In self-defence, eels have been seen leaping from the water to shock animals as big as horses.
family:
Electric eels breed in the dry season, from September to December, when pairs gather in small pools left as the water drops. The male builds a nest from his saliva, and the female lays around 1,200 eggs, adding more batches through the season.

The eggs hatch after 7 days, and once the larvae reach 15 mm they eat any leftover eggs, switching to other food at 9 cm. Males start breeding at 1.2 metres long, females at about 70 cm. Parental care lasts 4 months, with the male guarding the nest and young, though the two upland species seem to rely on it less.

Young eels can make electric discharges at just 7 cm long. They keep growing throughout life, adding vertebrae, up to about 300 in all, and captive eels have lived for more than 20 years.
remarkable:
An electric eel works like a living battery. It has 3 pairs of electric organs made of cells called electrocytes, which evolved from muscle cells. In the main organ, some 6,000 electrocytes are stacked in series, and around 35 such stacks run in parallel on each side of the body.

Each cell adds a little voltage, so together they produce at least 600 volts, with currents of about 1 ampere. Fresh water resists electricity, so a freshwater fish needs a very high voltage to deliver a strong shock, whereas marine electric rays manage with much less.
outlook:
Electric eels are found across a large part of northern South America, and their ability to breathe air lets them survive in shrinking dry-season pools and swamps where many fish could not. Until 2019, all electric eels were thought to be a single species, so scientists are only beginning to learn how the three species differ in their ranges, habits and needs.

Even the names are not quite settled: E. varii may turn out to be the same as a species described from the Peruvian Amazon in 1941.
people:
The Tupi name puraké means 'the one that numbs', and the first written mention, by the Jesuit priest Fernão Cardim, dates from 1583. In 1775, the surgeon John Hunter described the eel's electric organs to the Royal Society, and Hugh Williamson ran experiments showing it shocked fish with the same electricity he felt in his own hand.

Their work influenced Luigi Galvani and Alessandro Volta, whose electric battery followed in 1800. That year Alexander von Humboldt watched indigenous fishers drive about 30 horses into a pool, provoking the eels to leap up and shock them until the fish were exhausted and easy to catch; 2 horses were stunned and drowned. Michael Faraday later measured an eel's shocks with copper paddles, and engineers are now designing artificial electrocytes that might one day power medical implants.
relatives:
Electric eels are knifefish, members of the order Gymnotiformes, and form the subfamily Electrophorinae within the family Gymnotidae. Most knifefish are only weakly electric, using their fields to sense their surroundings but not to shock. The eel's lineage split from its closest relatives, the Gymnotus knifefish, in the Cretaceous. The genus name Electrophorus means 'electricity bearer'.

For more than 200 years it was thought to hold a single species, until a 2019 study split it into three: E. electricus, E. voltai and E. varii.
didYouKnow: In the 1870s the German zoologist Carl Sachs caught electric eels wearing rubber gloves, to the surprise of local people.

quiz.prompt: Which group of fish do electric eels actually belong to?
choices: Lungfish, which also breathe air at the surface
quiz.explanation: They are knifefish of the order Gymnotiformes, not true eels.

quiz.prompt: How does an electric eel get most of its oxygen?
choices: From bubbles trapped in the saliva nest the male builds
quiz.explanation: It breathes air through its mouth about every 2 minutes.

quiz.prompt: In which year were electric eels split into three species?
quiz.explanation: A 2019 study divided them into E. electricus, E. voltai and E. varii.

name: Asian Weaver Ant
range: Tropical Asia from India to the Philippines, and northern Australia
tagline: Ants that sew leaf tents with silk from their own young
lede: Asian weaver ants build their homes high in the trees by pulling living leaves together and stitching them with silk. The thread comes from their own larvae, which workers wave back and forth across the seams like tiny shuttles. A single colony can number half a million ants.
home:
This ant lives in tropical Asia and Australia, from India through Indonesia and the Philippines to the Northern Territory and Queensland. It is arboreal, nesting among the foliage of trees, and is an important part of the canopy ecosystem in humid tropical regions.

A colony may have several nests in one tree or spread across neighbouring trees; one colony occupied 151 nests in 12 trees. Nests are built at night, with major workers weaving the outside and smaller workers finishing the inside. In Singapore, colonies often live in sea hibiscus and great morinda trees, which offer the ants nectar and in return get protection from leaf-eating insects.
anatomy:
Weaver ants come in distinct sizes. Ordinary workers, 5 to 7 mm long, care for the larvae and farm scale insects for honeydew. Major workers, 8 to 10 mm long, have long, strong legs and large jaws, and do the foraging, assembling and expanding of nests.

Both are mostly orange. Queens are much bigger, at 20 to 25 mm, and usually greenish-brown, which gives the species its name smaragdina, Latin for emerald. They do not sting, but their bite is painful, and they can add irritant chemicals from their abdomens into the wound.
life:
Weaver ants hunt insects and other invertebrates, mainly beetles, flies, and wasps and their relatives. They also tend aphids, scale insects and other sap-suckers for their sweet honeydew, driving other ants away from the parts of the canopy where these insects live, especially where trees are linked by lianas. Shelters may even be built close to the nest to protect these assets.

The colony uses a two-level alarm system. Pheromones from one gland gather a local cluster of workers against intruders such as other ants or large insects. If the threat persists, this switches to long-range recruitment, using odour trails from another gland together with touching and body waggling, the same signals that mobilise the colony to claim new territory or exploit food.
family:
Each colony has a single queen, living in one of its nests, and her young are carried to the other nests. A mature colony lives for about 8 years on average. The colony's brood is a prize for some clever thieves.

A jumping spider, Cosmophasis bitaeniata, mimics the ants' chemical scent so it can walk into their nests and eat the larvae. It even lays its own eggs beside the nest, so that its spiderlings can easily reach the ant larvae too.
remarkable:
Building a leaf nest takes extraordinary teamwork. Workers spread out and tug at leaf edges independently, and when one manages to bend a leaf, others nearby stop and join it to pull in unison. Where a gap is too wide, they form living chains, climbing onto each other's backs and pulling backwards for leverage.

These chains act as a force ratchet: some ants pull while others hold the stored tension using the grip of their feet, which doubles the average force of each ant. In most groups, each member's effort drops as the team grows; here it rises. Once the leaves are in place, some workers hold them while others fetch larvae to spin the silk.
outlook:
Weaver ants are widespread and adaptable, nesting in plantation trees as readily as in forest. In Indonesia, colonies live in banana, coconut, oil palm, rubber, cacao, teak, mango, jackfruit and rambutan trees, among many others.

Their conservation status has not been formally evaluated. Rather than being threatened by people, they are often encouraged by them, and their young are harvested commercially in parts of Asia. Their communication has been called perhaps the most elaborate yet recognised in ants, and one of the most complex systems known among social insects.
people:
People have put weaver ants to work for a very long time. The oldest written record of their use against pests comes from China in 304 CE, where they guarded citrus trees, and colonies still protect crops such as cashew, mango, citrus, coconut, cocoa and coffee. In Sri Lanka, though, ant protection was abandoned in coffee because picking the crop proved too painful.

In Java, the larvae and pupae, called kroto, are sold as food for the island's popular captive songbirds, and mixed with eggs, maize, beans and honey as fishing bait. In Thailand and the Philippines they are eaten, with a taste described as creamy, sour and lemony, and in parts of India the adult ants are used in traditional medicine.
relatives:
The name Oecophylla comes from Greek and means 'leaf-house'. The species has many common names, including weaver ant, green ant, green tree ant and orange gaster. Several animals have evolved to exploit it.

The jumping spider Myrmaplata plataleoides looks like a weaver ant, with a pinched body and 2 black spots mimicking eyes on the side of its head, and it steals ant brood to pick up the colony's scent, though it generally steers clear of the nests. In Australia, three blue butterflies, the common, bright and purple oak-blues, depend on the ants and occur only where they are established.
didYouKnow: The smell-processing centres in a weaver ant's brain are arranged in clusters, a feature also seen in honeybees.

quiz.prompt: What do weaver ants use to stitch leaves together?
choices: Sticky sap collected from the trees they live in
quiz.explanation: Workers hold larvae against the leaf seams, and the larvae release silk threads.

quiz.prompt: What colour is a weaver ant queen?
choices: Bright red with yellow stripes along the abdomen
quiz.explanation: Queens are usually greenish-brown, giving the species its name smaragdina, meaning emerald.

quiz.prompt: Where does the oldest written record of using weaver ants against pests come from?
choices: Sri Lanka, where they guarded coffee plantations
quiz.explanation: It comes from China in 304 CE, where the ants protected citrus trees.

name: Common Wombat
range: Southeastern Australia, Tasmania and the Bass Strait islands
tagline: A burrowing marsupial with cube-shaped droppings
lede: The common wombat is a barrel-shaped Australian marsupial and a tireless digger that spends its days underground and its nights grazing. It is also famous for something unusual: its droppings come out as cubes.
home:
Common wombats live in the cooler, better-watered parts of southern and eastern Australia, including Victoria and Tasmania, and in mountain districts as far north as southern Queensland. In the south they can be found at any elevation, but in the north only in higher, mountainous country. They use a wide range of habitats, from rainforest, eucalyptus forest and woodland to alpine grassland, heathland and coast, and in some areas they graze in open fields alongside cattle and sheep.

Around 1.3 million are thought to remain in the wild, but more than two thirds of them live on islands, mostly Tasmania. On the mainland the species once ranged from South Australia's Limestone Coast across Victoria and along the Great Dividing Range, but its range and numbers have shrunk by more than half since European settlement, leaving populations in isolated pockets.
anatomy:
Wombats are sturdy and low-slung, with small ears and eyes, a large bald nose and short, strong legs ending in long claws. Their thick, coarse fur varies from light brown to grey and black. Size differs between the 3 subspecies. Mainland wombats average about 1 metre long and 27 kg, with the biggest reaching 1.2 metres and 35 kg.

Tasmanian wombats average 85 cm and 20 kg, and Flinders Island wombats are the smallest, at around 75 cm. Unlike any other marsupial, the wombat has a single pair of upper and lower incisors, and its teeth never stop growing. The structure of the enamel keeps a self-sharpening ridge on them, ideal for grazing tough native grasses.
life:
Common wombats are solitary and territorial, each living and feeding in an established home range. There they dig a tunnel system, with tunnels 2 to 20 metres long, many side branches and often more than one entrance, and build nests of sticks, leaves and grass.

A wombat usually has several burrows and switches the one it sleeps in every 1 to 9 days, though more than one wombat may nest in the same burrow. Many stay with the same burrows for life, unless farmers or other animals force them out or the burrow is destroyed.

They are herbivores, eating mainly grass, snow tussocks and other plants. They usually feed at night, but in cool weather they also come out in the early morning or late afternoon. Captive wombats are fed a range of vegetables too.
family:
The common wombat breeds mainly in winter and can breed every 2 years, producing a single joey. After a short pregnancy of about 20 to 30 days, the newborn spends around 5 months in its mother's pouch.

When it finally leaves, it weighs between 3.5 and 6.5 kg. The joey is weaned at 12 to 15 months and is usually independent by 18 months. Wombats live about 15 years on average in the wild and 20 in captivity. Their main predators are quolls, Tasmanian devils, dingoes and eagles.
remarkable: Wombats have been called ecological engineers. Their digging turns over and aerates the soil, helping plants grow, and their burrows become shelter for a remarkable range of other animals, including reptiles, rodents, rabbits, echidnas, wallabies, birds and even koalas. Wombats are usually fairly tolerant of these non-threatening lodgers.
outlook:
The common wombat is listed as Least Concern by the IUCN, but it still faces serious pressures, largely from people. Sarcoptic mange is widespread and remains the most troublesome problem, and wildlife carers regularly treat wombats in the field. Habitat loss and roadkill also take a toll, and wombats carry ticks and other parasites.

In Victoria, a $1 bounty from 1926 to 1966 branded wombats as farm pests for their burrowing and foraging, and wiped them out across much of their former range. The species had no protection in Victoria until 2020, and culling under licence there and in the Australian Capital Territory kills as many as 2,482 a year. In Tasmania, overall wombat counts rose between 1985 and 2019.
people:
The common wombat is also known as the bare-nosed wombat, after its large hairless nose. It was first described scientifically by George Shaw in 1800.

Today it is protected by law in South Australia under the National Parks and Wildlife Act 1972, in Queensland under the Nature Conservation Act 1992 and in New South Wales under the Biodiversity Conservation Act 2016. The treatment of mange by volunteer carers has become a big part of how people help wild wombats.
relatives:
The common wombat is one of 3 living wombat species and the only surviving member of its genus, Vombatus.

Its 3 subspecies were confirmed in 2019: the hirsute wombat of the mainland; the Tasmanian wombat, estimated at 840,000 animals in 2023; and the Bass Strait wombat, once found across the Bass Strait islands but now restricted to Flinders Island and to Maria Island, where it was introduced, with an estimated 74,000 in 2023. An extinct relative, Hackett's wombat, lived in southwestern Australia. It was about the same size, averaging 30 kg, and died out at the end of the Late Pleistocene.
didYouKnow: Wombats appear to mate lying on their sides.

quiz.prompt: What shape are common wombat droppings?
choices: Flat discs, which they stack on rocks to mark territory
quiz.explanation: Wombat dung is famously cube-shaped.

quiz.prompt: How long does a wombat joey stay in the pouch?
choices: About 3 years, until it is fully grown
quiz.explanation: Joeys spend around five months in the pouch before leaving it.

quiz.prompt: What is the most troublesome problem facing bare-nosed wombats?
choices: Competition with rabbits for burrows across the mainland
quiz.explanation: Sarcoptic mange is widespread and is the most problematic issue for the species.

name: Red King Crab
range: North Pacific from the Sea of Japan to Alaska; introduced to the Barents Sea
tagline: A giant crab that crossed a continent by plane
lede: With legs spanning up to 1.8 metres, the red king crab is the largest of the king crabs and the most prized by fishers. Oddly, it is named for the colour it turns when cooked: alive, it is more of a burgundy.
home:
The red king crab is native to the cold waters of the North Pacific and nearby seas, from the Bering Sea south to the Gulf of Alaska, and off the Kamchatka Peninsula, in the Sea of Okhotsk and in the Sea of Japan.

It has been seen in water from −1.8 to 12.8 °C, though 3.2 to 5.5 °C is typical, and young crabs prefer it below 6 °C. Where it lives depends on its age. Newly hatched larvae stay in shallow water, where food and protection are plentiful.

After about 2 years, young crabs move to depths of 20 to 50 metres and gather in tight groups of hundreds, a habit called podding. Adults usually live more than 200 metres down on sand and mud.
anatomy:
Its shell can reach 28 cm across, and it can weigh up to 12.7 kg. Males grow larger than females. Today, few crabs exceed 17 cm across the shell, and the average male landed in the Bering Sea weighs 2.9 kg. The crab breathes with 5 sets of gills, tucked into two chambers under the shell.

A paddle-like appendage beats back and forth to pull water in from behind the walking legs and push it out beside the mouth, and fine hairs filter out debris. It can clear sediment and parasites from its rear gills by moving its small fifth pair of legs. Its blood carries oxygen with haemocyanin, a copper-based pigment that turns from colourless to blue when it picks up oxygen.
life:
Red king crabs spend most of their lives in deep water, where they feed. In the Barents Sea, studies of its diet show it acting as a high-level predator on the seabed, and some evidence suggests it eats the egg masses of capelin, an important food for cod. In its native range it has many enemies, including Pacific cod, walleye pollock, halibut, several kinds of flatfish, sculpins, Greenland turbot, Pacific salmon and herring, sharks and rays, sea otters and seals.

Its growth depends on temperature: it moults slowly below 8 °C, and quite quickly at around 12 °C. It copes well with changes in salinity, but slightly more acidic water, at pH 7.8 rather than 8.0, slows its growth and eventually kills it.
family:
Mature females must stay in warmer water, near 4 °C, so their eggs develop in time to hatch, while males stay in colder water, near 1.5 °C, to save energy. In winter or early spring the crabs migrate towards shallower water to mate, and in May females move into shallow coastal areas to moult and spawn, with males joining them before moulting.

From mid-June to mid-November, the crabs return to fairly deep water below the summer thermocline. When it breaks down, they move back to intermediate depths, where they stay until the females release the eggs fertilised in the previous spawning. Juveniles tolerate low salinity slightly better than adults.
remarkable:
In the 1960s, the Soviet Union decided to give Europe a valuable new catch by moving red king crabs from the North Pacific to the Murmansk Fjord on the Barents Sea. Crabs sent overland died on the way, so a batch was flown in instead, and it survived, bred and spread.

First found in Norway in 1977, the crab had reached North Cape by the mid-1990s and has since reached Svalbard, and some scientists think it is advancing about 50 km a year. One was even caught south of Bergen in 2009. An important natural predator, the giant Pacific octopus, does not live in European waters.
outlook:
In its native Far East coastal waters, the red king crab has been declining steadily for unclear reasons. Overfishing, warmer water and more predation by fish have all been suggested, and US fishing controls set in the 1980s and 2000s have failed to stop the fall.

In the Barents Sea, by contrast, its population is increasing tremendously. Environmentalists and fishers there worry that it eats everything it comes across, 'creating a desert' on the seabed, and they fear what will happen if it reaches the cod breeding grounds off Lofoten. Fishers also complain that its claws ruin nets and long lines.
people:
The red king crab is the most coveted king crab on the market and the most expensive by weight. It is caught mostly in the Bering Sea and Norton Sound in Alaska, and although it is hard to catch, it is one of the most popular crabs to eat.

It is also called the Kamchatka crab or Alaskan king crab, and in Norway, because the Soviets introduced it, it is sometimes known as 'Stalin's crab'. East of North Cape, Norway and Russia manage the crab jointly through a fisheries commission that sets quotas, and in 2006 only 259 Norwegian fishermen were allowed to catch it there.

Processing waste can make up 69% of the catch, and enzymes from the crab's digestive gland interest various industries. A red king crab even appears as a boss in the video game Another Crab's Treasure.
relatives:
Paralithodes camtschaticus is the largest of the king crabs, and its species name refers to Kamchatka, one of its native strongholds. It is the most valuable of several king crab species sold commercially.

In January 2022, fishers in the United Kingdom reported catching red king crabs, raising fears of a new invasion, but the animals turned out to be a native species, Lithodes maja.
didYouKnow: A red king crab's heartbeat is set by a cluster of just 9 nerve cells attached to the wall of its heart.

quiz.prompt: Why is the red king crab called 'red'?
choices: It lives in the Red Sea
Its eggs glow red in the deep, dark water where it lives
quiz.explanation: Living crabs are more burgundy; the name comes from their cooked colour.

quiz.prompt: How were red king crabs brought to the Barents Sea?
choices: Flown in by the Soviet Union
They walked along the seabed around Siberia by themselves
quiz.explanation: Crabs sent overland died, so the Soviets flew in a batch that survived and spread.

quiz.prompt: What colour does the crab's haemocyanin turn when it carries oxygen?
choices: Bright yellow, like the copper inside it
quiz.explanation: Haemocyanin changes from colourless to blue when oxygenated.

name: Venus' Flower Basket
range: Deep seafloor of the western Pacific around the Philippines
tagline: A deep-sea sponge that builds itself out of glass
lede: Hundreds of metres down in the western Pacific stands an animal made of glass. The Venus' flower basket weaves its skeleton from silica into a lattice so fine and so strong that engineers, optical scientists and architects have all come to study it.
home:
This sponge lives in the western Pacific Ocean around the Philippine Islands, while other members of its genus turn up in oceans across the world, including near Japan and in the Indian Ocean. It has been found from 100 to 1,000 metres below the surface and is most common deeper than 500 metres.

It spends its whole life fixed in one spot on the seafloor. Although it is associated with rocky areas, it tends to anchor itself in soft, loose, muddy sediment, and grows a rooting structure that keeps it upright in the ooze.
anatomy:
The body is a curved tube shaped like a vase or basket, usually 10 to 30 centimetres tall. It is built entirely of silica, the main ingredient of glass, in the form of tiny six-pointed spicules, each made of three rays crossing at right angles.

These spicules weave together into a very fine mesh that gives the animal a rigidity other sponges lack and lets it survive at great depth. The walls are pierced by countless gaps leading into a central cavity, and water leaves through a single opening at the top.

At the base, a tuft of glassy anchoring fibres, 5 to 20 centimetres long and as thin as a human hair, holds it in the mud. The species is told apart from its relatives partly by these anchors, which end in six teeth.
life:
Like other sponges, the Venus' flower basket feeds by filtering seawater, straining out plankton and the drifting flakes of organic debris known as marine snow. Some scientists suspect it may use bioluminescence to lure plankton towards it.

Its lattice works as plumbing as well as a skeleton. Studies of water flow show that it reduces the drag the animal feels from passing currents and sets up gentle, orderly swirls inside the body cavity, which may help it feed selectively. In the Pacific, glass sponges of this group can build reefs, which may lock away carbon in the deep sea.
family:
Very little is known about how this sponge breeds. Sperm has been found in the connective tissue of one specimen, gathered in clusters within fine, thread-like structures, which supports the idea that each individual may be a hermaphrodite.

Because the adult cannot move, its sperm is thought to drift on the current until it reaches eggs held by another sponge. A team of Italian researchers built a three-dimensional model of the skeleton to simulate water moving in and out of it. They found that the lattice creates tiny vortices inside the body that help mix sperm and eggs.
remarkable:
The sponge often shelters a breeding pair of glass sponge shrimp. They slip into the lattice while young and small, then grow too large to squeeze back out, and spend the rest of their lives inside.

The shrimp eat particles the sponge collects, mate in its shelter and keep its interior clean, a partnership that lasts until they die.
outlook: This sponge has not been assessed for the IUCN Red List, and its deep, remote home makes it hard to study at all. Researchers have noted how inaccessible it is, which limits how much can be learned about its numbers or about any pressures it might face.
people:
In Japan, the dried skeletons are presented as wedding gifts, a symbol of undying love that may have been inspired by the shrimp couples sealed inside for life. Materials scientists prize the skeleton too. The sponge draws silicic acid from seawater and turns it into glass fibres in cold water, whereas factory-made optical fibres need high temperatures and come out brittle, so a sponge-inspired method could give finer control over fibres and perhaps cheaper solar cells.

Its geometry has inspired a lattice design with a better strength-to-weight ratio than other diagonally braced square grids, and an aluminium tube of the same size, with its material spread evenly, has only a hundredth of its stiffness. Writers on biomimicry have linked its form to Norman Foster's Gherkin tower in London.
relatives:
Euplectella aspergillum was described in 1841 by Sir Richard Owen, who called it one of the most singular and beautiful, as well as the rarest, of marine productions. Yet he doubted it was an animal at all and placed it in the very lowest class of living things.

The genus Euplectella was created for it, so it is the type species, and 4 subspecies are now accepted. It belongs to the glass sponges, named for their silica skeletons. Making glass is not unique to them, though: the orange puffball sponge, a demosponge from a different class, can also produce it biologically.
didYouKnow: When tested with alkali the skeletons proved highly resistant, hinting that they may also contain tough biomaterials such as chitin.

quiz.prompt: What is the Venus' flower basket's skeleton made of?
choices: Spongin fibres stiffened with iron from seawater
quiz.explanation: Its skeleton is made of six-pointed silica spicules woven into a mesh.

quiz.prompt: What often lives inside the sponge's lattice?
choices: A shoal of tiny fish that leave at night to feed
quiz.explanation: Glass sponge shrimp enter when young and grow too big to leave.

quiz.prompt: In Japan, what are the sponge's skeletons given as?
quiz.explanation: They symbolise undying love and are presented at weddings.

name: King Cobra
range: Forests of South and Southeast Asia, from India to southern China and the Philippines
tagline: The longest venomous snake, and it eats other snakes
lede: Rearing high off the forest floor with its narrow hood spread, the king cobra is the longest venomous snake in the world. It is also a specialist in eating other snakes, which is exactly what its scientific name means.
home:
King cobras range widely across tropical Asia, up to elevations of 2,000 metres. They are found from the Terai of India and southern Nepal through Bhutan, northeast India and Bangladesh to Myanmar, southern China, Cambodia, Thailand, Laos and Vietnam, and on to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia and the Philippines.

In India they live along both the Western and Eastern Ghats, in the Sundarbans and on Baratang Island in the Andamans. A few records come from as far west as eastern Pakistan, near Lahore, though it is uncertain whether any snakes survive there. Despite this huge range, the species is not commonly seen.
anatomy:
Adults are usually 3.18 to 4 metres long, and the longest known individual measured 5.85 metres. The skin is olive green with black and white bands that converge towards the head, which is covered by 15 large shields. The eyes are big, with golden irises and round pupils, the tongue is black, and the oval hood bears two black spots.

Juveniles are black with white, yellow or buff chevrons pointing towards the head. Males are larger than females and paler, especially in the breeding season. Males caught in Kerala reached 3.75 metres and 10 kg, while the biggest females measured 2.75 metres and weighed 5 kg.
life:
The king cobra hunts by day, tasting the air with its forked tongue and passing scent to a sensory organ in the roof of its mouth. It is an apex predator, dominant over every snake except large pythons, and eats mainly snakes and lizards: Indian cobras, banded kraits, rat snakes, monitor lizards and even reticulated pythons.

It tracks pit vipers by following their odour trails. Flexible jaws let it swallow prey much larger than its head, and after a big meal it may go months without eating.

It is not considered aggressive and usually slips away from people. Cornered, it raises the front of its body, flares its hood and strikes, and it can still glide forward while upright, so people often misjudge a safe distance.
family:
The king cobra is the only snake that builds a nest. Between late March and late May, the female gathers dry leaf litter into a layered mound, usually at the base of a tree, up to 55 centimetres high and 140 centimetres across, with a chamber for her eggs.

She lays 7 to 43 eggs and stays by the nest for anywhere from 2 to 77 days, defending it fiercely. The eggs hatch after 66 to 105 days. Hatchlings are 37.5 to 58.5 centimetres long, nervous and quick to bite, and their venom is already as potent as an adult's. Females have also been shown to produce young without mating. Wild king cobras live about 20 years on average.
remarkable:
Most snakes hiss across a broad range of frequencies centred near 7,500 Hz. The king cobra's warning sound stays below 2,500 Hz, centred near 600 Hz, closer in pitch to a human voice, so people liken it to a growl.

Pouches off its windpipe act as resonating chambers, and the rat snakes it preys on can growl in a similar way.
outlook:
The king cobra has been listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List since 2010. In Southeast Asia its greatest threat is the loss of forest to logging and farmland. It is also smuggled, and poached for bushmeat, snake leather and traditional Chinese medicine.

International trade is regulated under CITES Appendix II, and the snake is protected in China and Vietnam. In India, killing one can bring up to 6 years in prison, and in the Philippines, where it is called banakon, it is listed as a threatened species.
people:
A single bite can deliver up to 420 mg of dried venom, rich in nerve toxins, and without prompt treatment death can follow in as little as 30 minutes. Antivenoms produced in India and by the Thai Red Cross Society can neutralise it.

The snake holds a special place in the folklore of India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Myanmar, and is India's national reptile. In one Myanmar ritual, a tattooed priestess kisses a king cobra on the top of its head.

An Indian myth claims the killer's image stays in the dead snake's eyes for its mate to find, so slain cobras often have their heads crushed or burned. In Bangkok, a roadside shrine was built after a female's nest and young were destroyed during roadworks.
relatives:
Despite its name, the king cobra is not a true cobra. Genetic studies show it split early from the lineage that gave rise to the mambas, rather than from the Naja cobras. Albert Günther coined the genus Ophiophagus, 'snake-eater', in 1864, because the earlier name Hamadryas already belonged to the cracker butterflies.

What was long treated as one species is now seen as a complex. Three more have been proposed: the Sunda king cobra, the Western Ghats king cobra and the Luzon king cobra, each a separate genetic lineage adapted to its own region.
didYouKnow: One early specimen, described in 1840, was reportedly caught floating in a basket off the coast near Chennai, where wild king cobras have never lived.

quiz.prompt: What does the king cobra mainly eat?
choices: Birds' eggs stolen from nests high in the canopy
quiz.explanation: Its genus name means 'snake-eater', and snakes and lizards are its main prey.

quiz.prompt: What does the female king cobra build for her eggs?
choices: A floating raft of reeds bound with silk
quiz.explanation: It is the only snake known to build a nest, from dry leaf litter.

quiz.prompt: Which snakes is the king cobra most closely related to?
choices: True cobras of the genus Naja
quiz.explanation: It split early from the lineage that led to the mambas, not the Naja cobras.

name: Common Ostrich
range: Savannas, Sahel and semi-deserts of Africa
tagline: The biggest bird alive, and the fastest on two legs
lede: Standing up to 2.75 metres tall, the common ostrich is the tallest and heaviest bird on Earth. It cannot fly, but it can outrun almost any predator, and it lays the largest eggs of any living bird.
home:
Ostriches once roamed Africa north and south of the Sahara and much of Asia Minor. Today they live in open country, on the savannas and in the Sahel on both sides of the equatorial forest, and in southwest Africa they inhabit semi-desert and true desert. Temperatures there can swing by 40 °C between night and day.

The Arabian population of the Middle East was hunted to extinction by the middle of the 20th century, and attempts to reintroduce ostriches to Israel have failed. Birds brought to Australia for farming have escaped to form a small feral population in the outback. DNA from fossil eggshells shows that ostriches also lived in India 25,000 years ago.
anatomy:
Males stand 2.1 to 2.75 metres tall and weigh 100 to 130 kg; females are smaller and lighter. Adult males are mostly black with white wing tips and tail, while females and young males are greyish-brown and white.

The head and neck are almost bare, and the eyes, 50 mm across, are the largest of any land vertebrate, letting the bird spot predators far away. Each foot has just two toes, the larger bearing a nail like a hoof, which helps with running, and the bird can cover 3 to 5 metres in a stride.

Its feathers lack the tiny hooks that zip together a flying bird's plumage, so they stay soft and fluffy. The wings, spanning about 2 metres, act as stabilisers for braking, turning and zigzagging at speed.
life:
Ostriches eat mainly seeds, shrubs, grass, fruit and flowers, with the occasional locust, mouse, lizard or scrap from a predator's kill. Having no teeth, they swallow pebbles that grind food in the gizzard, which can hold 1,300 g, up to 45% of it sand and stones.

They can go several days without drinking and survive losing a quarter of their body weight to dehydration. Outside the breeding season they live alone or in pairs, but they may gather in nomadic groups of 5 to 100, led by a top hen and often mixing with zebras and antelopes.

An ostrich can hold a steady 50 km/h and sprint at over 70 km/h. To hide, it lays its head and neck flat on the ground, looking like a mound of earth, and if cornered it kicks forward with enough force to kill a lion.
family:
Ostriches mature at 2 to 4 years. Territorial males boom by inflating their necks and gather a harem of 2 to 7 hens, then court with alternating wing beats and spiralling head movements. The male scrapes a communal nest, a shallow pit about 3 metres wide, and the dominant female lays first, later pushing out extra eggs from weaker hens until about 20 remain. She can tell her own eggs from the others.

Each egg is about 15 centimetres long and weighs 1.4 kg, over 20 times a hen's egg. The drab female sits on them by day and the black male by night, so the nest stays hard to see.

Chicks hatch after 35 to 45 days, but fewer than 10% of nests survive and only 15% of chicks reach their first birthday. Survivors can live long lives: one in captivity reached 62 years and 7 months.
remarkable: As the largest bird alive, the ostrich is also the largest living dinosaur, and scientists use it to study how extinct dinosaurs moved. It is unlike every other living bird in one more curious way: it produces urine separately from its faeces.
outlook:
Wild ostriches have declined drastically over the past 200 years, and most now survive in reserves or on farms.

Even so, the species still occupies a vast range of about 9,800,000 square kilometres, and the IUCN and BirdLife International list it as Least Concern. The Arabian subspecies died out around 1966, and North African populations are protected under CITES Appendix I, which bans commercial international trade.
people:
Ostriches have inspired people for at least 5,000 years, in Mesopotamia, Egypt and the Kingdom of Kush. Kalahari hunter-gatherers use the eggshells as water flasks and jewellery, and engraved shells at Diepkloof Rock Shelter in South Africa date back about 60,000 years.

The idea that ostriches bury their heads in sand is false, probably dating to Pliny the Elder, and it gave us the phrase 'ostrich effect' for ignoring bad news. The birds were nearly wiped out in the 18th century for their plumes, and feather farming took off in South Africa in the 19th century; by the early 1900s more than 700,000 were in captivity.

Today they are farmed for leather, feathers and lean red meat, and in South Africa people even race them. Near Oudtshoorn, where farms sit beside wild birds, 2 or 3 serious or fatal attacks happen each year.
relatives:
Carl Linnaeus named the species in the 18th century. Struthio is Late Latin for ostrich, and camelus recalls the Ancient Greek name meaning 'camel-sparrow', a nod to its dry home. Only one other ostrich survives, the Somali ostrich, recognised as a separate species by BirdLife International since 2014; it split off around 4 million years ago as the East African Rift formed. Ostriches are ratites, alongside rheas, emus, cassowaries and kiwis.

Genetic work now places them alone in their order and as the sister group to all other members of this ancient group of birds, which also includes the flying tinamous.
didYouKnow: Ostriches raised entirely by people may direct their courtship displays at their keepers instead of at other ostriches.

quiz.prompt: How many toes does an ostrich have on each foot?
choices: Five, with the outer pair fused into a hoof
quiz.explanation: It has just two toes, an adaptation that helps it run.

quiz.prompt: Who sits on the ostrich eggs at night?
choices: Nobody, because the warm sand heats them until morning
quiz.explanation: The black male sits by night and the drab female by day, keeping the nest hidden.

quiz.prompt: Where does the 'head in the sand' myth seem to have begun?
quiz.explanation: It probably started with Pliny the Elder, who misunderstood ostrich behaviour.

name: Giant Oceanic Manta Ray
range: Tropical, subtropical and temperate oceans worldwide
tagline: The largest ray, with the biggest brain of any fish
lede: With a disc up to 7 metres across, the giant oceanic manta ray is the largest ray in the world. It spends most of its life far out at sea, sweeping up plankton with its mouth open wide, and it may be one of the few animals that recognise themselves in a mirror.
home:
This manta lives in tropical, subtropical and temperate waters around the globe. It has been recorded as far north as southern California, New Jersey, northern Japan, the Sinai Peninsula and the Azores, and as far south as Peru, Uruguay, South Africa and New Zealand.

It is an ocean-going fish that travels with the currents, migrating to places where upwellings of nutrient-rich water bring blooms of zooplankton. It is often found around offshore oceanic islands, and it visits coastlines to hunt.
anatomy:
The giant manta can reach 9 metres long and weigh around 3,000 kg, though a typical adult is about 4.5 metres. Its flattened body carries huge triangular pectoral fins. At the front, a pair of cephalic fins can be rolled into spirals while swimming or unfurled to funnel water into its wide, rectangular mouth.

Its teeth are tiny, in a band of 18 rows on the lower jaw only, and unlike its devil ray cousins it has no spine on its whip-like tail, just a knob at the base. The back is black, dark brown or steely blue, and the belly white with dark spots, a pattern unique enough to identify individuals.

Two sharply marked white patches on the shoulders are divided by a line shaped like a T.
life:
In deep water the manta swims steadily in a straight line, while closer to shore it tends to bask or cruise idly, alone or in groups of up to 50. When feeding it circles slowly to herd plankton into a tight ball, then speeds through it with its mouth agape, sieving copepods, shrimp, krill and larvae from the water with tissue between its gill arches.

Research published in 2016 found that about 73% of its diet comes from deep-water sources, including fish, overturning the old idea that it fed only by filtering at the surface. It must swim constantly to push water over its gills, so it never rests on the seabed. It can reach 24 km/h, and only large sharks, false killer whales and orcas are big enough to kill it, though most adults carry scars from shark bites.
family:
Males can breed once their disc is about 4 metres wide, females at about 5 metres. When a female is ready, one or several males may follow her in a 'train'. During mating, the male grips her pectoral fin with his teeth and the pair swim belly to belly for several minutes.

The young develop inside the mother. At first each embryo lives on yolk inside an egg case; after hatching it stays in the oviduct, feeding on a milky secretion.

Usually just 1 pup is born after a pregnancy of about 12 to 13 months. It is already 1.4 metres across and weighs 9 kg, and it spends its first few years growing in shallow coastal water. Females breed only every 2 or 3 years.
remarkable: The oceanic manta has the largest brain of any fish, weighing up to 200 g, five to ten times heavier than a whale shark's. A network of blood vessels called the rete mirabile warms the blood flowing to it, and mantas are among the few animals, on land or at sea, that might pass the mirror test, seemingly showing self-awareness.
outlook:
The giant oceanic manta ray is listed as Endangered by the IUCN because its numbers have fallen drastically over the past 20 years through overfishing. Because it feeds in shallow water, it is easily caught in drifting gillnets and bottom nets, whether targeted or taken as bycatch.

With late maturity, a long pregnancy and usually a single pup, it cannot make up such losses for decades. Pollution adds to the pressure. A 2019 study in Indonesia's Coral Triangle found filter-feeders, including oceanic mantas, regularly swallowing microplastics, and tissue from carcasses in Ghana contained high levels of arsenic and mercury.
people:
Since the 1970s, fishing for mantas has been driven by demand for their gill rakers, the comb-like filters on their gills. These are the main ingredient in a tonic sold in traditional Chinese medicine under the trade name pengyusai, fetching up to 400 US dollars a kilogram, though there is no strong evidence that it does any good. Few aquariums have managed to keep this species.

Since 2018 it has been displayed at Nausicaá in France and at the Okinawa Churaumi Aquarium in Japan. It goes by many names, including giant manta, oceanic manta and pelagic manta ray.
relatives:
The giant manta belongs to the family Mobulidae. Until 2017 it was placed in the genus Manta with the smaller reef manta ray, but DNA showed that both mantas sit within the devil rays of the genus Mobula, so they were moved there.

The two mantas overlap in range and are easily confused, especially when young. The oceanic manta is larger, typically 4 to 5 metres across against 3 to 3.5 metres, and the pale shoulder patches of the reef manta blend gradually into the back and form a Y rather than a T.
didYouKnow: At reef cleaning stations, oceanic mantas hover almost motionless for several minutes while small fish pick off loose skin and parasites, mostly at high tide.

quiz.prompt: Roughly how much of the giant manta's diet comes from deep-water sources?
choices: Almost all of it, as it never feeds at the surface
quiz.explanation: A 2016 study found about 73% of its diet is deep-water food, including fish.

quiz.prompt: Why does the giant manta never rest on the seabed?
choices: Bottom-dwelling stingrays chase it out of their territory
quiz.explanation: It has to keep swimming to push water over its gills.

quiz.prompt: What does a manta's T-shaped back marking help tell it apart from?
choices: The common stingray of shallow coastal lagoons
quiz.explanation: Oceanic mantas have a T between their white shoulder patches; reef mantas have a Y.

name: Painted Lady
range: Every continent except Antarctica; rare in South America
tagline: A butterfly that flies from Africa to the Arctic
lede: The painted lady is the most widespread butterfly on Earth, found on every continent except Antarctica. Each year, relay teams of successive generations shuttle between tropical Africa and the Arctic Circle, and some have even crossed an ocean.
home:
Painted ladies can turn up in almost any temperate region, including mountains in the tropics, but they live year-round only in warmer areas. In South America they are rare visitors, and in Australia they are limited to a small area around Bunbury, Fremantle and Rottnest Island.

They like sunny, brightly lit, open places, and are drawn to meadows full of flowers and clover. Males set up territories in spots sheltered by hedgerows, and on overcast days the adults settle into small hollows in the ground.
anatomy:
The upper wings are a warm reddish orange, browner towards the body, with black-and-white chequered fringes. Each forewing has an irregular black band, a black tip with a short white streak, and a curved row of 4 round spots near the corner. The hindwing carries a row of 5 small black spots between bands of dark markings.

Underneath, the hindwing is marbled olive brown, speckled with black and crossed by white veins, with a row of 5 eyespots. Painted ladies see much like honey bees, with receptors for ultraviolet, blue and green light, but they lack red receptors, so red light is invisible to them.
life:
Caterpillars feed mainly on plants of the daisy family, such as thistles, knapweeds, burdock, sunflowers and wormwoods, and more than 300 host plants have been recorded.

Adults sip flower nectar and the sugary honeydew left by aphids. In spring, painted ladies pour out of North Africa and the Mediterranean into Britain and Europe in May and June, sometimes reaching Iceland, while others travel from the Red Sea through Israel and Cyprus to Turkey. Radar studies show that the return flight south in autumn happens at high altitude, which is why it was overlooked for so long.

The butterflies appear to steer by a sun compass, and in the laboratory they lost their bearings when cut off from the sky. Their main defences are flight and camouflage, while caterpillars hide in small silk tents on leaves.
family:
Courtship begins with small groups of 2 to 8 butterflies circling one another for a few seconds. Males perch in the late afternoon on hilltops, meadow edges and other landmarks where females are likely to pass, and chase off rival males. A male often mates with several females. Unusually, painted ladies breed continuously through every season, even winter, and keep reproducing throughout their migrations, so no overwintering stage has ever been found.

Females lay their eggs one by one, choosing plants with plenty of nectar for adults even when those plants are poor food for caterpillars, a strategy that favours quantity over quality. They also seem to fly towards rain, which may help more eggs and larvae thrive.
remarkable:
In 2024, scientists reported painted ladies on a beach in French Guiana, far outside their usual range. Pollen on their bodies came from West African shrubs, and genetic and isotope tests confirmed the butterflies were born in Europe or Africa.

Helped by unusually favourable trade winds, they had flown over 4,200 kilometres, the first evidence of any insect crossing an ocean.
outlook:
With an enormous range and females that produce large numbers of offspring, the painted lady is one of the most successful butterflies on the planet. Its numbers swing wildly from year to year because migrations are erratic.

Heavy winter rain in deserts grows the plants that caterpillars need, and in March 2019 it sent millions streaming across Southern California, while a migration through Israel the same spring was estimated at a billion butterflies. Global climate events such as El Niño may also trigger large movements.
people:
In North America the butterfly was once called the cosmopolitan, a fitting name for a species found almost everywhere. It is bred in schools for teaching, and released at weddings, memorial events and hospices. Ordinary people have helped reveal its travels.

The Worldwide Painted Lady Migration project, a citizen science effort led by the Institute of Evolutionary Biology in Barcelona, has tracked butterflies flying from Iceland all the way to the Sahara and beyond. Other research suggests that British painted ladies complete a round trip of about 14,500 kilometres from tropical Africa to the Arctic Circle over as many as 6 generations.
relatives:
The painted lady belongs to the genus Vanessa. Its close relatives include the Australian painted lady, sometimes treated as a subspecies, which ranges over half of Australia, as well as the American painted lady and the West Coast lady of North America.

Studies of colour vision in another cousin, the red admiral, show that it cannot tell yellow light from orange, or orange from red.
didYouKnow: Groups of courting painted ladies rarely stray more than 4.5 metres from the point where their circling flight began.

quiz.prompt: Which colour can painted ladies not see?
choices: Green, which is why they ignore leaves
quiz.explanation: They have ultraviolet, blue and green receptors but no red ones.

quiz.prompt: Over how many generations can the Africa to Arctic round trip take place?
choices: Exactly 2, one flying north and one returning south
quiz.explanation: British painted ladies complete the 14,500 km round trip over as many as 6 generations.

quiz.prompt: Where were the ocean-crossing painted ladies found in 2024?
choices: The Azores, after drifting on the trade winds
quiz.explanation: Pollen and genetic tests showed the French Guiana butterflies had flown from Africa or Europe.

name: Giant Clam
range: Shallow coral reefs of the Indo-Pacific
tagline: The largest clam alive, powered by sunlight
lede: The giant clam is the biggest bivalve mollusc alive, able to top 200 kg and live for more than a century. It gets most of its food by farming tiny algae in its own flesh, gaping open each day so they can soak up the sun.
home:
Giant clams live on the shallow coral reefs of the South Pacific and Indian oceans, including the Philippines and the reefs of Malaysia in the South China Sea. They settle on flat coral sand or broken coral, at depths of up to 20 metres.

The species ranges across the Indo-Pacific, but its populations are shrinking fast, and it has vanished from many areas where it was once common. The South China Sea is a hotspot for the whole group: 7 of the 10 known kinds of giant clam live on its reefs.
anatomy:
A giant clam can measure up to 120 centimetres across. The largest known specimen, found off Sumatra around 1817, was 137 centimetres long and weighed an estimated 250 kg alive, and its shells are now in a museum in Northern Ireland. A heavier clam found off the Japanese island of Ishigaki in 1956 was shorter, at 115 centimetres, but weighed an estimated 340 kg alive.

Adults are the only giant clams that cannot close their shells completely, so part of the brownish-yellow mantle always shows. The shell has 4 or 5 deep vertical folds, which separates it from the similar Tridacna derasa, with 6 or 7.
life:
Giant clams filter food from the water, yet 65 to 70% of their nutrition comes from single-celled algae called zooxanthellae living in their mantle. The algae use carbon dioxide, phosphates and nitrates supplied by the clam, which keeps them in a special circulatory system at far higher densities than usual.

This partnership lets the clam grow to 1 metre long in nutrient-poor reef water. The balance shifts with size: very small clams get about 65% of their carbon from filter feeding, but larger ones only 34%. Recent modelling suggests the algae are stacked in vertical columns and fed light by shimmering cells called iridocytes, turning sunlight into energy with an efficiency of up to about 67%, among the best natural solar collectors known.
family:
Each clam is a hermaphrodite, producing both eggs and sperm, though it cannot fertilise itself. Because adults cannot move, they spawn into open water, coordinated by a chemical signal: when one clam releases it, its neighbours detect it and respond.

Spawning tends to follow incoming tides around certain phases of the moon, and an adult can release more than 500 million eggs at once. About 12 hours after fertilisation a larva hatches and starts to build a shell. Within a week it settles on the bottom, using a small foot to crawl and shift position.

At first it has no algae and depends on plankton, picking up its partners from the water later. Many die at this stage. Laboratory-reared clams grow about 12 centimetres a year, and in the wild giant clams live on average for more than 100 years.
remarkable:
The edge of the mantle is dotted with several hundred to several thousand pinhole eyes, each about 0.5 mm across.

Each contains a pupil-like opening over a bed of 100 or more light receptors, sensitive to three ranges of light including ultraviolet, which may be unique among molluscs. When a shadow passes or the light dims, the clam partly closes its shell.
outlook:
The main reason giant clams are disappearing is heavy harvesting, both for food and for the aquarium trade, and it is the large, most profitable adults that are taken. The species has been reported as locally extinct in peninsular Malaysia. International trade, including in parts and shells, is regulated under CITES Appendix II. Farming offers hope.

Mass culture began at the Micronesian Mariculture Demonstration Center in Palau, and an Australian project ran from 1985 to 1992 at James Cook University's Orpheus Island Research Station, helping to set up hatcheries across the Pacific Islands and the Philippines. Clams have been introduced to Hawaii and Micronesia, and restocked clams in the Philippines spread their own larvae to sites hundreds of metres away within 10 years.
people:
Peoples of East Asia have known giant clams for thousands of years, and the Venetian explorer Antonio Pigafetta described them in his journal in 1521. The meat is a delicacy in Japan, where it is called himejako, as well as in France, Southeast Asia and many Pacific Islands.

In parts of China high prices are paid for the adductor muscle, believed to be an aphrodisiac, and the shells sell on the black market as decorations. Folklore has long cast the clam as a killer.

A Polynesian tale tells of one biting off a monkey's hand, a Maori legend describes one attacking a canoe, and versions of the US Navy Diving Manual explained how to escape its grip. In reality its slow-closing muscle, and the need to squeeze water out first, mean it cannot trap a person.
relatives:
Tridacna gigas is the best-known species of the genus Tridacna, and several other giant clams are often mistaken for it. Its relatives include Tridacna derasa and Hippopus porcellanus, both found on the reefs of eastern Malaysia.

Giant clams have reorganised the basic bivalve body plan, growing fleshy mantles that spill over the edges of their shells. Biologists have long debated how: Sir Yonge argued the internal organs rotated 180 degrees relative to the shell, while Stasek proposed that the body simply grows backwards rather than downwards.
didYouKnow: Chemical traces locked in a giant clam's shell, including oxygen isotopes and the ratio of strontium to calcium, can reveal past sea surface temperatures.

quiz.prompt: Where does the giant clam get most of its nutrition?
choices: Dead material that drifts down from the reef
quiz.explanation: Zooxanthellae living in its mantle supply 65 to 70% of its needs.

quiz.prompt: What do the pinhole spots on the clam's mantle do?
choices: Squirt jets of water at approaching fish
quiz.explanation: They are tiny eyes that make the clam close up when light dims or something moves.

quiz.prompt: How many eggs can an adult giant clam release at once?
choices: Roughly a million, spread out over a week
quiz.explanation: Giant clams spawn into open water and can release over 500 million eggs at a time.

name: Reticulated Python
range: Rainforests, woodlands and river margins of South and Southeast Asia
tagline: The world's longest snake, and a superb swimmer
lede: The reticulated python is the longest snake in the world, a non-venomous constrictor wrapped in a net of diamond markings. It swims so well that it has been seen far out at sea and has made its own way to many small islands.
home:
This python ranges across South and Southeast Asia, from the Nicobar Islands, India and Bangladesh through Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, Malaysia and Singapore. It is found on a long chain of Indonesian islands, from Sumatra and Borneo to Sulawesi, Java, Flores and Timor, as well as in Timor-Leste and on many islands of the Philippines.

It lives in rainforests, woodlands and nearby grasslands, usually close to rivers, streams or lakes. In the early 20th century it was said to be common even in busy parts of Bangkok, where it sometimes ate domestic animals.
anatomy:
A study of more than a thousand wild pythons in southern Sumatra found lengths of 1.5 to 6.5 metres and weights of 1 to 75 kg. Snakes over 6 metres are rare, but this is the only living species that regularly exceeds that length. It is the third heaviest snake, after the green anaconda and the Burmese python.

Its smooth scales are arranged in 69 to 79 rows around the middle of the body, and deep pits line some of the scales along its lips. The back carries a complex geometric pattern of irregular diamonds flanked by smaller, pale-centred markings.

In a zoo it can look garish, but among shadows and fallen leaves this disruptive colouring makes the snake almost vanish, hiding it from predators and prey alike.
life:
The reticulated python is an ambush hunter. It waits until an animal wanders within range, seizes it, wraps it in its coils and kills it by constriction. Pythons up to 3 or 4 metres long eat mainly rats and other rodents, bats and treeshrews.

Larger ones take civets, binturongs, primates, wild boar and deer weighing more than 60 kg. It can swallow prey up to a quarter of its own length and as heavy as itself. Near villages it sometimes snatches stray chickens, cats and dogs.
family:
Reticulated pythons lay eggs, with females producing clutches of 15 to 80. At an ideal incubation temperature of 31 to 32 °C, the eggs take an average of 88 days to hatch, and the hatchlings are already at least 0.61 metres long.

On some small islands, pythons have shrunk over time. The Tanahjampea population south of Sulawesi rarely grows much beyond 2 metres, and the Selayar population does not exceed 4 metres. Island-bred pythons are now selectively bred in captivity into 'super dwarfs' that grow only 1.82 to 2.4 metres long.
remarkable: One of the largest pythons ever scientifically measured, from Balikpapan in East Kalimantan, was 6.95 metres long. It was measured under anaesthetic while surgeons removed a radio collar from its intestines: it had eaten a half-starved, radio-collared sun bear weighing 23 kg, a meal that took about 10 weeks to digest.
outlook:
Because it is so widespread, the reticulated python is listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. Even so, in several countries it is hunted for its skin, for traditional medicine and for the pet trade, which makes it one of the most economically important reptiles in the world.

In 2015 the United States added it to its list of injurious wildlife, banning imports. A court decision in 2017 overturned the ban on moving it between states.
people:
This is one of the very few snakes known to prey on people, and the only one for which photographs and video prove it has swallowed humans. Most recent fatal cases have been in Indonesia, especially on Sulawesi and nearby islands; in 2017 a farmer in West Sulawesi became the first fully confirmed case of a person found inside a python.

Even a huge snake can struggle to get past an adult's shoulders. Size claims are notoriously unreliable. Colossus, a zoo python in Pittsburgh, was once credited with 8.7 metres, but its skeleton measured 6.35 metres, and a snake in Indonesia claimed at 14.85 metres turned out to be about 7 metres.

Scientists accept only measurements of dead or anaesthetised animals. Even so, a captive python in Kansas City called Medusa was recorded at 7.67 metres in 2011.
relatives:
Johann Gottlob Schneider described the species in 1801 as Boa reticulata. The name reticulatus is Latin for 'net-like', after its complex pattern. Genetic studies later showed that it is more closely related to the pythons of Australia and New Guinea than to the Indian python and its kin.

A proposal in 2004 to give it the genus Broghammerus was widely rejected because it lacked scientific rigour. In 2014 researchers named the genus Malayopython for this species and its sister, the Timor python, and that name is now in general use.
didYouKnow: In 2012 an albino reticulated python called Twinkie, 7 metres long, was named the largest albino snake in captivity.

quiz.prompt: What does the name reticulatus mean?
choices: Strangler of deer, from an old Javanese word
quiz.explanation: It is Latin for 'net-like', after the python's patterned scales.

quiz.prompt: How does the reticulated python kill its prey?
choices: By crushing it with its powerful jaws and teeth
quiz.explanation: It is non-venomous and kills by squeezing prey in its coils.

quiz.prompt: How has the reticulated python reached many small islands?
choices: As eggs carried on rafts of floating vegetation
quiz.explanation: It is an excellent swimmer and has been reported far out at sea.

name: Common Raven
range: Across the Northern Hemisphere, from Arctic tundra to North African desert
tagline: The heaviest perching bird, and one of the cleverest
lede: The common raven is a big, glossy black bird with a deep, rolling croak and a mind to match. It is the heaviest of all perching birds, and its knack for solving problems places it among the most intelligent animals known.
home:
Ravens have the largest range of any member of their genus and one of the largest of any perching bird. They live right across the Northern Hemisphere, from the Arctic and temperate lands of North America and Eurasia to the deserts of North Africa and islands in the Pacific. In Tibet they have been recorded at 5,000 metres, and on Mount Everest as high as 6,350 metres.

Most prefer wooded country with wide open land nearby, or coasts with sea cliffs for nesting. They generally stay put all year, even in Arctic Canada and Alaska. In Britain they were wiped out of many areas by gamekeepers, but are now spreading again under legal protection.
anatomy:
An adult raven is 54 to 71 centimetres long, with a wingspan of 116 to 153 centimetres, and weighs from 0.69 to 2.25 kg. Birds from cold places such as Greenland and the Himalayas tend to be bigger, with larger bills. Compared with crows, ravens have a heavier, slightly curved bill, shaggy throat feathers, longer bristles above the beak and a long, wedge-shaped tail. The plumage is iridescent black and the eyes dark brown.

In the air they soar steadily with fewer wingbeats than crows, yet are just as agile, and their feathers creak in flight like rustling silk. A pied form once lived in the Faroe Islands, and pale, leucistic ravens are occasionally seen in British Columbia.
life:
Ravens will eat almost anything: carrion and the maggots on it, grain, acorns, berries, eggs, small mammals, frogs, lizards and human rubbish. On Alaska's Arctic tundra, birds got about half their energy from hunting rodents and half from scavenging caribou and ptarmigan.

They follow wolves to scavenge their kills, and have even been seen leading packs to prey they could spot from the air. Surplus food, especially fat, is hidden away, and ravens learn to cache it out of sight of other ravens, which steal from one another freely.

Their voice is just as varied, with 15 to 30 types of call, and they can mimic sounds including human speech. Young ravens are famously playful, sliding down snowbanks, playing chase with wolves, otters and dogs, and breaking off twigs to play with together.
family:
Young ravens start courting early but may not pair up for another 2 or 3 years. Once paired, they usually stay together for life, nesting in the same place year after year and defending a territory.

The nest is a deep bowl of large sticks, some 150 centimetres long, lined with soft material such as deer fur, built in a tall tree, on a cliff ledge or on a utility pole. The female lays 4 to 6 pale bluish-green, brown-blotched eggs and incubates them alone for 18 to 21 days.

Both parents feed the chicks, which fledge at 35 to 49 days and stay with them for another 6 months. Wild ravens typically live 10 to 15 years, the record being 23 years and 3 months, while birds at the Tower of London have passed 40.
remarkable:
In one test, meat hung from a perch on a string. To reach it, a raven had to pull up a loop, pin it with a foot and repeat.

Four of five birds succeeded, with no obvious trial and error, suggesting genuine insight. Other studies show ravens remember unfair trades, pretend to bury food to fool onlookers, and by 4 months old match adult chimpanzees and orangutans on tests of reasoning.
outlook:
With its size, sociability and fierce defence of its nest, the raven has few natural predators, mainly eagles and large owls that take eggs and fledglings. People have been its main enemy: gamekeepers still persecute it illegally in parts of Britain, and Finland paid a bounty for ravens from the mid-18th century until 1923. Elsewhere ravens have boomed alongside people.

In the western Mojave Desert, towns, landfills and roads helped the population grow about 16-fold in 25 years, and the birds now threaten young desert tortoises, prompting shooting, trapping and efforts to cover rubbish. Limited culling in Alaska aims to protect the vulnerable Steller's eider.
people:
Few birds loom so large in human stories. To the Tlingit and Haida, Raven was a trickster and creator, and in Siberian legend the raven god Kutkh made the Kamchatka Peninsula.

In Norse myth the ravens Huginn and Muninn flew over the world to bring news to Odin, and in Jewish, Christian and Islamic tradition the raven was the first animal Noah released from the Ark. In parts of Europe, though, its black plumage and taste for carrion made it a bird of ill omen.

The raven is the national bird of Bhutan, whose kings wear the Raven Crown, and the official bird of the Yukon. The legend that England will fall if the Tower of London's ravens leave is probably a Victorian invention. A group of ravens is called an unkindness or a conspiracy.
relatives:
Carl Linnaeus named the raven in 1758, and it is the type species of the genus Corvus. Both names simply mean 'raven', corvus in Latin and corax in Greek. Most authorities recognise 11 subspecies, and it shares the title of largest corvid with the thick-billed raven.

Its closest relatives are the brown-necked raven, the pied crow of Africa and the Chihuahuan raven. Genetic studies reveal a surprise: ravens of the southwestern United States form a separate lineage that split off about 2 million years ago and is closer to the Chihuahuan raven than to other common ravens, though the two groups can still interbreed.
didYouKnow: Ravens often steal shiny objects such as golf balls, perhaps because young birds are drawn to bright, round things that resemble eggs.

quiz.prompt: Which two ravens brought news to the Norse god Odin?
choices: Geri and Freki, the twin storm birds of the north
quiz.explanation: In Norse myth, Huginn and Muninn flew over the world to report to Odin.

quiz.prompt: In the string-pulling test, what did ravens have to do?
choices: Fly through a maze of mirrors to reach a hidden nest of eggs
quiz.explanation: Four of five ravens worked out how to haul up meat hanging on a string.

quiz.prompt: Who incubates a raven's eggs?
choices: Young birds from the previous year's brood
quiz.explanation: The female incubates alone for 18 to 21 days while the male shelters the young.
