Scent glands on the thighs help them communicate.
family:
Solenodons breed all year, though a female is receptive only briefly, about once every 10 days. After a pregnancy of more than 84 days she gives birth to 1 to 3 young, but usually only two survive, because she has just two teats, set near the groin.

The babies are born blind and hairless, weighing 40 to 55 g. The mother carries her young about for their first 2 months; how long they take to be fully weaned is unknown. In captivity solenodons have lived for more than 11 years.
remarkable: Its venom is potent: in tests, doses of around half a milligram per gram of body weight killed mice within 2 to 6 minutes. Genome studies show the solenodon evolved venom independently of venomous shrews, yet recruited similar families of genes to do it, a striking case of evolution arriving at the same answer twice.
outlook:
The species was long listed as Endangered, but in 2020 the IUCN downlisted it to Least Concern as more became known about its population and range. Threats remain: national parks in both countries are being cleared for farming and charcoal, and introduced dogs, cats and small Asian mongooses, brought in to control rats in sugar cane fields, can all kill solenodons.

With no native land predators, it never evolved defences and is a slow, clumsy runner; its only natural enemies are owls. It is fully protected by law. Since 2009, projects involving the EDGE programme, Durrell, BirdLife International and local partners have studied it and raised awareness in both countries.
people:
Science first met the animal in 1833, when a puzzling specimen from Haiti reached the Russian Academy of Sciences; its curator, Johann Friedrich von Brandt, named it Solenodon paradoxus.

It was later thought extinct until naturalists rediscovered it in the Dominican Republic in 1907, and by 1964 it was again feared lost. In 1981 it was declared 'functionally extinct' in Haiti, surviving only in remote southern mountains. Its local name is agouta.
relatives:
Solenodons belong to an ancient lineage that split from other placental mammals about 73.6 to 78 million years ago, in the Late Cretaceous.

The only other living species is the Cuban solenodon; a smaller sister species, Marcano's solenodon, died out on Hispaniola after European colonisation. Together with the Hispaniolan hutia, a rat-like rodent, the solenodon is one of only two native land mammals surviving on the island.
didYouKnow: In 2007 the EDGE of Existence programme named the Hispaniolan solenodon one of its top ten focal species.

quiz.prompt: How does the solenodon deliver its venom?
choices: Through spurs on its hind feet
By spraying it from scent glands on its thighs
quiz.explanation: Venomous saliva flows through a groove in its second lower incisor.

quiz.prompt: Why do usually only two of a solenodon's young survive?
choices: The mother has only two teats
The largest pup pushes its siblings out of the burrow soon after birth
quiz.explanation: A female has just two teats, so she can only feed two young.

quiz.prompt: What does the name solenodon mean?
choices: Night digger of the Caribbean forest floor
quiz.explanation: It refers to the groove in the tooth that carries its venom.

charities.name: Durrell Wildlife Conservation Trust
charities.blurb: Saves threatened species from extinction and has worked to protect Hispaniola's solenodons.

name: King Penguin
range: Subantarctic islands of the Southern Ocean, from the Falklands to Macquarie Island
tagline: The orange-cheeked diver with a 14-month nursery
lede: Standing nearly a metre tall with blazing orange cheeks, the king penguin is the second largest penguin in the world. It hunts in the dark depths of the Southern Ocean, and raising a single chick takes it well over a year. Its colonies, crowded with woolly brown youngsters, can hold hundreds of thousands of birds.
home:
King penguins breed on subantarctic islands between 45 and 55°S, including South Georgia, the Crozet, Kerguelen and Prince Edward Islands, Macquarie Island, the Falklands and the Argentine part of Tierra del Fuego. The largest populations are on the Crozet Islands, with around 455,000 pairs.

Where they go outside the breeding season is unknown, and stray birds have turned up on the Antarctic Peninsula and in South Africa, Australia and New Zealand. The total population is estimated at 2.23 million pairs and is increasing. Single colonies are vast: St Andrew's Bay on South Georgia holds over 150,000 pairs.
anatomy:
Kings stand 70 to 100 centimetres tall and weigh 9.3 to 18 kg, up to about 20 kg before moulting. They are about 25% shorter and a third lighter than the emperor penguin. The cheek patch is solid bright orange, the upper chest orange-yellow, and the bill long and straight with orange markings on the lower half, while the back is a grizzled sooty grey rather than black.

Males are slightly larger, but the sexes look alike and are best told apart by their calls. Chicks look nothing like their parents, wrapped in heavy dark brown down. Kings can also smell the feathers and droppings of their own kind, which may help them sense their colony.
life:
Fish make up about 80% of the diet for most of the year, mainly lanternfish, along with squid and krill; in July and August fish drop to around 30%.

By day kings dive to 100 to 300 metres, staying under for about 5 minutes, but at night they keep above 30 metres. The deepest recorded dive is 343 metres, and the longest lasted 552 seconds. Most dives are flat-bottomed: the bird descends to a set depth and hunts there for about half the dive before returning. They swim at 6.5 to 10 km/h and porpoise, leaping clear of the water, to breathe without slowing.

On land they waddle or toboggan on their bellies. Predators include leopard seals and orcas at sea, and giant petrels and skuas that take eggs and chicks.
family:
Kings first breed at around 5 to 6 years old. Each season a pair stays faithful, but fewer than 30% keep the same partner the following year. They build no nest.

The female lays a single pear-shaped egg of about 300 g, and both parents take turns, in shifts of 6 to 18 days, balancing it on their feet under a fold of belly skin for about 55 days. The chick then sits on its parents' feet for 30 to 40 days before joining a crèche guarded by a few adults while the parents fish.

Fed on regurgitated fish, it is almost full-grown by April, then fasts and loses weight through winter before fledging in late spring. The whole cycle takes 14 to 16 months, so a pair usually succeeds only once every two years, or twice in three.
remarkable: That long cycle is a clever bit of timing. Rather than rushing a youngster through one summer, as smaller penguins do, kings carry their young through the harshest season, so that by the time it is finally ready to go to sea, it is summer again and food is plentiful.
outlook:
The king penguin is listed as Least Concern, and its numbers have grown since it was protected. In the early 1920s whalers on South Georgia and the Falklands nearly wiped it out, burning millions of oily penguins as fuel for the fires that rendered whale blubber, since the islands had no trees.

The future is less certain. One huge colony on Île aux Cochons in the Crozets fell from about half a million pairs in the 1980s to about 60,000 in 2017, possibly because warming is pushing its food farther away.

Kings rely on the Antarctic Convergence for 80% of their food, and as it shifts south they may need to travel an extra 200 km; some projections suggest 70% of the population could disappear within 80 years. Commercial fishing for lanternfish adds further pressure.
people:
The English illustrator John Frederick Miller engraved and named the species in 1778. Kings were once harvested for blubber, oil, meat and feathers, but today they are fully protected, and tourism at breeding sites is tightly restricted. They are flagship birds in zoos around the world.

At Edinburgh Zoo, a king penguin called Sir Nils Olav holds the rank of major general as mascot of the Royal Norwegian Guard. In Japan, Lala became a viral star for walking to a market to fetch fish wearing a special backpack, and in 2024 Pesto, a chick at Sea Life Melbourne, became famous for his enormous size.
relatives:
The king penguin's closest relative is the larger emperor penguin, with which it shares the genus Aptenodytes and the habit of incubating on its feet.

The two rarely meet in the wild, but can be told apart by the king's longer, straighter bill, larger flippers and sleeker body. The International Ornithologists' Union recognises no subspecies, though some authorities separate South Atlantic birds from those of the Indian Ocean and Macquarie Island.
didYouKnow: In 1936 king penguins were released in northern Norway, and they were seen there until 1949.

quiz.prompt: How long does a king penguin take to raise a chick from egg to fledging?
choices: 3 months, during the short southern summer when fish are easy to catch
quiz.explanation: Its long breeding cycle means pairs usually succeed only every other year.

quiz.prompt: Where does a king penguin keep its egg during incubation?
choices: In a burrow dug into soft peat on the hillside above the beach
quiz.explanation: It balances the egg on its feet under a fold of belly skin.

quiz.prompt: What colour is a king penguin chick's down?
choices: Pale grey with a black and white mask
quiz.explanation: Chicks are wrapped in heavy dark brown down, unlike their parents.

charities.name: BirdLife International
charities.blurb: A global partnership protecting birds and their habitats, including seabirds of the Southern Ocean.

name: Red-bellied Piranha
range: Amazon, Paraguay, Paraná and Essequibo river basins of South America
tagline: A fearsome reputation, but mostly a timid scavenger
lede: Few fish are as feared as the red-bellied piranha, star of horror films and tall tales of bloodthirsty shoals. The truth is tamer. It is mostly a timid scavenger that schools for safety and happily eats fruit, seeds and insects.
home:
The red-bellied piranha ranges more widely than any other piranha, through the rivers of Argentina, Brazil, Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, Guyana, Suriname, Paraguay, Peru, Uruguay and Venezuela. It lives in the Amazon, Paraguay, Paraná and Essequibo basins and smaller coastal rivers of north-eastern Brazil, in rivers, streams, oxbow lakes, reservoirs, floodplains and flooded forests.

It prefers warm water of 15 to 35 °C but can survive brief spells as cold as 10 °C. It is found mainly in whitewater rivers, but also in blackwater and clearwater. Introduced to China, probably through the aquarium trade, it was first detected there in 1990 and has since become invasive.
anatomy:
Adults can reach 50 centimetres and 3.9 kg, though they rarely exceed 35 centimetres. The body is deep and flattened from side to side, mostly grey with silver-flecked scales, and grown fish have the reddish belly that gives the species its name.

Females have a slightly deeper red belly than males. The pectoral and pelvic fins range from red to orange, the base of the anal fin is usually black, and dark spots sometimes appear behind the gills. Juveniles are silver with darker spots. The piranha can make sounds by rapidly contracting special muscles, with its swim bladder probably acting as a resonator.
life:
Red-bellied piranhas are omnivores. They eat insects, worms, crustaceans, snails and fish, but also fruit, nuts, seeds, leaves and debris, and in the rainy season, when food is plentiful, they live mostly on plants and insects.

In the wild they tend to take only weak, injured, dying or dead animals, playing a role rather like vultures on land. Small piranhas forage by day, larger ones at dawn and dusk, lurking in dark places or among plants to ambush prey. They travel in shoals, but mainly for protection from dolphins, caimans, large fish and wading birds such as herons and storks, and there is no evidence that they hunt cooperatively.

Rare feeding frenzies, when a school strips a large animal within minutes, are usually triggered by provocation or starvation. They make three kinds of call, linked to face-offs, fights over food and chasing.
family:
Breeding is tied to the floods of the rainy season, with two reproductive seasons a year. Piranhas can breed at about a year old. Ready to spawn, they actually lose their red colouring and move into flooded grasses at the margins of lakes. Nests about 4 to 5 centimetres deep are dug among the water grasses, and females lay several thousand eggs, often around 5,000, which stick to the plant stems.

Adults swim side by side in tight circles over the nest, not courting but guarding it from egg thieves such as smaller characins. The eggs hatch in 2 to 3 days, and the young hide in the vegetation until they are big enough to turn from hiding to hunting.
remarkable:
Much of the piranha's bloodthirsty image goes back to Theodore Roosevelt. After his expedition to Brazil, the former US president told of a cow devoured to the bones within minutes.

It later emerged that the scene had been staged by local guides, who had penned piranhas in a stretch of river and starved them for over a week before driving the cow in.
outlook:
The red-bellied piranha is widespread and locally abundant, and in parts of its range it is among the commonest fish. Collecting for the aquarium trade may pose a small local risk. The bigger concern runs the other way: where it is introduced elsewhere in the Americas, it tends to harm local fish, partly because of its aggressive behaviour.

No piranhas live wild in the United States, but a single red-bellied piranha turned up in a golf-course lake in Simi Valley, California, in 1998, and California and Washington now ban the species and watch for it.
people:
The species name nattereri honours the naturalist Johann Natterer. Hollywood has made the most of the fish's reputation, from Joe Dante's 1978 film Piranha, which cast it much as Jaws cast sharks, to Piranha 3D in 2010 and its sequel. Red-bellied piranhas are popular aquarium fish.

They are messy eaters that need clean water and dim hiding places, will refuse rotten meat and need not be fed every day. Young ones often nip each other's fins, which grow back surprisingly fast, and hungry piranhas may eat each other.
relatives:
The red-bellied piranha belongs to the family Serrasalmidae, which also includes the pacus. These are medium to large fish with deep, flattened bodies and long dorsal fins, and most members of the family that are not piranhas mainly eat plants.

Within the family it is placed in the genus Pygocentrus, set apart by its unusual teeth and the width of its head.
didYouKnow: Red-bellied piranhas are almost immune to gas bubble disease, which devastates nearly every other fish sharing their waters.

quiz.prompt: Why do red-bellied piranhas mostly gather in shoals?
choices: To keep warm in cooler blackwater rivers during the dry season
quiz.explanation: Shoaling mainly guards them against dolphins, caimans and birds; there is no evidence of pack hunting.

quiz.prompt: How was the 'feeding frenzy' shown to Theodore Roosevelt staged?
choices: Cattle blood was poured into the river upstream for several days beforehand
A different species was swapped in
quiz.explanation: Local guides corralled the fish and starved them for over a week before driving in a cow.

quiz.prompt: What happens to a piranha's colour when it is ready to breed?
choices: Its fins turn black and gold and its belly turns silver
quiz.explanation: Breeding fish lose their red colouring and move into flooded grasses.

charities.blurb: Buys and protects threatened tropical forests, including flooded forests of the Amazon.

charities.name: Wildlife Conservation Society
charities.blurb: Protects wildlife and wild places worldwide, including Amazon rivers and freshwater fish.

name: Indri
range: Eastern rainforests of Madagascar
tagline: Madagascar's singing lemur, sacred in local legend
lede: Every morning the eastern rainforests of Madagascar ring with eerie, wailing songs that carry far across the canopy. They belong to the indri, a big black-and-white lemur that bounds between tree trunks. Revered in Malagasy legend as an ancestor, it is now in grave danger.
home:
The indri lives in lowland and montane rainforest along Madagascar's eastern coast, from the Anjanaharibe-Sud Special Reserve in the north to the Mangoro River in the south. Strangely, it is missing from the Masoala Peninsula and Marojejy National Park, even though forests where indris do live lie less than 40 km away.

It is a creature of the trees, sleeping 10 to 30 metres above the ground, alone or in pairs, and eating little that does not grow on trees. Family groups move 300 to 700 metres a day through their territory, travelling farthest in midsummer as they search for fruit.
anatomy:
Along with the diademed sifaka, the indri is the largest living lemur. It averages about 6.5 kg and can weigh 9.5 kg or perhaps more, with a head and body length of 64 to 72 centimetres; with its legs stretched out it reaches nearly 120 centimetres.

Unlike any other living lemur, it has only a stub of a tail. The indri is a vertical clinger and leaper, holding its body upright and launching itself from trunk to trunk with long, muscular legs.

Its silky fur is mostly black, with white patches on the limbs, neck, crown and lower back, and its large greenish eyes sit in a bare dark face framed by round, fuzzy ears. Colour varies from place to place, and some northern indris are almost entirely black.
life:
The indri is active by day and eats plants, mainly young, tender leaves, along with seeds, fruit and flowers. It plucks food with its teeth and pulls branches towards its mouth with its hands. Members of the laurel family feature heavily in its diet.

Mature females get first access to food and forage higher in the trees than males. Indri society is led by females, who push males to lower branches and poorer feeding spots and usually lead the group when it travels. Groups are small, typically a mated pair with their growing young, though in fragmented forests several generations may stay together.

Young females play-wrestle silently for up to 15 minutes, and the whole group uses shared toilet spots. A roar warns of hawks overhead, and a honk warns of a fossa on the ground.
family:
Indris are monogamous for the long term, seeking a new mate only when their partner dies. They mature late, at 7 to 9 years, and females give birth only every 2 to 3 years, after a pregnancy of 120 to 150 days. The single infant is usually born in May or June.

The mother does most of the caring, but the father stays with the family and helps. Babies are born mostly or completely black and develop any white markings at 4 to 6 months. The infant clings to its mother's belly for 4 or 5 months before moving onto her back, starts to show independence at 8 months and is fully independent only at 2 years or more.
remarkable:
The indri's song lasts from 45 seconds to more than 3 minutes. It begins with a roar from the whole group, followed by long notes of up to 5 seconds, then a descending wail, often sung as a duet by the adult pair.

Neighbouring groups answer one another in turn, perhaps marking territories and sharing news. A group sings almost daily, up to 7 times a day, mostly between 7 and 11 in the morning, climbing to the treetops first so the sound carries up to 4 km.
outlook:
The indri is critically endangered. Estimates of its numbers range from 1,000 to 10,000, and the population may shrink by 80% over the next three generations, around 36 years. Slash-and-burn farming, firewood gathering and logging destroy and fragment its forest, even inside protected areas. Hunting is also a threat, despite traditional taboos.

As old beliefs erode, some people find ways around them, selling indri meat they are forbidden to eat or buying it when they are forbidden to kill, and in some regions it is prized as a delicacy. Captive breeding offers no fallback: only one indri has ever lived more than a year in captivity, and none has bred.
people:
Malagasy people revere the indri and protect it with fady, or taboos. One legend tells of a man who went hunting and never returned; his son went looking and vanished too, and the villagers found only two large lemurs in the trees, the first indris. In some versions only the son is transformed, and the indri's wail is the father mourning him.

Its local name, babakoto, is usually translated as 'ancestor' or 'father', and may mean 'father of a little boy'. Each morning indris sit facing the rising sun, legs crossed and palms out, and many Malagasy believe they worship it. The name indri probably comes from the Malagasy endrina, not, as an old story claims, from a word meaning 'there it is'.
relatives:
The indri is related to the sifakas and, like all lemurs, is native only to Madagascar. It was first described by the French naturalist Pierre Sonnerat.

In 2005 Colin Groves listed two subspecies, a dark northern form and a paler southern one, but later work suggests the colour simply changes gradually across the range.
didYouKnow: The first film of wild indris was made by luring them with recorded calls, for David Attenborough's 1961 BBC series Zoo Quest to Madagascar.

quiz.prompt: What is unusual about the indri's tail?
choices: It is longer than its body
It is striped black and white like a ring-tailed lemur's
quiz.explanation: It is the only living lemur with merely a rudimentary tail.

quiz.prompt: Who leads an indri group?
choices: Whichever young male wins the wrestling bouts each spring
quiz.explanation: Indris live in a female-dominated society, and the dominant female usually leads.

quiz.prompt: What does the Malagasy name 'babakoto' usually translate as?
choices: There it is, as pointed out to an early French explorer
quiz.explanation: Babakoto is most often translated as 'ancestor' or 'father'.

name: Laughing Kookaburra
range: Eastern Australia, introduced to Tasmania, south-west Australia and New Zealand
tagline: The giant kingfisher whose laugh fills the Australian bush
lede: At dawn and dusk the Australian bush erupts with manic laughter, swelling into a raucous chorus. The laughing kookaburra, the heaviest kingfisher in the world, is announcing that this patch of woodland belongs to its family. That family may include grown-up children who stay home to help raise their siblings.
home:
The laughing kookaburra is native to eastern Australia, from Cape York Peninsula in the north to Cape Otway in the south, on both sides of the Great Dividing Range, and west through Victoria to South Australia's Yorke Peninsula and Flinders Ranges. Partly because of its reputation for killing snakes, it was introduced to south-west Western Australia from 1883, to Tasmania from 1906, and to Kangaroo and Flinders islands.

In the 1860s Governor George Grey released birds on Kawau Island in New Zealand, and a small population now breeds north of Auckland. It lives in open eucalypt forest and woodland, especially where the ground is grassy and open, and it needs tree holes to nest. It is also at home on farmland with trees along roads and fences, and in city parks and gardens, and it stays in the same territory all year.
anatomy:
This is a stocky bird 41 to 47 centimetres long, with a big head, brown eyes and a long, heavy bill, black above and pale below. Females are usually bigger, averaging about 352 g against the male's 307 g. The head and underparts are white or cream, with a dark brown stripe through each eye.

The wings and back are brown with sky-blue spots on the shoulders, and the rusty tail is barred with dark brown and tipped with white. Its voice box, a tracheo-bronchial syrinx, has two sources of vibration, letting it produce two notes at the same time, each with many harmonics.
life:
Kookaburras hunt by perching on a branch or wire and waiting, then dropping onto prey on the ground. They take mice and other small mammals, insects, earthworms, snails, yabbies, small fish, frogs, lizards, small birds and, most famously, snakes, sometimes venomous ones much longer than themselves. In gardens they even snatch goldfish from ponds. The laugh is a territorial call.

One bird begins with a low chuckle, then throws back its head and cackles, and the rest of the family joins in, with neighbouring groups answering in turn without overlapping. Calling increases in the months before breeding. Kookaburras also defend borders with displays, swooping back and forth along territory edges in 'trapeze flights' that can last half an hour.
family:
Kookaburras pair for life and live in family groups. A breeding pair may be helped by up to five grown offspring from earlier years, which defend the territory, incubate the eggs and feed the chicks. Nests are in unlined tree holes or dug into termite nests in trees, and egg-laying peaks from September to November.

The female usually lays 3 white eggs about 2 days apart, and they hatch after 24 to 26 days. Chicks carry a hook on the bill, and when food is short they fight with it; the smallest may be killed by its older siblings. Young fledge at 32 to 40 days and are fed by the group for 6 to 10 weeks more.
remarkable:
The famous laugh is not instinctive but learned. After the young leave the nest, the adult male sings short snatches of the call and the fledglings try to copy him, usually without success at first.

These singing lessons last about 2 weeks before the young can take part in the family's dawn and dusk chorus.
outlook:
The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists the laughing kookaburra as Least Concern, given its large range and population.

Estimates suggest there could be as many as 65 million birds, though that may be far too high: Birdata recorded a 50% drop in sightings between 2000 and 2019, suggesting a marked decline. The New Zealand population is probably fewer than 500 birds.
people:
The kookaburra is famously bold around people. In suburbs it will eat from people's hands, let them rub its belly, or swoop in to snatch food without warning.

In the 19th century it was usually called the laughing jackass, and 'kookaburra' became the official name only in 1926; it comes from the Wiradjuri word gugubarra. Marion Sinclair wrote the popular children's song 'Kookaburra' in 1934. Recordings of the call have been edited into Hollywood films for decades, beginning with the Tarzan series in the 1930s, usually to set a jungle scene.
relatives:
The laughing kookaburra belongs to the tree kingfisher subfamily Halcyoninae. Its genus, Dacelo, is an anagram of Alcedo, the Latin for kingfisher, and holds four kookaburras: the blue-winged kookaburra, which also lives in Australia, and two New Guinea species, the rufous-bellied and spangled kookaburras.

Compared with the blue-winged, the laughing kookaburra has a darker eye, a shorter bill and smaller, duller blue patches. The species name novaeguineae, 'of New Guinea', is a mistake. Pierre Sonnerat claimed to have seen the bird there in 1776, but he never visited New Guinea and the kookaburra does not live there.
didYouKnow: A lone laughing kookaburra has lived wild in the English county of Suffolk since at least 2015.

quiz.prompt: How do young kookaburras learn to laugh?
choices: They are born knowing the call
By copying neighbouring families across the territory border at dawn
quiz.explanation: The adult male sings parts of the call and the fledglings practise for about 2 weeks.

quiz.prompt: What is wrong with the kookaburra's scientific name?
choices: It doesn't live in New Guinea
It was first given to a different bird and then moved across by mistake
quiz.explanation: Novaeguineae means 'of New Guinea', but the species does not occur there.

quiz.prompt: Who helps a breeding pair raise its chicks?
choices: Blue-winged kookaburras sharing the same tree hollow
quiz.explanation: Up to five grown young from earlier years help incubate and feed the chicks.

charities.name: BirdLife Australia
charities.blurb: Australia's largest bird conservation organisation, protecting native birds and their habitats.

name: Red Lionfish
range: Indo-Pacific reefs; invasive in the western Atlantic and Caribbean
tagline: A venomous beauty that conquered the Caribbean
lede: Striped in red and white and trailing long, feathery fins like a lion's mane, the red lionfish is one of the most striking fish on a coral reef. It is also one of the most troublesome: carried far from home by the aquarium trade, it has spread across the western Atlantic, where almost nothing eats it.
home:
The red lionfish is native to the Indo-Pacific, including the western and central Pacific and the waters off western Australia. Linnaeus based his description on a fish from Ambon Island in Indonesia. Outside that range it has become firmly established.

Adults now live along the East Coast of the United States from Cape Hatteras in North Carolina to Florida, in Bermuda and the Bahamas, in the northern Gulf of Mexico, and right across the Caribbean, from Cuba and Puerto Rico to Belize, Honduras, Colombia and Mexico. It has also reached the eastern Mediterranean and the Brazilian island of Fernando de Noronha.
anatomy:
Adults can reach 47 centimetres, making this one of the largest lionfish species, while juveniles are usually under 2.5 centimetres long. The body is banded with white stripes alternating with red, maroon or brown ones.

Its weapons are its spines: 13 venomous spines along the dorsal fin, 2 on the pelvic fins and 3 on the anal fin. Together with its long, non-venomous fins, they create the mane-like look that gives the fish its name. The larvae look quite different, with a large head, a long triangular snout, serrated head spines and colour only on the pelvic fins.
life:
Lionfish are mostly solitary and mostly nocturnal, hunting from late afternoon to dawn. They feed largely on crustaceans such as shrimps, crabs, amphipods and isopods, along with other invertebrates and small fish, including young lionfish. A hunting lionfish uses its broad fins to corner prey, then swallows it whole with a quick strike. One of its tactics is a slow, unbroken approach.

Many small fish swim in bursts with brief pauses, and the lionfish creeps closer during each pause, which lets it catch fish twice as fast as itself. Once within about 9 centimetres, it rapidly expands its mouth, and the low pressure inside sucks the prey in.
family:
Courtship is the only time lionfish gather, usually one male with several females, and it takes place around nightfall and through the night. Courting fish circle, sidewind, follow and lead one another. The sexes look alike except while breeding. After courtship the female releases two masses of eggs, which the male fertilises before they float to the surface.

A female can lay up to 30,000 eggs in one session, and more in warmer months. The embryos produce a sticky mucus that lets them cling to rocks and corals, and they hatch about 36 hours after fertilisation. The larvae swim well, start eating tiny ciliates within four days, and spend about a month drifting before settling. An average red lionfish lives around 10 years.
remarkable: Genetic studies suggest the red lionfish began as a hybrid. Its DNA appears to carry contributions from two other lineages, one formed by the common lionfish and another by the luna and Russell's lionfishes, hinting that the species arose when those fish interbred.
outlook:
Within its native range, moray eels and the ambush-hunting bobbit worm have been seen eating lionfish. In the Atlantic, though, few predators recognise it as food, probably because it is so new there. Lionfish have turned up in the stomachs of Nassau and tiger groupers in the Bahamas, but the Nassau grouper is itself critically endangered and unlikely to make a dent.

About 93% of invasive lionfish belong to this species. They eat a huge range of prey, become abundant quickly, and have moved into the role left by overfished snappers and groupers. Scientists link them to falling numbers of other reef fish and to declines in reef diversity, so many organisations now encourage people to catch and eat lionfish.
people:
The red lionfish probably first escaped into the wild off Florida in the early to mid-1980s, almost certainly from the aquarium trade. Within a few decades it had become one of the best-known marine invaders in the Americas.

Its dorsal spines are purely defensive. A threatened lionfish turns its spines towards the attacker, even if that means swimming upside down. A sting is rarely fatal to people but causes extreme pain, and sometimes headaches, vomiting and difficulty breathing. Soaking the wound in hot water is a common treatment, since few hospitals carry anything specific, but medical help is strongly recommended because some people react badly.
relatives:
The red lionfish belongs to the scorpionfish family, Scorpaenidae, many of whose members carry venomous spines. It is one of five species in the genus Pterois, and the Atlantic invasion involves two of them: the red lionfish and its close look-alike, the common lionfish, Pterois miles.

Linnaeus first named it Gasterosteus volitans in 1758, and it was later made the type species of Pterois. The name volitans means 'flying', probably after the big, wing-like pectoral fins.
didYouKnow: Red lionfish breed every month, which helped their drifting larvae spread rapidly across their new Atlantic range.

quiz.prompt: What does the species name volitans mean?
quiz.explanation: Volitans means 'flying', probably a nod to the large, wing-like pectoral fins.

quiz.prompt: How did red lionfish most likely reach the Atlantic?
choices: By swimming through the Suez Canal and around Africa
quiz.explanation: They were almost certainly released or escaped from aquariums off Florida in the 1980s.

quiz.prompt: Roughly how many eggs can a female lay in one mating session?
choices: Over 10 million in a single batch
quiz.explanation: A female can release up to 30,000 eggs at a time, and more in warmer months.

name: Kinkajou
range: Tropical forests from southern Mexico to Bolivia and south-eastern Brazil
tagline: The 'honey bear' that is really a raccoon cousin
lede: With a monkey's grasping tail, a teddy-bear face and a tongue long enough to lick nectar from flowers, the kinkajou is a puzzle of a mammal. It is actually a relative of the raccoon, and it spends its nights clambering through the rainforest canopy in search of ripe fruit.
home:
Kinkajous range from east and south of the Sierra Madre in Mexico, through Central America, to Bolivia east of the Andes and the Atlantic Forest of south-eastern Brazil. They live from sea level up to 2,500 metres.

They need closed-canopy tropical forest, but many kinds will do: lowland rainforest, montane forest, dry forest, gallery forest along rivers, and secondary forest. During the day they sleep in tree hollows or in shady tangles of leaves, out of direct sunlight.
anatomy:
A kinkajou has a round head, large eyes that shine green or bright yellow in torchlight, a short pointed snout, short limbs and small rounded ears. Including its tail, it measures 82 to 133 centimetres, of which the tail is 39 to 57 centimetres, and it weighs 1.4 to 4.6 kg. Females are generally smaller than males.

Its fur is short, dense and woolly, in shades from tawny olive to wood brown above and buff to brownish yellow below. Some have a dark stripe down the back. The coat mixes pale hairs with darker, brown-tipped ones that reflect less light, which can create an illusion of spots and lines. The tail is furred right to the tip.
life:
Kinkajous are strictly nocturnal, busiest between about 7 pm and midnight and again an hour before dawn. They are superb climbers: the tail serves as a fifth hand, though never for holding food, and the ankles and feet can rotate 180°, so a kinkajou can run backwards along a branch or descend a trunk head first. About 90% of the diet is ripe fruit, especially figs.

A kinkajou holds soft fruit in its forepaws and scoops out the pulp with its tongue, and it probably helps spread seeds. Leaves, flowers, nectar and herbs make up most of the rest, with the occasional ants, bird eggs or small vertebrates. Its slender 13-centimetre tongue reaches into blossoms for nectar, so it may also act as a pollinator.
family:
Kinkajous breed throughout the year. After a pregnancy of 112 to 118 days, the female gives birth to one small baby, or occasionally two. Although they usually forage alone, kinkajous sleep in family units and groom one another.

Scent glands near the mouth, on the throat and on the belly let them mark their territories and travel routes. They sometimes gather to feed in large groups, and may even forage alongside olingos. In captivity they typically live about 23 years, and the record is 42 years.
remarkable: The kinkajou is one of only two carnivorans with a prehensile tail; the other is the binturong of South-east Asia, a much larger animal with similar limb proportions. Despite belonging to the Carnivora and having sharp teeth, it lives mainly on fruit, and its habits mirror those of spider monkeys, which fill a similar role by day where the two overlap.
outlook:
Kinkajous are seldom seen because of their strict nocturnal habits, but they have a much larger range than olingos and tend to be more common. Still, they are hunted for the pet trade, for meat, and for their skins, which are made into wallets and horse saddles.

Because they depend on closed-canopy forest, deforestation is a potential threat. Honduras has listed the species on Appendix III of CITES, so exports from Honduras need a permit and exports from elsewhere need a certificate of origin.
people:
The name kinkajou comes from the French quincajou, which was based on an Algonquian name for the wolverine. In English it has also been called the honey bear, night ape and night walker. Captive kinkajous eagerly eat honey, hence that name, though honey is not well recorded in the wild diet. Kinkajous are sometimes kept as exotic pets.

They are playful, quiet and have little odour, but they dislike noise, sudden movements and being woken by day, and an agitated one may scream, claw and bite deeply. In El Salvador, Guatemala and Honduras pet kinkajous are called micoleón, 'lion monkey', and escaped pets have been reported living wild in Florida.
relatives:
The kinkajou belongs to the raccoon family, Procyonidae, along with olingos, coatis, raccoons, the ringtail and the cacomistle, and it is the only member of its genus, Potos. DNA studies show it is the sister group to all the others, having split from them 24 to 21.6 million years ago.

Its ancestors probably evolved in North America and moved south after the Isthmus of Panama formed. Olingos look so similar that many local cultures do not tell them apart, but kinkajous are larger, have shorter muzzles and lack anal scent glands. When food is scarce, the bigger kinkajous drive olingos away.
didYouKnow: A 2016 genetic study found five distinct regional lineages of kinkajou, suggesting that some of its eight proposed subspecies might be separate species.

quiz.prompt: Roughly what share of a kinkajou's diet is fruit?
choices: Almost none, as it mainly hunts insects and lizards
quiz.explanation: Some 90% of its diet is ripe fruit, especially figs.

quiz.prompt: Which family does the kinkajou belong to?
choices: The bear family, as its 'honey bear' nickname suggests
quiz.explanation: It is a procyonid, related to raccoons, coatis and olingos.

quiz.prompt: How far can a kinkajou rotate its ankles and feet?
choices: A full 360°, like an owl turning its head
quiz.explanation: Rotating its feet 180° lets it run backwards along branches and climb down head first.

name: Lilac-breasted Roller
range: Open savanna and woodland across eastern and southern Africa
tagline: A savanna jewel that tumbles through the sky
lede: Lilac, azure, olive and deep purple-blue, the lilac-breasted roller looks like a bird painted by someone who could not choose a colour. It sits on a high perch scanning the savanna, then drops to snatch insects, scorpions and lizards from the ground.
home:
This roller is found across eastern and southern Africa, from the Red Sea coast of Eritrea through East Africa, including Zanzibar, down to Namibia, Botswana, Zimbabwe and north-eastern South Africa. It lives from sea level to 2,000 metres or more, and has wandered as far as Oman and Yemen. It is most abundant in Kenya.

Its home is open savanna with scattered trees and shrubs, because it needs high perches for hunting and nesting. It is largely absent from treeless places and avoids towns and farmland unless they are abandoned. The southern subspecies is mostly resident, while the northern lilac-throated roller migrates from north-east Kenya to north-west Somalia to breed.
anatomy:
A sturdy, large-headed bird, it weighs about 104 grams and measures 36 to 38 centimetres, including the 8 to 9 centimetre tail streamers. Its wingspan is 50 to 58 centimetres. The throat is lilac, deepening to a darker lilac breast, with an olive crown and back and lilac-rufous cheeks. In flight the wings flash brilliant azure, black and dark purple-blue.

Males and females look alike, though males may be slightly larger. Juveniles lack the long black outer tail streamers and have rufous-tawny, streaked breasts. Like all rollers, it has syndactyl feet, with the second and third toes fused together.
life:
Usually alone or in pairs, the roller perches at the top of a tree, a pole or even a large grazing mammal, watching for movement below. It feeds on ground-dwelling insects, spiders, scorpions, centipedes, millipedes and snails, and on small vertebrates including lizards, chameleons, snakes and small birds. Small prey is swallowed on the spot; larger prey is carried to a perch and beaten until it falls apart. Fire is an opportunity.

When grassland burns, rollers gather with fiscals, flycatchers, kites, storks, swallows and bee-eaters to pick off animals fleeing the flames, and in parks they hunt slow lizards and snakes crossing the roads. Its call is a harsh, sawing 'rak rak rak', given in flight.
family:
Pairs are probably monogamous and nest on their own. They do not dig their own holes, instead taking over cavities made by woodpeckers or kingfishers, about 5 metres up in a baobab, palm or other tree, or even in the side of a termite mound. The nest is a flat pad of grass.

The female lays 2 to 4 eggs, and both parents take turns incubating them for 22 to 24 days. The chicks hatch helpless and are fully feathered after 19 days. The parents are fiercely protective, taking on raptors and other birds that come too close, and one of the pair may fly in a rolling pattern to drive off intruders.
remarkable:
Its courtship flight is a spectacle. The bird climbs high, sometimes between 69 and 144 metres, then tips forward with closed wings and plunges towards the ground.

At top speed it rocks from side to side several times, calling a harsh 'kaaa, kaarsh', before swooping up again. Rival males that meet in the air fight by beating wings and clawing at each other as they climb.
outlook:
The IUCN lists the lilac-breasted roller as Least Concern, thanks to its large range and stable population. It is less abundant in Kenya than it once was, however, and because it shuns farmland and towns it depends on open savanna staying intact.

Outside national parks it is seen less often, sometimes appearing only when farmers burn land and stir up insects.
people:
The lilac-breasted roller is unofficially considered the national bird of Kenya. Over the years it has collected other names too, including fork-tailed roller, lilac-throated roller, Mosilikatze's roller and troupand.

Linnaeus gave it its scientific name in 1766, basing his account on 'le Rollier d'Angola', a bird described and illustrated by the French zoologist Mathurin Jacques Brisson in 1760. The name caudatus is Latin for 'tailed', after its streamers.
relatives:
It is one of nine species in the genus Coracias, a group of rollers native to the open woodlands of Africa and western Eurasia. Two subspecies are recognised.

The lilac-throated or blue-breasted roller of the Horn of Africa, with a greenish-blue crown and an azure breast, was first described as a separate species, but there is no behavioural or ecological evidence to keep it apart. In Kenya's Turkana Basin it can be confused with the sleeker Abyssinian roller, which has dark blue upper tail coverts and distinctly spatulate tail streamers.
didYouKnow: Immature lilac-breasted rollers have buffy breasts with just the occasional lilac feather and pale streaks.

quiz.prompt: Which country unofficially treats this roller as its national bird?
choices: Ethiopia, where it was first described
quiz.explanation: It is unofficially considered the national bird of Kenya, where it is most abundant.

quiz.prompt: Where does the lilac-breasted roller usually nest?
choices: In a burrow it digs in a riverbank
In a hanging basket woven from grass
quiz.explanation: It takes over cavities made by woodpeckers or kingfishers rather than digging its own.

quiz.prompt: Which toes are fused on a roller's foot?
choices: All four, forming a single grasping pad
quiz.explanation: Rollers have syndactyl feet, with the second and third toes joined.

name: Sea Lamprey
range: North Atlantic coasts and rivers; invasive in the Great Lakes
tagline: The jawless 'vampire fish' that drinks blood
lede: The sea lamprey has no jaws and no paired fins, just an eel-like body and a round sucking mouth ringed with rows of sharp teeth. It clamps on to living fish and feeds on their blood, which has earned it the nickname 'vampire fish' and made it a notorious invader of North America's Great Lakes.
home:
The sea lamprey lives in the northern and western Atlantic along the coasts of Europe and North America, as well as in the western Mediterranean and the Black Sea. It has been found as deep as 4,000 metres and tolerates water from 1 to 20 °C.

In North America it is native to the Connecticut River basin, and the largest European populations are in north-central Portugal, north-western Spain and western France. It is anadromous: adults live in the sea or a large lake and travel up rivers to spawn.

Its body copes with a wide range of salinity, and the membranes of its gills change their chemistry as young lampreys move towards salt water. Some populations, like those in the Great Lakes, live entirely in fresh water.
anatomy:
Adults can reach 120 centimetres and weigh up to 2.3 kg. The body is olive or brownish-yellow on the back and sides with black marbling, and paler underneath. Behind each eye is a row of seven gill openings. The mouth is the remarkable part.

Jawless and round, it is as wide as or wider than the head, and lined with many concentric rows of sharp, keratinised teeth surrounding a rasping tongue. The lamprey also tolerates very high levels of urea, which lets it feed on sharks and rays, whose blood is rich in this compound that is toxic to most fish.
life:
A feeding lamprey attaches its suction-cup mouth to a fish's skin and rasps through the flesh with its tongue and teeth. A fluid in its mouth called lamphredin stops the victim's blood from clotting, and many hosts die from blood loss or infection.

The lamprey is not choosy, preying on a wide variety of fish. The adult feeding stage lasts only 12 to 18 months, but in that time a single lamprey can kill around 18 kg of fish. Its whole lifespan can stretch to 7 years, much of it spent as a burrowing larva.
family:
Males build nests in the gravel or sand of streams with a moderately strong current, and females lay large numbers of eggs in them. Spawning is the last act of their lives: the adults die soon afterwards. The larvae, called ammocoetes, burrow into the soft bottom of quiet water downstream and filter plankton and detritus for several years.

Then they metamorphose into the adult form and head for the sea or a lake, though some begin feeding on blood while still in the river. About a year and a half after metamorphosis, the adults return upstream to breed.
remarkable:
Its genome is one of the strangest among vertebrates. During early development, the lamprey sheds about 20% of its DNA from the cells that build its body, keeping the full set only in the line of cells that will make eggs and sperm.

Northern lampreys, the group it belongs to, also have more chromosomes than any other vertebrate, between 164 and 174.
outlook:
In its native range the sea lamprey coevolved with its hosts, which developed some resistance. Lake Ontario was walled off from the other Great Lakes by Niagara Falls, but once the Welland Canal let lampreys bypass the falls, they reached Lake Erie by 1921 and Lake Superior by 1938.

Lake trout, lake whitefish, chub and lake herring had no defences, and together with overfishing the lamprey helped devastate lake trout in the 1930s and 1940s. With those predators gone, the invasive alewife boomed. The Great Lakes Fishery Commission, a joint Canada–US body, fights back with electric currents, barriers that let most other fish pass and, most effectively, the selective pesticide TFM, applied to rivers.

Researchers are also studying lamprey pheromones as a gentler lure. Meanwhile, in the Connecticut River basin, managers help lampreys past dams, because adults that die after spawning feed native freshwater fish.
people:
Lampreys are a delicacy in parts of Europe and are sold seasonally in France, Spain and Portugal, which also hold the main fisheries for the species. In Finland they are eaten pickled, and in Latvia sea lampreys are sometimes caught alongside river lampreys.

Scientists value the sea lamprey too. Its genome was sequenced in 2013 and serves as a model for studying development and evolution, and two immune genes, CDA1 and CDA2, were first discovered in it before being found across lampreys.
relatives:
The sea lamprey is a northern lamprey, one of a group of jawless, eel-like fish; despite its shape and its old nickname, it is not an eel.

Its genus name, Petromyzon, comes from the Greek for 'stone' and 'to suck', so it means 'stone sucker', while marinus is Latin for 'of the sea'. The larvae are so unlike adults that they have their own name, and they tolerate a far narrower range of salt levels than adults can.
didYouKnow: Sea lampreys can rid their bodies of excess acid faster than most other saltwater fish, mostly across the surface of their gills.

quiz.prompt: What does a lamprey's mouth produce to stop blood clotting?
choices: A digestive acid that dissolves fish scales
quiz.explanation: A fluid called lamphredin keeps the host's blood flowing while the lamprey feeds.

quiz.prompt: What happens to sea lampreys after they spawn?
choices: They turn back into filter-feeding larvae
quiz.explanation: Spawning is followed by the death of the adults.

quiz.prompt: Which canal let sea lampreys bypass Niagara Falls?
choices: A short canal dug beside Lake Superior
quiz.explanation: Once the Welland Canal was built, lampreys spread from Lake Ontario to the other Great Lakes.

name: Koala
range: Eucalypt woodlands of eastern and south-eastern Australia
tagline: Australia's sleepy, leaf-eating marsupial icon
lede: Dozing up to 20 hours a day in the fork of a gum tree, the koala lives on leaves that would poison most mammals. Its round fluffy ears and teddy-bear face have made it one of the most famous animals on Earth, yet beneath the charm is a creature tuned to survive on almost no energy.
home:
Koalas live in eastern and south-eastern mainland Australia, in Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria and South Australia, over a range of roughly 1,000,000 square kilometres spanning 30 ecoregions. They have been introduced to several nearby islands, and Magnetic Island marks the northern limit of the range.

In the late Pleistocene they lived as far west as south-western Western Australia. They usually inhabit open eucalypt woodland, in both tropical and temperate climates. In semi-arid country they keep to trees along streams and creeks, which offer refuge during drought and extreme heat.
anatomy:
A koala is stout, with a large head and a vestigial tail or none at all. It measures 60 to 90 centimetres and weighs 4 to 15 kg, and koalas from Victoria are twice as heavy as those from Queensland.

Males are 50% larger than females and have bald chest patches marking their scent glands. The back fur, light grey to chocolate brown, is the best insulating coat of any marsupial. Sharp curved claws and two opposable digits on each forepaw give a firm grip, while two fused toes on each hind foot work as a grooming comb.

Its brain is unusually small, about 19.2 grams, and does not fill the skull, perhaps because its diet cannot fuel a bigger one. A low larynx and extra folds in the soft palate let koalas make surprisingly deep sounds for their size.
life:
Koalas eat mostly eucalypt leaves and favour around 30 of the more than 600 species available, choosing leaves with more protein and less fibre. They rarely need to drink. A koala clips leaves with its front teeth, grinds them with cusped molars and sometimes brings food back up to chew again.

A caecum 200 centimetres long ferments the fibre, food may stay in the gut for 100 hours, and liver enzymes neutralise the toxins. The diet is so poor that its metabolic rate is only half that of a typical mammal.

It is active mostly at night, spends just 15 minutes a day on social behaviour, and comes down to the ground only 2 or 3 times a night. Males bellow with a series of deep, snoring inhalations and belching exhalations that carries far through the forest.
family:
Koalas give birth between October and May after a pregnancy of only 33 to 35 days. The newborn joey weighs no more than 0.5 grams, yet crawls into its mother's pouch and latches on to a teat.

At about 26 weeks it is fully furred and peeks out, and at 6 or 7 months it leaves the pouch for the first time. Around then, the mother produces a soft, bacteria-rich pap from her caecum that the joey eats, preparing its gut for eucalyptus.

The young rides on her back and stays nearby until it is 1.5 to 2 years old. Females mature at about 3 years and males at about 4, and koalas live 13 to 18 years in the wild. Once their teeth wear down, chewing gets harder, and old koalas may eventually starve.
remarkable: Unusually among marsupials, koala milk gets less fatty as the joey grows, and a mother keeps lactating for up to a year to make up for her own low energy. She also never cleans her pouch, which is held shut by a ring of muscle that keeps the young safely inside.
outlook:
The IUCN moved the koala from Least Concern to Vulnerable in 2014, and in 2022 it was listed as endangered in Queensland, New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory. Threats include clearing for farming and housing, drought and bushfires, which trap koalas in flammable treetops. Chlamydia bacteria and koala retrovirus cause disease, and cars and dogs kill about 4,000 a year.

Population estimates vary hugely, from 92,000 in 2021 to as many as 918,000 using newer survey methods in 2025, compared with 8 to 10 million in the early 1900s. In parts of South Australia and Victoria, such as Cape Otway and French Island, koalas are now so abundant that they overgraze their trees.
people:
The word koala comes from the Dharug word gula, meaning 'no water'. In Dreamtime stories, the Tharawal people believed the koala helped them reach Australia by rowing their boat, and many tales explain how it lost its tail. Settlers called it the 'native bear', which is why it is still wrongly called the koala bear.

In the early 20th century koalas were killed in vast numbers for fur: about 8 million between 1888 and 1927. Sanctuaries in Brisbane and Sydney led the first conservation efforts in the 1920s and 1930s. Since then the koala has brought Australian tourism over $1 billion in 1998 alone, starred as Blinky Bill, and inspired 'koala diplomacy' after world leaders held koalas at the 2014 G20 summit in Brisbane.
relatives:
The koala is the only living member of the family Phascolarctidae. Its closest living relatives are the wombats, and together they sit in the suborder Vombatiformes alongside extinct animals such as marsupial lions and giant wombats.

The koala lineage probably branched off around 40 million years ago. Ancient koalas lived in rainforests and ate a broader diet. As Australia dried out in the Miocene and eucalypt woodland spread, the koala's ancestors adapted to it. Its scientific name, Phascolarctos cinereus, means 'ash-coloured pouched bear'.
didYouKnow: A koala will not eat plucked eucalyptus leaves laid out on a flat surface, because that does not match its normal feeding routine.

quiz.prompt: What does the Dharug word gula, the origin of 'koala', mean?
choices: Little bear, after its rounded fluffy ears
quiz.explanation: Koalas get most of their water from leaves and rarely need to drink.

quiz.prompt: What are the koala's closest living relatives?
choices: Possums, which also live in trees
quiz.explanation: Koalas and wombats together form the suborder Vombatiformes.

quiz.prompt: How much does a newborn koala weigh?
choices: Around 300 g, about the weight of an apple
quiz.explanation: The tiny, barely formed joey crawls into the pouch to finish developing.

name: Mandarin Duck
range: Wooded rivers and lakes of East Asia; introduced in Western Europe
tagline: A dazzling duck that stands for faithful love
lede: The drake mandarin duck looks almost too ornate to be real, with a red bill, a white crescent over each eye, orange 'whiskers' and two upright orange sail feathers on its back. In China, Korea and Japan these birds have long stood for love and fidelity.
home:
Mandarin ducks are native to East and North-east Asia. The Asian birds are migratory, wintering in lowland eastern China and southern Japan. They breed along dense, shrubby, wooded edges of rivers and lakes, mostly at low altitude but up to 1,500 metres in valleys, and in winter also use marshes, flooded fields, coastal lagoons and estuaries.

Escapes from collections founded a large feral population in Great Britain during the 20th century, now about 7,000 birds, with smaller numbers in the parks of Dublin, a large population around Berlin, and isolated groups in North Carolina and Sonoma County, California. In Europe they use more open habitat than at home.
anatomy:
This is a fairly small duck, 41 to 49 centimetres long with a wingspan of 65 to 75 centimetres, slightly smaller than its American relative the wood duck. The male's breast is purple with two vertical white bars, and his flanks are ruddy. The sails are modified flight feathers whose enlarged inner vane sticks up like the sail of a boat.

The female is greyish brown, paler below, with a slender white eye-ring, a stripe running back from the eye and a pale tip to her bill. Both sexes have crests. After breeding, the male moults into a drab eclipse plumage that resembles the female's, though his bill stays bright. Ducklings can be told from mallard ducklings because their eye-stripe stops at the eye.
life:
Mandarins are shy, preferring cover under overhanging trees such as willows, and they gather in smaller flocks than many ducks. They feed by dabbling or walking on land, mainly near dawn and dusk, and spend the day perched in trees or resting on the ground.

Their diet changes with the seasons. In autumn and winter they eat mostly acorns, beech mast and grain. In spring they switch to insects, snails, fish and water plants, and in summer they add worms, frogs, molluscs and even small snakes. Predators include mink, raccoon dogs, otters, polecats, Eurasian eagle-owls and grass snakes.
family:
Mandarins breed in densely wooded areas near shallow lakes, marshes or ponds, nesting in tree holes close to water. The female lays a single clutch of 9 to 12 eggs in April or May. The male may guard her during incubation, but he does not sit on the eggs and leaves before they hatch.

Soon after hatching, the mother flies down and coaxes the ducklings to leap from the nest hole to the ground, then leads them to water. Females also often lay eggs in other mandarins' nests: in one reserve in north-east China, 46.1% did so. This saves them effort and risk, and the extra eggs did not harm the hosts' own chances.
remarkable: Mandarin ducks have 84 chromosomes, all of a similar shape, while other ducks typically have 80. This may make hybridising with other ducks very difficult or even impossible, and though hybrids with six other species have been reported, none has been verified.
outlook:
By the 1980s, mass exports and the destruction of forest habitat had cut numbers in eastern Russia and China to below 1,000 pairs each, while Japan still held around 5,000 pairs. China has since protected the species, and a 2009 survey estimated 12,000 to 14,000 birds there. Logging remains the greatest threat.

Hunters also shoot mandarins by accident because they are hard to identify in flight, and some are poached for their beauty. In Britain the introduced population seems to cause no harm, since it fills an empty niche, although it might come to compete with the tree-nesting common goldeneye.
people:
The German explorer Engelbert Kaempfer described the bird in 1727, writing that he could hardly believe his eyes when shown a picture of the drake until he saw one alive. In China mandarins are called yuanyang, from the words for the male and female, and 'two mandarin ducks playing in water' describes a loving couple.

Because the sexes look so different, yuanyang in Cantonese also means an odd pair, as in the drink of that name. In Korea, carved wooden wedding ducks are traditional marriage gifts, and in Japan a happily married couple is oshidori fūfu. Mandarins are also popular in zoos and waterfowl collections, where breeders have produced silver and white forms.
relatives:
The mandarin's only close relative is the North American wood duck; together they form the genus Aix, created in 1828. Linnaeus had placed it in Anas with other ducks in 1758.

Aix was Aristotle's word for an unknown diving bird, and galericulata comes from the Latin for a wig. The species has no subspecies. A fossil bone from West Runton in England, once thought to show that mandarins ranged far more widely, has been reinterpreted as an unidentified duck.
didYouKnow: In 1747 the naturalist George Edwards called it 'the Chinese teal', drawing it from a live bird kept on an estate in Richmond, Surrey.

quiz.prompt: What are the drake's orange 'sails'?

quiz.explanation: They are enlarged secondary flight feathers whose vane sticks up like a sail.

They climb down the trunk using their claws

name: Swordfish
range: Tropical and temperate Atlantic, Pacific and Indian Oceans
tagline: An ocean hunter with heated eyes and a sword
lede: Built like a torpedo and armed with a long, flat bill, the swordfish is one of the ocean's great hunters. It warms its own eyes to see better in cold, dark water, and it has been known to drive its sword clean through the hull of a boat.
home:
Swordfish roam tropical and temperate waters of the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian Oceans, including the Mediterranean. They prefer water of 18 to 22 °C but tolerate anything from 5 to 27 °C, the widest range of any billfish, and they typically move towards cooler regions to feed in summer.

By day they usually stay at depths of up to 550 metres, and one has been recorded at 2,878 metres. At night they rise to the surface and near-surface waters to feed. They are also often seen basking at the surface with the first dorsal fin out of the water.
anatomy:
Swordfish commonly reach 3 metres long, and the largest reported measured 4.55 metres and weighed around 650 kg. Females grow larger than males, and Pacific fish are bigger than those of the north-west Atlantic and Mediterranean. The body is long and round, and adults have lost all their teeth and scales; young fish shed their scales at around 1 metre long.

Next to each eye is a special heater organ that keeps the eyes and brain warm, with the eyes 10 to 15 °C above the surrounding water. Warm eyes see far better, which makes the fish a more effective predator. It is one of 22 fish species, along with marlin, tuna and some sharks, known to have a heat-conserving mechanism.
life:
Contrary to the popular image, swordfish probably do not skewer their prey. Instead they slash at it with the bill to injure it, then rely on speed and agility; small prey is simply swallowed whole. They are certainly among the fastest fish, but the often-quoted 100 km/h is unreliable, and something nearer 36 km/h is more likely.

They eat mackerel, barracudinas, hake, herring, lanternfish and other open-water fish, plus bottom fish, squid and crustaceans. In one north-west Atlantic study, 82% of stomachs held squid. Swordfish are loners or gather in very loose groups, sometimes 10 metres apart, and they leap clear of the water, perhaps to shake off remoras and lampreys.
family:
Swordfish spawn in batches in warm water, above about 24 °C in the North Pacific and 23 °C in the North Atlantic, where the Sargasso Sea is a known spawning ground. In the Caribbean and other warm parts of the western Atlantic they spawn all year round. A large female may carry between 1 million and 29 million eggs, each 1.6 to 1.8 millimetres across, which float in open water.

The larvae hatch at 4 millimetres long, and the bill appears when they reach about 1 centimetre. Swordfish mature at 4 to 5 years, and the oldest found in one study were a 16-year-old female and a 12-year-old male. Their age is read from growth rings in their fin rays.
remarkable: A wounded swordfish can be dangerous. Harpooned fish have rammed their swords through the planking of small boats, and museums hold hull fragments of large sailing ships with swordfish bills embedded in them, sometimes piercing several layers of heavy timber and even copper sheathing.
outlook:
Fully grown swordfish have few natural enemies, though killer whales sometimes take them, and shortfin mako sharks will attack them at their peril: makos have been found dead with broken-off swords in their heads. Young swordfish are eaten by many predators, and almost 50 kinds of parasites live on or in them. People are the main predator.

After a 1998 'Give Swordfish a Break' campaign in which 750 US chefs dropped North Atlantic swordfish from their menus, a large area of the Atlantic was closed to fishing, and the North Atlantic stock is now fully rebuilt. Stocks in the Indian Ocean and Mediterranean, however, are of high concern, and others are poorly known.
people:
Swordfish have been fished since ancient times, and in the Strait of Messina they are still hunted from traditional wooden boats called feluccas. Long-lining later spread around the world, while sport anglers developed swordfishing, often dropping baits hundreds of metres deep with glowing lights.

The firm meat is usually sold as steaks for grilling, and orange-tinted 'pumpkin swordfish' sells at a premium, but health authorities warn about high mercury levels. Swordfish is also at the centre of a long debate over whether it is kosher, since it sheds its scales as it grows. 'Swordfish' was the password in the Marx Brothers film Horse Feathers in 1932.
relatives:
The swordfish is the only member of its family, Xiphiidae. It looks like marlins and sailfish, but they belong to a different family, and the swordfish lineage split from all other billfish at least as far back as the middle Paleocene.

Its closest known relatives are the small, extinct blochiids of the early Eocene. Both parts of its scientific name mean 'sword': Xiphias from Greek and gladius from Latin. In some countries it is known as the broadbill.
didYouKnow: The International Game Fish Association's all-tackle record swordfish weighed 536 kg and was caught off Chile in 1953.

quiz.prompt: How do swordfish usually use their bill when hunting?
choices: To stun prey with a burst of electricity from its tip
quiz.explanation: They most likely slash at prey to weaken it rather than skewering it.

quiz.prompt: Why does a swordfish heat its eyes?
choices: To keep its blood from freezing in polar waters
quiz.explanation: Warmer eyes give sharper vision, making it a more effective predator.

quiz.prompt: What do adult swordfish lack?
choices: Fins on the back and belly, since they glide instead
quiz.explanation: Swordfish lose all their teeth and scales by adulthood.

name: Leopard Seal
range: Antarctic pack ice, wandering to southern coasts and islands
tagline: The spotted, singing top predator of the ice
lede: Sleek, spotted and armed with massive jaws, the leopard seal is the top predator of the Antarctic pack ice. It lurks beneath the floe edge waiting for penguins to enter the water, and its eerie underwater songs fill the Southern Ocean each summer.
home:
Leopard seals are 'ice-loving' seals that live mainly in the Antarctic pack ice between 50° and 80° south, with higher densities in West Antarctica. A population appears to be resident in Chilean Patagonia, and some consider them residents of New Zealand too, where they breed and are seen year-round.

Most stay in the pack ice all year, but in the southern winter mothers with pups may move north to sub-Antarctic islands and southern coasts. Wanderers have turned up in Australia, South Africa, Brazil, Uruguay, Easter Island and Tristan da Cunha, and one reached the Cook Islands in 1960, the most northerly sighting.
anatomy:
Leopard seals are long and muscular, 2.4 to 3.5 metres long and 200 to 600 kg, as long as a walrus but usually less than half its weight. Females are up to 50% larger than males. The coat is countershaded, dark grey above with leopard-like spots and white to light grey below, and a thick layer of blubber keeps the seal warm and streamlined.

The canine teeth are up to 2.5 centimetres long, yet the molars lock together to form a sieve for straining krill. The front flippers are unusually large for a true seal and let it steer with great agility. It has no external ears, but its hearing and short, clear whiskers work together to track prey underwater.
life:
Young leopard seals eat mostly krill, squid and fish, while adults tackle penguins, including emperor, king, Adélie, gentoo and chinstrap, and other seals such as crabeaters, young elephant seals and fur seal pups. To catch a penguin, the seal patrols the ice edge almost fully submerged, seizes the bird by the feet and beats it against the water.

Lacking slicing teeth, it shakes its prey from side to side to tear it apart. They are mostly shallow divers but can go deeper than 80 metres, collapsing their lungs on the way down. In winter, juveniles cannot dive deep enough to reach krill, and pairs have been seen hunting fur seal pups together. Their only natural predator is the orca.
family:
Leopard seals are solitary except for mothers and pups, and their breeding system is polygynous. Mating takes place in the water from December to January, and after an average pregnancy of 274 days the female gives birth to a single pup on the floating pack ice, in a circular hole she has dug in the ice.

The pup weighs about 30 kg at birth and stays with its mother for around a month before weaning; the father plays no part. Nearly a quarter of pups die in their first year. Females mature at 3 to 7 years and males at 6 or 7, and leopard seals can live up to 26 years.
remarkable:
In the southern summer, males sing underwater for hours each day, hanging upside down and rocking from side to side with their chests pulsing.

Their calls reach 153 to 177 decibels and include trills like birds or crickets and low, haunting moans. Young males use many varied calls, while mature males arrange a few stylised ones into their own distinctive songs.
outlook:
The IUCN lists the leopard seal as Least Concern. It is widespread and faces no major threats from human activity. A 2012 survey counted 35,000, probably a big underestimate, while other estimates run to 220,000 to 440,000; because the seals spend so long underwater, they are best surveyed by listening.

Hunting is regulated by the Convention for the Conservation of Antarctic Seals, and none currently occurs. Because it depends on sea ice, the leopard seal may suffer as polar ice shrinks with global warming. Commercial krill fishing, growing tourism, entanglement in marine debris and canine distemper virus are further concerns.
people:
Encounters with people are rare but memorable. During Shackleton's 1914–1917 expedition, a leopard seal about 3.7 metres long chased Thomas Orde-Lees across the ice until Frank Wild shot it. In 2003 biologist Kirsty Brown was killed while snorkelling near Rothera Research Station, the first recorded human death caused by a leopard seal.

The seals also have a habit of attacking the black pontoons of inflatable boats. Other meetings are gentler. A female leopard seal brought penguins to photographer Paul Nicklen for four days, perhaps trying to feed him. In New Zealand, a female named Owha frequented the North Island coast from 2012 to at least 2022.
relatives:
The leopard seal is the only species in the genus Hydrurga, named in 1848. It is a true seal and belongs to the Lobodontini, a tribe of Antarctic seals that also includes its closest relatives, the Ross, crabeater and Weddell seals.

The interlocking, krill-sieving molars they share are the trait that gives the tribe its name. Henri de Blainville described the species in 1820 from a stuffed specimen in Le Havre, which he believed came from around the Falkland Islands.
didYouKnow: Fossils show that leopard seals also lived along the coast of South Africa during the Late Pleistocene.

quiz.prompt: What is the leopard seal's only natural predator?
choices: The great white shark, which hunts near the ice
quiz.explanation: Orcas are the only animals known to prey on leopard seals.

quiz.prompt: How do leopard seals eat krill?
choices: They sieve it through their teeth
They lick it off the ice
They scoop it with their flippers
They chase single krill one at a time near the ice edge
quiz.explanation: Their molars lock together so they can strain krill from the water.

quiz.prompt: Which leopard seals sing long underwater songs?
choices: Both sexes equally, in winter duets under the ice
quiz.explanation: Males call for hours each day in summer, linked to breeding.
