name: Orca
range: All oceans and most seas, commonest in cooler coastal waters
tagline: The ocean's top predator, with its own family dialects
lede: Black and white, with a fin like a raised sword, the orca is the largest of the dolphins and the top predator of every ocean. It hunts in family teams with tactics passed down through generations, and different groups speak their own dialects and eat entirely different prey.
home:
Orcas are found in all oceans and most seas, from the polar ice edge to the tropics, though they are commonest in cooler coastal waters at higher latitudes. The densest populations live off the Norwegian coast, along the Aleutian Islands and in the Gulf of Alaska, and in the Southern Ocean around Antarctica.

Worldwide there are probably at least 50,000, including roughly 25,000 in the Antarctic. Their movements are poorly understood: the same whales appear off British Columbia and Washington each summer, yet where they spend the rest of the year remains unknown.
anatomy:
Males are usually 6 to 8 metres long and weigh more than 6 tonnes, and the largest reach 10 metres and over 10 tonnes; females are smaller, typically 5 to 7 metres. A male's dorsal fin is a tall triangle up to about 1.8 metres high, more than twice the height of the female's curved fin.

The body is black with a white lower jaw and belly, oval white patches above and behind the eyes, and a grey saddle behind the fin. Calves are born about 2.4 metres long, with patches that look yellow or orange.

Orcas have strong, interlocking teeth, good eyesight in and out of water and sophisticated echolocation. A layer of blubber 7.6 to 10 centimetres thick keeps them warm, and the heart slows from about 60 beats a minute at the surface to 30 when submerged.
life:
With no natural predators, orcas hunt in groups like wolf packs and eat an average of 227 kg a day. Each population specialises. Resident orcas of the northeast Pacific live mainly on salmon, especially Chinook, while transients hunt seals, sea lions and dolphins.

Off Norway, orcas herd herring into a tight ball with bubbles and flashes of their white bellies, then stun the fish with tail slaps. Others take sharks and rays, flip great white sharks upside down to paralyse them and eat their livers, or wear down the calves of large whales, including blue whales. In Antarctica, some orcas swim in formation to make waves that wash seals off ice floes.

At Península Valdés and the Crozet Islands they deliberately beach themselves to snatch sea lions and elephant seals, a technique that takes young whales years to learn.
family:
Resident orca society is unlike that of any other known mammal: sons and daughters stay with their mother for life. A matriline, averaging 5.5 animals, is led by the eldest female, and because females can reach 90, up to six generations may travel together. Related matrilines form pods, pods with similar calls form clans, and each pod has its own dialect of 7 to 17 call types that calves learn from their family.

Males mate with females from other pods. Females begin breeding at around 10 to 13 and usually have one calf about every 5 years after a pregnancy of 15 to 18 months.

Between 37 and 50 percent of calves die in their first 7 months. Fertility drops sharply after about 40, and orcas are among the few animals that go through menopause and live for decades afterwards; wild females average 50 to 80 years, males around 30.
remarkable:
Orcas have more cortical neurons than any other mammal, humans included, and their hunting methods and dialects are passed on by learning, which scientists describe as culture. They even seem to teach deliberately: off the Crozet Islands, mothers push calves onto the beach to practise and pull them back if needed.

In 2025, a Salish Sea orca was seen tearing off strands of bull kelp and rolling them over its body, the first recorded tool use by a killer whale.
outlook:
The IUCN lists the orca as Data Deficient, because several types may turn out to be separate species, some of them endangered. The main threats are dwindling prey, pollution, oil spills, noise and conflict with boats. As top predators, orcas concentrate toxins such as PCBs; some in the Norwegian Arctic carry more than polar bears.

After the Exxon Valdez spill, one transient group in Alaska fell to seven animals that had still not reproduced by 2009. The southern residents of Washington and British Columbia, which depend on declining Chinook salmon, were listed as endangered in the United States in 2005 and numbered only about 75 by 2019.
people:
The name killer whale may come from Basque sailors who called them whale killers after seeing them attack larger whales. Peoples of the Pacific Northwest give orcas a central place in art and belief: to the Haida they were the most powerful animals in the ocean, and the Lummi call them qwe'lhol'mechen, 'our relations under the waves'.

In Western cultures they were long feared, and fishermen once shot them as pests. Attitudes shifted after 1964, when a captured orca named Moby Doll proved gentle, and the photo-identification work of Michael Bigg revealed orca family life. Captivity remains controversial. Wild orcas have never killed a person, though captive animals have, and since 2020 orcas off Iberia have damaged hundreds of boats, often biting their rudders.
relatives:
Orcinus orca is the only living species in its genus and one of 35 species in the oceanic dolphin family, which appeared about 11 million years ago. Despite resemblances to false killer whales and pilot whales, its exact place in the family is unclear, with different genetic studies pointing to snubfin dolphins or to other branches.

The species itself may be several. Off western North America, fish-eating residents, mammal-eating transients and offshores rarely mix, and in 2024 researchers proposed raising residents and transients to full species. Four types, A to D, are known around Antarctica, and some of these may also prove distinct.
didYouKnow: At Eden in Australia, orcas once helped whalers hunt larger whales, and a male called Old Tom was reportedly seen there every winter from the 1840s to 1930.

name: Rock Ptarmigan
range: Arctic and Subarctic tundra and mountains, with outposts in the Alps, Pyrenees and Japan
tagline: The grouse that turns white for winter
lede: On bare Arctic mountainsides, a plump grouse turns from mottled grey-brown in summer to snow white in winter, vanishing against rock and snow alike. The rock ptarmigan thrives in some of the harshest places any bird lives, and even its feet are wrapped in feathers.
home:
Rock ptarmigans breed across Arctic and Subarctic Eurasia and North America, including Greenland, on rocky mountainsides and tundra. Beyond the Arctic they hang on in isolated mountain populations in Scotland, the Pyrenees, the Alps, Bulgaria, the Urals, the Pamirs, the Altai and Japan, where they live only in the Japanese Alps and on Mount Haku.

They prefer higher, barer ground than the willow ptarmigan. Southern birds barely move, dropping to lower, sheltered sites in winter, but in the far north they wander widely. Birds have crossed the 300 km Denmark Strait from Greenland to Iceland, carrying Greenland minerals in their gizzards. In Britain the species once lived in the Lake District, but now survives only in the Scottish Highlands.
anatomy:
The rock ptarmigan is 34 to 36 centimetres long, with a wingspan of 54 to 60 centimetres and a weight of 440 to 640 g, about 10 percent smaller than the willow ptarmigan. It moults to match the seasons. In winter it is entirely white except for black outer tail feathers and a black line through the eye.

In summer the breeding male is greyish above with white wings and belly, while the female is mottled grey and brown. Males have bright red combs above the eyes. The legs and feet are densely feathered. The bird can store little fat, so it must feed often in winter, and long blind-ended guts called ceca help it squeeze nutrition from poor food.
life:
Ptarmigans eat buds, catkins, leaves, flowers, berries and seeds, changing menu through the year. In Alaska, winter food is aspen, dwarf birch and willow buds and catkins; in spring they turn to crowberries and lingonberries; early summer brings the widest choice, including willow leaves and the flowers of Dryas, and late summer more berries and seeds.

Chicks eat insects, larvae and snails. In its remote habitat the rock ptarmigan has few predators, chiefly gyrfalcons, golden eagles and Arctic foxes, and it can be surprisingly approachable. On Franz Josef Land in the Russian High Arctic, a small population survives the dark polar winter by feeding on the rich plants that grow on and beneath seabird cliffs.
family:
In spring, males defend territories with snores, rattles and chases. In the aerial display a male flies fast on rapid wingbeats, glides upwards with tail fanned and then sails down, belting out a rasping call often compared to a stick dragged along a picket fence.

On the ground he fans his tail, stretches his neck, lowers his wings and circles a female. The red comb matters. In a study in Nunavut, males with larger, better-conditioned combs mated more often, and males with two mates had larger combs than those with one. Rock ptarmigans can breed at 6 months old and commonly raise up to six chicks, so hunting has little effect on their numbers.
remarkable:
The Svalbard subspecies is the only rock ptarmigan that fattens up significantly for winter. Most rock ptarmigans carry no more than 20 g of fat at any time, enough to last about 2 days without food, but Svalbard birds put on about 100 g, enough for up to 10 days of starvation.

Food there is scarcer than anywhere else in the range, and the extra weight does not seem to make walking any more costly.
outlook:
With its huge Arctic range and fast breeding, the rock ptarmigan is widespread, but some populations have declined. Its range in Britain has shrunk since the 1800s, and in Iceland, where ptarmigan is a traditional festive dish, hunting was banned in 2003 and 2004 because numbers had fallen.

Hunting has been allowed again since 2005 on a limited number of days set each year, and all trade in the birds is illegal there. In Japan the raichō is protected nationwide. During the last ice age the species was far more widespread across continental Europe.
people:
The rock ptarmigan is the official bird of Nunavut, where it is called aqiggiq, and the official game bird of Newfoundland and Labrador. In Japan its name, raichō, means 'thunder bird', and it is the emblem of Gifu, Nagano and Toyama Prefectures.

It has been introduced to New Zealand, South Georgia and the Kerguelen and Crozet Islands, while attempts in the Faroes and Ireland failed. In 1797 Thomas Bewick called it the White Grouse and noted that its dark meat tasted somewhat like hare, sometimes bitter from the hill plants it eats. It even has its own song, 'The Ptarmigan's Cry', by the heavy metal artist Sgaile.
relatives:
The rock ptarmigan belongs to the grouse tribe and is easily confused with the willow ptarmigan in winter. It can be told apart by its slimmer bill, its liking for higher and barer ground and, in males, black lores.

There are 23 recognised subspecies, from the Aleutian Islands to the Alps, the Pyrenees and Japan. The genus name Lagopus means 'hare-foot', after the feathered legs. The species name muta means 'mute' in Neo-Latin, a nod to the male's simple croaking song, and was long misspelt mutus until it was realised that Lagopus is feminine.
didYouKnow: The word ptarmigan comes from the Gaelic tarmachan, 'croaker', and its silent p was added by people who wrongly thought the word was Greek.

quiz.explanation: Raichō means 'thunder bird'; it is protected throughout Japan.

quiz.explanation: Svalbard birds gain about 100 g of fat, enough for up to 10 days without food.

name: Pallas's Cat
range: Cold, rocky steppes and mountains from the Caucasus to Mongolia and Tibet
tagline: The fluffy, grumpy-looking cat of the high steppe
lede: With its flat face, low-set ears and dense, smoky fur, Pallas's cat looks permanently unimpressed. About the size of a house cat but far stockier, it hunts pikas and voles across the cold, high steppes of Central Asia, and has become one of the internet's favourite wild animals.
home:
Pallas's cat, or manul, lives in widely scattered places from the Caucasus and the Iranian Plateau through the Hindu Kush, the Himalayas and the Tibetan Plateau to Mongolia, the Altai-Sayan region and the mountains of southern Siberia. It favours rocky montane grassland and shrubland, scree slopes and ravines where snow lies no deeper than about 15 to 20 centimetres.

Its climate is harsh. In the centre of its range air temperatures swing across 80 °C between summer and winter, falling to −50 °C. The cat has been recorded remarkably high: its droppings were found at 5,593 metres in Nepal's Shey Phoksundo National Park, the highest record yet.
anatomy:
Pallas's cat has a head-and-body length of 46 to 65 centimetres and a bushy tail of 21 to 31 centimetres, and it weighs 2.5 to 4.5 kg. Its long, dense fur, with up to 9,000 hairs in every square centimetre, makes it look stout and plush. The coat is light grey tinged with ochre, greyer and plainer in winter, with small black spots on the forehead, two black zigzag lines on each cheek, thin dark bars across the lower back and a ringed tail with a black tip.

The rounded ears sit low on the sides of the head, so the cat can peer over a rock while showing very little of itself, which gives its face a fierce look. Its legs are short, its claws short and sharp, and its bite powerful for its size.
life:
Pallas's cat is solitary and a specialised hunter of small mammals. It stalks or ambushes pikas, voles, gerbils and ground squirrels near burrow entrances, and scoops rodents out of shallow burrows with its paws; it also takes birds, beetles and grasshoppers. In Mongolia it switched to Brandt's vole when that species boomed between 2017 and 2020. It shelters in caves, rock crevices and old marmot burrows.

In central Mongolia, 29 radio-collared cats used 101 dens over two years. Home ranges vary enormously, from about 7 to 125 square kilometres for females and up to 207 square kilometres for males, and cats there were mostly active at dawn and dusk in summer but by day in autumn. They mark their ground with urine, droppings and scrapes.
family:
Females mature at about a year old, and pregnancy lasts 66 to 75 days. Between late April and late May the female gives birth to two to six kittens in a den among rocks or in an old marmot burrow with at least two entrances; in Iran one used hollows in ancient junipers. The fuzzy kittens open their eyes at about two weeks.

By 2 months they weigh 500 to 600 g, and their fur grows steadily longer. They begin hunting at about 5 months and are fully grown by 6 to 7 months.

In zoos the species is notoriously hard to raise: almost half of the kittens born in North American member zoos died within 30 days, the highest rate for any small wild cat.
remarkable:
Unlike most small cats, Pallas's cat has round pupils that shrink to tiny circles in bright sunlight rather than narrowing into slits.

Within its subfamily it shares this trait only with the puma, the jaguarundi and the cheetah. Framed by white rings around the eyes, the round pupils give the manul a stare unlike any other small cat's.
outlook:
Pallas's cat has been listed as Least Concern since 2020 because of its wide range and assumed large population, but some populations are in trouble. It was once hunted for fur in huge numbers, more than 10,000 skins a year in China, Mongolia and Russia. International trade ended in 1988, but domestic trade in skins and body parts for medicine continues in Mongolia, where it may still be hunted.

Poisoning campaigns against rodents and pikas destroy its prey, as on the Tibetan Plateau, where more than 54,000 square kilometres of grassland were poisoned between 2005 and 2009. Herding dogs, traps, poaching, mining and new roads add to the pressure. China lists it as Endangered, and Mongolia as Near Threatened.
people:
Manul is the cat's Mongolian name, and Pallas's cat honours the naturalist Peter Simon Pallas, who described it in 1776 from near Lake Baikal; the English name was coined by William Thomas Blanford. The species has been kept in zoos since the early 1950s, and by 2018, 177 lived in 60 zoos across Europe, Russia, North America and Japan.

It has also become an online celebrity. A Russian meme from 2008 shows a manul with a caption inviting you to pet the cat, Moscow Zoo made it its mascot in 2012, and a Novosibirsk Zoo manul called Zelenogorsk went viral for holding his own tail in his paws.
relatives:
Pallas described the cat as Felis manul, but in 1842 Johann Friedrich von Brandt proposed the genus name Otocolobus, which Reginald Pocock accepted in 1907. Genetic studies suggest it split from its relatives several million years ago, from the line leading to the genus Prionailurus according to nuclear DNA, or to Felis according to mitochondrial DNA.

Since 2017 cat specialists have recognised two subspecies: manul in the west and north of Central Asia, from Iran to Mongolia, and nigripectus in the Himalayas from Kashmir to Bhutan.
didYouKnow: In 2011, a Pallas's cat at Cincinnati Zoo became the first of her kind to be artificially inseminated, giving birth to four kittens 69 days later.

quiz.explanation: Its pupils contract to small circles, a trait it shares with the puma, jaguarundi and cheetah.

name: Philippine Tarsier
range: Forests of the southeastern Philippines, including Bohol, Samar, Leyte and Mindanao
tagline: A fist-sized primate with enormous eyes
lede: Small enough to sit in a human fist, the Philippine tarsier peers out of the night with the largest eyes, for its size, of any mammal. It can swivel its head 180 degrees, leap 3 metres between trees and call in ultrasound far too high for us to hear.
home:
The Philippine tarsier is found only in the southeastern Philippines, with established populations on Bohol, Samar, Leyte and Mindanao and others on smaller islands such as Maripipi, Siargao, Basilan and Dinagat. It lives in primary and secondary forest from sea level to about 700 metres, favouring dense, low vegetation such as tall grass, bushes and bamboo, and perches on average about 2 metres above the ground.

Recent studies found home ranges averaging 6.45 hectares for males and 2.45 hectares for females. In a night a tarsier may travel up to 1.5 km through the forest, and by day it sleeps in dark hollows close to the ground, deep in thick bush.
anatomy:
Standing just 85 to 160 millimetres tall, it is one of the smallest primates. Males weigh 80 to 160 g, and females are usually lighter. The fur is thin, rough and grey to dark brown, and the thin, nearly bald tail, about twice the length of the body, ends in a tuft and helps with balance.

The eyes are fixed in the skull and cannot move, so instead the tarsier turns its round head. In bright light the pupils shrink to tiny spots; in darkness they fill almost the whole eye. The thin, mobile ears are almost always twitching after sounds. Long fingers end in rounded pads that grip almost any surface, and the second and third toes carry sharp claws used for grooming.
life:
Tarsiers are hunters. They eat mainly live insects, especially crickets and grasshoppers, along with spiders, small crustaceans and the occasional small lizard or bird, grabbing prey and bringing it to the mouth with both hands. Clinging upright to trunks, they leap from branch to branch, powered by the long ankle bones that give the family its name.

They are solitary and shy, crossing paths only now and then at night. Calls include a piercing single-note loud call and a soft, bird-like trill of contentment; when several chirp together, the sound resembles locusts. Owls, small carnivores and large birds prey on them, and feral cats from nearby villages are a major threat.
family:
The mating season runs from April to May, and a pregnancy of about 6 months produces a single baby. It is born furry and with its eyes open, with a body about 70 millimetres long and a 115-millimetre tail. The mother carries it in her mouth, and the newborn can already cling to branches, beginning to leap in less than a month.

Females have several pairs of nipples, but only the pair on the chest gives milk; the others serve as anchor points for the infant. Babies nurse for about 60 days and reach maturity at 2 years. Tarsiers can live for 24 years in the wild. Depending on the population, they may pair with one partner or several.
remarkable:
Philippine tarsiers talk in ultrasound. They can call at around 70 kHz and hear frequencies above 90 kHz, well beyond the limit of human hearing.

Infants use these silent calls as distress signals when separated from their mothers, and males use them to call their mates in the breeding season. Females also mark their mates with scent from a gland around the mouth.
outlook:
The Philippine tarsier was last assessed by the IUCN in 2008 as Near Threatened, after a decline estimated at under 30 percent over about 20 years, driven by habitat loss and poaching for the pet trade. Illegal logging, firewood cutting, slash-and-burn farming and spreading towns and roads are eating into its forests.

On Bohol, where it was a common sight in the south until the 1960s, the Philippine Tarsier Foundation estimates only about 700 remain. Tarsiers do badly in captivity, where poor diet, bright lights and stress shorten their lives, and roadside displays may encourage tourists to buy them illegally. The species is protected under Philippine law, and the foundation runs a sanctuary at Corella on Bohol.
people:
Locally the tarsier goes by many names, including mawumag in Cebuano and other Visayan languages, magô in Waray, and mamag, magau and malmag. It first reached Western scientists through the missionary J. G. Camel, whose description was published by J. Petiver in 1705 and later formed the basis of Linnaeus's name Simia syrichta.

In Sarangani province, indigenous people leave tarsiers alone because they believe the animals bring bad luck, a superstition that, together with thick forest, has helped protect them. Today the tarsier is a flagship species for conservation, and Endangered Species International has created a sanctuary on Mindanao.
relatives:
Tarsiers belong to the family Tarsiidae, a lineage around 45 million years old. Until 2010 all living tarsiers were placed in the genus Tarsius, but a revision by Shekelle and Groves moved the Philippine species into its own genus, Carlito, named after the Filipino conservationist Carlito Pizarras.

The other genera are Tarsius of Sulawesi and Cephalopachus of Sundaland. Three subspecies are recognised, on Leyte and Samar, on Bohol, and on Mindanao, though how distinct they really are has long been debated.
didYouKnow: Tarsiers groom one another, with females removing dead skin and parasites from adult males and from their own young.

choices: It hops in a circle while keeping its body upright
quiz.explanation: Its eyes are fixed in the skull, so it rotates its head instead.

choices: In a fold of skin like a pouch on her side
quiz.explanation: Females carry their infants in their mouths.

quiz.prompt: Who is the tarsier's genus, Carlito, named after?
choices: An old Visayan spirit said to guard the night forest
quiz.explanation: It honours the Filipino conservationist Carlito Pizarras.

name: Snow Bunting
range: Breeds right around the Arctic, winters in northern temperate fields and shores
tagline: The songbird that lives farthest north
lede: When the Arctic is still locked in snow and the temperature can drop to −30 °C, the first migrant to return is a small black-and-white bunting. The snow bunting is the most northerly recorded perching bird in the world, and in winter its flocks swirl over fields and shores like blown snowflakes.
home:
Snow buntings breed right around the Arctic, on high tundra in North America, Ellesmere Island, Greenland, Iceland, Norway, Russia, Siberia, Novaya Zemlya and Franz Josef Land. Small isolated populations live on a few mountain tops further south, including the Cairngorms of Scotland, the Saint Elias Mountains on the Alaska–Yukon border and the Cape Breton Highlands.

There seems to be no northern limit to the range, while in the south it is limited by day length. In winter, buntings move to the northern temperate zone, from southern Canada and the northern United States to the coasts and plains of northern Europe and east into central Asia. There they roam open farmland, barren fields and lakeshores in flocks that can number in the hundreds.
anatomy:
The snow bunting is a ground-dwelling bird about 15 centimetres long, with a wingspan of 32 to 38 centimetres and a weight of 30 to 40 g; it is fairly large and long-winged for a bunting. In summer the male is white with a black back and black wingtips, and his yellow bill turns all black. The female has brown fringes to her black back feathers. In winter both sexes wear broad orange-brown fringes.

Instead of moulting into breeding colours, snow buntings let the brown feather tips wear away in spring to reveal the black beneath. Unlike most perching birds, they have feathered legs, a protection against the cold. Apart from the common raven, no other passerine winters as far north.
life:
From autumn to spring, snow buntings eat seeds of weeds and grasses such as knotweed, ragweed, goosefoot and goldenrod, often picking them from stems poking through the snow. In summer they add crowberry, bilberry, poppy and saxifrage seeds and invertebrates such as butterflies, flies, wasps and spiders. They even flip stones to uncover basking spiders, and sometimes catch insects in flight.

Their call is a rippling whistle, per-r-r-rit, and the male's song a brief, loud warble. Each male's song is unique, built from repeating motifs and lasting about 2 seconds, and how often he sings reveals how well he forages, since singing time competes with feeding time. Females use this to choose good providers.
family:
Males reach the Arctic first, at the beginning of April, to claim the best nest sites; females follow four to six weeks later as the snow begins to melt. In Greenland a male defends his territory with loud calls and head-lowered threats, and courts by rising 10 to 15 metres, gliding and singing loudly.

Pairs are monogamous, and the male shadows his mate during her fertile period. The nest is tucked into a rock crack or crevice, safe from predators but cold.

The female lays blue-green, brown-spotted eggs once the air rises above 0 °C, and the male brings her food while she sits so she can keep the eggs warm. They hatch in 12 to 13 days, the nestlings are fed only on invertebrates, and the young can fly 12 to 14 days later.
remarkable:
Snow buntings migrate by night and steer by the Earth's magnetic field, without relying on any visual cues. Only birds with enough stored energy pick the right seasonal direction.

Before heading north they feast, raising their fat mass by 30 percent while lean mass falls by 15 percent, and they enlarge their breast muscles, which also lets them shiver harder to stay warm on arrival.
outlook:
Snow buntings remain widespread, but climate change is a concern. For the past 40 years the Arctic oscillation, a regional climate pattern, has stayed in its positive phase, bringing warmer springs.

These trigger earlier breeding that can miss the peak of the insects the chicks need, reducing hatching success, and warmer conditions may draw competing species north. There may be some gains too, since higher temperatures could allow more second broods to survive. During the last ice age, the species was widespread throughout continental Europe.
people:
Linnaeus described the snow bunting in 1758 from Lapland, calling it Emberiza nivalis; nivalis is Latin for 'snow-white'. Its current genus name, Plectrophenax, coined by the Norwegian-born zoologist Leonhard Stejneger in 1882, joins Greek words for 'cock's spur' and 'impostor'.

For birdwatchers in winter, the challenge is telling it from look-alikes. The Lapland longspur has little white in the wing and a drier, more rattling call than the bunting's liquid ripple, and the horned lark has a black-and-yellow head pattern and no white on its wings.
relatives:
The snow bunting was once placed with the American sparrows and Old World buntings in the family Emberizidae, but it now belongs to the smaller family Calcariidae with the longspurs. Its closest relative is McKay's bunting of the Bering Sea region, which is even whiter; the two hybridise in Alaska, and some authors treat them as one species.

Four subspecies differ slightly in the plumage of breeding males: nivalis in Arctic Europe and North America, insulae in Iceland, the Faroes and Scotland, vlasowae in Arctic Asia, and the slightly larger townsendi of the Aleutians and Kamchatka. A hybrid with a Lapland longspur was photographed in Newfoundland and Labrador in 2011.
didYouKnow: In autumn, female snow buntings leave the Arctic first and winter further south than males, while juveniles linger longest.

quiz.prompt: How do male snow buntings get their black breeding plumage?
choices: They roll in dark soil to cover their winter feathers
quiz.explanation: The brown fringes wear away to reveal the black feather centres beneath.

quiz.prompt: Which other passerine winters as far north as the snow bunting?
choices: The Lapland longspur, which often flocks alongside it
quiz.explanation: Apart from the common raven, no other passerine winters so far north.

quiz.prompt: How do snow buntings find their way on migration?
choices: Following older birds along familiar coastlines by day
quiz.explanation: They migrate at night and sense the geomagnetic field, without using visual cues.

name: Proboscis Monkey
range: Mangroves, swamps and riverside forests of Borneo
tagline: Borneo's big-nosed, pot-bellied swimmer
lede: Few faces are as unforgettable as that of a male proboscis monkey, whose fleshy nose can be more than 10 centimetres long and hangs down past his mouth. This pot-bellied monkey of Borneo's mangroves is perhaps the most aquatic of all primates, as at home in a river as in the treetops.
home:
The proboscis monkey lives only on Borneo and is found in all three countries that share the island: Brunei, Indonesia and Malaysia. It is restricted to lowland habitats that may be reached by tides, especially mangroves, riverine forest and dipterocarp forest, but also uses swamp forests, nipa and nibong palm swamps, heath forest, limestone hills, rubber plantations and even steep cliffs.

It rarely strays more than a kilometre from water. Groups follow a daily rhythm tied to rivers. They sleep in neighbouring trees near the bank, forage there in the morning and then move inland to rest, returning to the river to feed again as night approaches.
anatomy:
This is one of the largest monkeys in Asia, and the sexes differ hugely. Males measure 66 to 76 centimetres in head-and-body length and usually weigh 16 to 22.5 kg, up to 30 kg; females are 53 to 62 centimetres long and weigh 7 to 12 kg.

The coat is orange, reddish-brown or brick-red on the back and paler below, and both sexes have a bulging, pot-bellied stomach and many webbed toes. The male's huge nose is supported by special cartilage, and one idea is that it evolved because females prefer males with louder calls, which a bigger nose amplifies.

Females have smaller noses, still large for a primate, and youngsters' noses are upturned. Babies are born with a blue face that darkens to grey at about 2.5 months and turns cream like the adults' by about 8.5 months.
life:
Proboscis monkeys eat mainly young leaves and unripe fruit, with some flowers, seeds and insects, from at least 55 plant species. They eat mostly fruit from January to May and mostly leaves from June to December, and occasionally chew the cud to digest more efficiently.

Their days are spent resting, travelling, feeding and keeping watch. A typical group has one adult male, several females and their young, though there are all-male groups and lone males. Groups gather at sleeping sites at night into bands of up to 60, then split and rejoin in a loose fission-fusion society.

Males honk to keep the group together, and both sexes roar, snarl and shake branches in disputes. Predators include false gharials and possibly pythons, saltwater crocodiles, Sunda clouded leopards and eagles.
family:
Females mature at about 5 years. At one site, mating took place mainly between February and November and births between March and May. Both sexes invite mating with a pouting face, and pregnancy lasts about 166 to 200 days.

Births usually happen at night or in the early morning, and the mother eats the placenta and licks her baby clean. Other group members are allowed to hold the infant.

Young start eating solid food at 6 weeks and are weaned at 7 months, while a young male's nose grows slowly until adulthood. Resident males may hold a group for 6 to 8 years; when one is replaced, infants risk being killed by the newcomer. Young males leave to join all-male groups, and females sometimes move too.
remarkable:
For a primate, the proboscis monkey is an astonishing swimmer. It regularly crosses rivers, can swim up to 20 metres underwater, and will jump from overhanging branches straight into the water.

Where it can, it crosses at narrow points or through the canopy, perhaps to avoid the crocodiles and false gharials waiting below.
outlook:
The proboscis monkey is listed as Endangered by the IUCN and in Appendix I of CITES. Its population fell by more than half in the 36 to 40 years up to 2008, as logging and oil palm plantations destroyed its forests, and in some areas it is hunted as a delicacy and for traditional Chinese medicine.

The largest populations remain in Kalimantan, with far fewer in Sarawak, Brunei and Sabah. It is protected by law throughout Borneo and occurs in 16 protected areas, including Tanjung Puting and Kutai National Parks in Indonesia and Bako National Park and the Lower Kinabatangan Wildlife Sanctuary in Malaysia.
people:
Westerners first learned of the proboscis monkey from Baron Friedrich von Wurmb in 1781, who later sent specimens to Stamford Raffles. Its genus name, Nasalis, comes from the Latin nasus, 'nose', and in English it is also called the long-nosed monkey.

It shares its forests with the Bornean orangutan and with other monkeys such as the silvery lutung. In Malaysia it is protected by federal law and by state laws in Sarawak and Sabah.
relatives:
The proboscis monkey is the only species in the genus Nasalis and belongs to the Colobinae, a subfamily of Old World monkeys. Two subspecies have been described, larvatus over most of the range and orientalis in northeast Kalimantan, though the difference is small and not all authorities accept it.

In Sabah, proboscis monkeys squeezed by oil palm clearing into small patches of riverside forest have formed mixed groups with silvery lutungs, and a possible hybrid has been seen in the Lower Kinabatangan. The two lineages split roughly 9 million years ago, so confirmed hybrids would be a surprise and a concern for conservation.
didYouKnow: Female proboscis monkeys arrange themselves in a strict linear pecking order.

quiz.prompt: On which island does the proboscis monkey live?
choices: Sulawesi and the small islands around it
quiz.explanation: It is found only on Borneo, in Brunei, Indonesia and Malaysia.

quiz.prompt: What colour is a newborn proboscis monkey's face?
choices: Black with pale pink patches around the eyes
quiz.explanation: Babies have blue faces that turn grey and then cream as they grow.

quiz.prompt: Why might male proboscis monkeys have such big noses?
choices: To help them breathe while swimming long distances underwater
quiz.explanation: A bigger nose may make a louder call, which females seem to prefer.

name: Southern Cassowary
range: Rainforests of New Guinea, nearby Indonesian islands and northeastern Australia
tagline: A helmeted giant of the rainforest floor
lede: A helmeted, blue-faced bird as tall as a person stalks the rainforests of New Guinea and northern Australia, red wattles swinging at its throat. The southern cassowary is one of the heaviest birds on Earth, and each foot carries a dagger-like claw.
home:
The southern cassowary lives in Indonesia, Papua New Guinea and northeastern Australia. It mainly inhabits tropical rainforest but also uses nearby savannah forest and mangroves, generally below about 1,100 metres in Australia and 500 metres in New Guinea.

Its total range covers some 396,000 square kilometres. Cassowaries are strong swimmers and can cross rivers and streams. People have traded live cassowaries for hundreds or perhaps thousands of years, and some birds probably escaped or were released far from where they came from, which blurs the picture of their natural range.
anatomy:
Southern cassowaries usually stand 1.5 to 1.8 metres tall, and the largest modern birds reach about 2 metres and 85 kg; on average only ostriches are heavier.

Females are larger and dominant, weighing roughly 47 to 76 kg against 29 to 55 kg for males, with a taller casque, bigger bill and brighter skin. The plumage is stiff, bristly and black, the face blue, the long neck red at the back, and two red wattles up to 18 centimetres long hang from the throat.

On top of the head sits a brown, horn-like casque 13 to 20 centimetres high. The three-toed feet are thick and powerful, and the inner toe bears a claw up to 12 centimetres long. Strong legs let a cassowary run at up to 50 km/h and jump nearly 2 metres straight up.
life:
Cassowaries forage on the forest floor for fallen fruit and seeds, and can safely digest some fruits that are toxic to other animals. Their droppings show they often eat Davidsonia plums and fruits of the palm, quandong, laurel and myrtle families.

They also take fungi, snails and insects, small animals such as fish, frogs, birds and mammals, and carrion, and when food is scarce they have been seen eating soil, perhaps for minerals. They are solitary and generally quiet, communicating with hisses and rumbles, but give a thunderous call in the breeding season. Chicks keep in touch with their father using high-pitched whistles and chirps.
family:
Pairs form only in the breeding season, usually in late winter or spring. The male builds a ground nest, a mattress of plants 5 to 10 centimetres thick and up to 1 metre wide that lets moisture drain away, and the female lays three to five eggs, each about 12 to 16 centimetres long and weighing around 600 g. They are granular and bright pea-green at first, fading with age.

After that, the female's job is done. The male incubates the eggs alone for about 50 days and then raises the striped, fluffy chicks, which can walk and explore within hours of hatching.

Young become independent at 9 to 12 months, and take 4 to 5 years to grow the full casque and adult plumage, when they usually start breeding.
remarkable:
The cassowary's fearsome reputation is mostly undeserved. A 2003 study of 221 attacks found that 150 were against people, and 75 percent of those came from birds that had been fed by humans; most involved birds expecting or snatching food.

Only two human deaths have been recorded since 1900, one in Queensland in 1926 when two boys tried to club a bird, and one in Florida in 2019 when a captive bird's owner fell.
outlook:
The IUCN evaluated the southern cassowary as Least Concern in 2018, and a 2002 study estimated 10,000 to 20,000 birds, but it faces habitat loss from logging, hunting, feral animals that eat its eggs, and road traffic. In Australia it is listed as Endangered under federal law, with around 5,000 birds estimated in 2023, when a draft recovery plan was published.

Vehicle strikes are a major cause of death, and feeding by people draws birds onto roads. Queensland has trialled AI cameras that detect cassowaries near roads and trigger warning signs. Some scientists argue that the Australian population has stabilised, thanks to protected habitat and laws that stopped rapid forest loss.
people:
The name cassowary, and the scientific name Casuarius, come from the Malay name kesuari. Linnaeus described the bird in 1758 as Struthio casuarius, from a specimen from the island of Seram.

In the late 1800s, Queensland hunters such as Archibald Meston shot and weighed birds they claimed reached 119 kg, far above typical weights, and Meston even reported a white bird he took for an albino. The writer Karl Brandt has suggested that Aboriginal encounters with cassowaries may have inspired the myth of the bunyip. Southern cassowaries have been bred in zoos around the world.
relatives:
The southern cassowary is one of three living cassowaries, alongside the northern and dwarf cassowaries, and is the type species of the genus Casuarius. Cassowaries are ratites, related to the emu, ostrich, rhea and kiwi, and are the sister lineage of the emus within the family Casuariidae.

Several subspecies have been described, mostly from the colours of the bare head and neck, but these fade in museum specimens and vary with age and between individuals. Most authorities now treat the species as having no subspecies, and its many old scientific names are considered synonyms.
didYouKnow: In 2026, scientists discovered that southern cassowary casques glow under ultraviolet light, in patterns different from those of northern cassowaries.

quiz.prompt: Who incubates southern cassowary eggs?
choices: Nobody, the eggs are buried in warm rotting leaves
quiz.explanation: The male incubates the eggs alone for about 50 days and raises the chicks.

quiz.prompt: What colour are freshly laid cassowary eggs?
choices: Pale blue with dark red spots at the narrow end
quiz.explanation: They start bright pea-green and fade with age.

quiz.prompt: What lay behind most cassowary attacks on people?
choices: Mistaking people for predators during the breeding season
quiz.explanation: Most attacks involved birds that had been fed by people expecting or snatching food.

name: Pronghorn
range: Open plains of western North America, from southern Canada to Mexico
tagline: The fastest runner in the Americas
lede: Across the open plains of the American West, a tan-and-white animal can outrun anything else on the continent. The pronghorn is the fastest land mammal in the Americas, reaching 88.5 km/h, and despite its nickname it is not an antelope at all but the last survivor of an ancient North American family.
home:
Pronghorns live west of the Mississippi, from southern Alberta and Saskatchewan through the western United States into Mexico, where the Sonoran subspecies ranges from Baja California Sur through Sonora to San Luis Potosí. They have disappeared from Iowa, Minnesota and Manitoba. They prefer open country between about 910 and 1,800 metres, with the densest populations where 254 to 406 millimetres of rain falls a year, and most stay within 8 km of water.

Some make epic journeys. In Idaho, researchers tracked a migration route of more than 260 km from the foothills of the Pioneer Mountains through Craters of the Moon National Monument to the Continental Divide, a route that narrows at one point to a bottleneck only about 180 metres wide.
anatomy:
Adult males are 1.3 to 1.5 metres long, stand 82 to 104 centimetres at the shoulder and weigh 40 to 65 kg; females are as tall but lighter, at 34 to 48 kg. The coat is tan with bold white on the rump, sides, belly, chest and throat, and the very large eyes, set high in the skull, give a 320° field of view.

Each foot has two hooves and no dewclaws. The horns are unique. A permanent bony core is covered by a keratin sheath that is shed and regrown every year, and in males the sheath, averaging about 25 centimetres, carries a forward-pointing prong.

Females' horns are small, sometimes barely visible, and very rarely pronged. Males also have a patch of black hair at the angle of the jaw.
life:
Pronghorns eat a wide variety of plants, including some that are unpalatable or poisonous to livestock. In one study forbs made up 62 percent of the diet, shrubs 23 and grasses 15; another found cacti made up 40 percent. Like cattle, they chew the cud. Their predators include cougars, wolves, coyotes, grizzly bears and bobcats, and golden eagles take fawns.

When a pronghorn spots danger, the white hair on its rump flares open, exposing glands that release a smell like buttered popcorn and warning others by sight and scent; people have smelled it 20 to 30 metres downwind. Built for running rather than jumping, pronghorns tend to slip under fences instead of leaping them.
family:
Pronghorns gather in mixed herds in winter, then split in spring into bachelor groups, female harems and solitary adult males. Some males defend a territory, others a harem, and they may switch strategy.

Females choose in different ways: some visit several males, some provoke fights between males and mate with the winner, and some stay quietly with one. A courting male approaches softly vocalising and waving his head to show his cheek patches. They breed in mid-September, and pregnancy lasts 7 to 8 months, unusually long for a North American hoofed animal. Twins are common, and newborns weigh 2 to 4 kg.

For their first 3 weeks or so fawns hide in vegetation, meeting their mothers for only 20 to 25 minutes a day. Pronghorns mature at 15 to 16 months and live up to 10 years, rarely 15.
remarkable:
The pronghorn's real gift is stamina. It can run at 56 km/h for 6.5 km and at 68 km/h for 1.5 km. Although slower than a cheetah, it holds high speed far longer, thanks to an oversized windpipe, heart and lungs, a large blood volume, very light bones, hollow hair and cushioned hooves.

It has at least 13 distinct gaits, with a stride of nearly 7.3 metres at full stretch. Why it evolved such speed is debated. One idea links it to the extinct cat Miracinonyx, but fossils suggest pronghorn ancestors were already built for running before that predator appeared.
outlook:
Around 1900, conservationists of the Boone and Crockett Club feared the pronghorn would go extinct, and by the 1920s hunting had cut the population to about 13,000. Refuges followed, including the Charles Alexander Sheldon Antelope Refuge in Nevada, created with the National Audubon Society and greatly expanded by President Franklin Roosevelt in 1936. With habitat protection and hunting limits, numbers recovered to an estimated 500,000 to 1,000,000.

Today pronghorns are legally hunted for food and population control, and no major range-wide threat exists, though fences and roads block migration corridors and bluetongue disease from sheep has caused local declines. The Sonoran and Baja California subspecies are endangered, with fewer than 300 Sonoran pronghorns left in the United States.
people:
Plains peoples and those of the Northwest Plateau hunted pronghorns as a principal food, and the animal features prominently in Native American mythology. Lewis and Clark described how the Mandan drove herds into a large pen through gradually narrowing fences of bushes, and were struck by the animal's 'wonderful fleetness'.

Clark was among the first Euro-Americans to describe killing one, near the mouth of the Niobrara River. Spanish explorers saw pronghorns in the 16th century, but George Ord gave the formal description only in 1815. The species is the symbol of the American Society of Mammalogists, and pronghorns once outnumbered people in Wyoming.
relatives:
Despite names like American antelope and prairie antelope, the pronghorn is not an antelope; it resembles Old World antelopes through parallel evolution. It is the only surviving member of the family Antilocapridae, and its closest living relatives are the giraffe and the okapi.

During the Pleistocene about 11 other antilocaprids roamed North America, many with long or spectacularly twisted horns, and three other genera still existed when humans arrived. Recognised subspecies include the Rocky Mountain, Mexican, Oregon, Sonoran and critically endangered Baja California pronghorns.
didYouKnow: Unlike deer, pronghorns have a gallbladder.

quiz.prompt: What are the pronghorn's closest living relatives?
choices: Mountain goats and bighorn sheep of the Rockies
quiz.explanation: Despite its looks, the pronghorn's closest living relatives are the giraffe and okapi.

quiz.prompt: What does a pronghorn's alarm scent smell like to people?
choices: Wet dog after a long walk in the rain
quiz.explanation: The main compound in the rump gland smells like buttered popcorn.

quiz.prompt: What happens to the pronghorn's horn sheath every year?
choices: It splits lengthways into two separate spikes
quiz.explanation: The keratin sheath over the bony core is shed and regrown annually.

name: Saola
range: Wet mountain forests of the Annamite Range in Vietnam and Laos
tagline: The 'Asian unicorn', found by science only in 1992
lede: In 1992, scientists surveying a new national park in Vietnam were handed a skull with a pair of long, straight horns unlike anything they knew. It belonged to the saola, a forest bovid so secretive that no trained scientist has ever watched one in the wild. Today it may be teetering on the edge of extinction.
home:
The saola lives only in the Annamite Range, the mountain chain along the border of Vietnam and Laos, and has one of the smallest ranges of any large mammal, covering roughly 5,000 square kilometres including four nature reserves. It favours wet evergreen or deciduous forest, especially steep river valleys between about 300 and 1,800 metres above sea level.

In the northern Annamites it has mostly been reported near streams at around 600 to 1,100 metres, and it is said to move down to the lowlands in winter. Above all, it needs forest that is remote from people.
anatomy:
A saola stands about 84 centimetres at the shoulder, with a head-and-body length of about 1.5 metres, and weighs roughly 80 to 100 kg.

Its soft, thin coat is chocolate brown, paler on the neck and belly, with a narrow black stripe down the back and bold white patches on the face, throat and sides of the neck. The short tail is banded brown, white and black. Both sexes carry nearly parallel horns, dark brown or black and about 35 to 50 centimetres long, twice the length of the head.

On each side of the muzzle is a maxillary gland, probably the largest of any animal, covered by a flap and filled with a pungent, greyish-green paste. Its skin thickens to 5 mm around the nape and shoulders, perhaps as armour against predators and the horns of rivals.
life:
Almost everything known about saola behaviour comes from local hunters and from a handful of captive animals. Villagers say saola are active by day and by night but rest through the hot middle of the day.

They seem to be mostly solitary, though groups of two or three, and occasionally six or seven, have been reported. A female kept briefly in Laos fed on spleenwort ferns, Homalomena and the leaves of broad-leaved shrubs and trees, and the species is said to eat Schismatoglottis plants that other herbivores ignore.

She was calm with people but terrified of dogs, snorting and lowering her horns at them. She marked rocks and plants by opening the flaps of her facial glands and smearing on their musky secretion, and occasionally gave short bleats.
family:
Very little is known about how saola breed. Mating probably happens between late August and mid-November, and single calves appear to be born mainly between mid-April and late June. Pregnancy is guessed to last about 33 weeks, similar to bushbuck and their relatives, though no one has measured it.

Villagers who killed mothers with young reported calves whose horns ranged from 9.5 to nearly 19 centimetres long, which suggests the birth season is spread over at least two or three months. Zoos have taught us nothing about the life cycle, because every saola kept in captivity has died within weeks or months.
remarkable: The saola was the first large mammal discovered in the region for 50 years, and it was so unlike any other hoofed animal that it was placed in a genus of its own. DNA has since shown that it is the earliest branch of the wild cattle tribe, having split from the ancestors of buffalo, bison and yaks between about 11 and 16 million years ago.
outlook:
The saola is listed as Critically Endangered, with an estimated 50 to 300 animals left as of 2015. The last confirmed record is a camera-trap photograph from central Vietnam in 2013, and some fear it is already extinct.

Its biggest threat is snares set for wild boar, sambar and muntjac; conservation groups have removed more than 26,000 of them from saola forests. It is also hunted for meat and traditional medicine, and its forest is being lost and fragmented.

The Saola Working Group, formed in 2006, and the Saola Foundation are searching remote forests with local trackers, dung-sniffing dogs and a field DNA test, hoping to catch survivors and start a breeding programme. One conservationist warned in 2025 that extinction within a decade is inevitable without such intervention.
people:
The name comes from a Tai language of Vietnam and is usually translated as 'spindle horn', though it more precisely means 'spinning-wheel post horn', after the parallel wooden posts that hold a spinning wheel. The Hmong in Laos call it 'the polite animal' because it moves so quietly through the forest.

Newspapers dubbed it the 'Asian unicorn' for its rarity and gentle nature, though it has no link to unicorn legends. In local villages a hunter who brings in a saola wins great esteem, which makes protection harder, and the intense scientific interest even encouraged hunters to try to capture live animals. A cartoon saola named Sao La was the mascot of the 2021 Southeast Asian Games.
relatives:
The saola is the only species in the genus Pseudoryx, a name that nods to its resemblance to the oryx of Arabia and Africa; its species name refers to the Vietnamese provinces of Nghệ An and Hà Tĩnh. Before genetic studies, experts had variously grouped it with goats and sheep or with three different tribes of wild cattle and antelopes.

It now sits firmly in the tribe Bovini. A 2025 study of its genome found that saola split into northern and southern populations between 5,000 and 20,000 years ago, and that their numbers have stayed small for at least 10,000 years.
didYouKnow: A captive saola could stretch its tongue about 16 centimetres, far enough to reach its own eyes, and the tongue's upper surface is covered in fine backward-pointing barbs.

quiz.prompt: In what year did scientists first find evidence of the saola?
choices: 2013, from a camera-trap photograph in Laos
quiz.explanation: A survey team in Vietnam's Vũ Quang National Park obtained a skull with its strange horns in May 1992.

quiz.prompt: What is the biggest threat to the saola?
choices: Disease spread by domestic cattle grazing in its forests
quiz.explanation: Snares meant for wild boar, sambar and muntjac also catch saola; more than 26,000 have been removed.

quiz.prompt: Which animals are the saola's closest relatives?
choices: Goats and sheep of the high mountains
quiz.explanation: DNA places it as the earliest branch of the tribe Bovini, with buffalo, bison and yaks.

name: Western Barn Owl
range: Open country across Europe, West Asia and Africa
tagline: The ghostly, heart-faced owl that screeches, not hoots
lede: Pale as a ghost and silent in flight, the western barn owl drifts low over fields at dusk, listening. Its heart-shaped face works like a satellite dish, funnelling the faintest rustle to ears so sharp it can catch a mouse in total darkness.
home:
The western barn owl is found across most of Europe, West Asia and Africa, with its densest populations in Western and Central Europe and around the Mediterranean. Smaller clusters live in East Africa and Madagascar, and it occurs in scattered pockets across West Africa. People have introduced it to some Pacific islands and Malaysia to control rats.

It hunts over open wetlands, grassland, savanna, heath and shrubland up to 4,000 metres, as well as farmland and the edges of towns. It needs open ground to hunt over and a cavity to nest in: a hollow tree, a crack in a cliff, or increasingly a barn, farm shed or church tower.
anatomy:
This is a medium-sized, pale owl about 33 to 35 centimetres long with a wingspan of 80 to 95 centimetres, long wings and a short, square tail. Its back and head are a mottled grey or golden brown finely speckled with black and white, while the underparts range from white to reddish buff.

Females average about 10% heavier than males and tend to have more spots, which may signal resistance to parasites. Its flight is almost soundless: tiny serrations on the leading edges of its flight feathers and a soft fringe on the trailing edges break up the turbulence that makes noise.

Its ears sit at different heights on its head, which helps it judge both the direction and the distance of a sound. It has a much higher metabolism than other owls its size, so it needs relatively more food.
life:
Barn owls hunt mainly at dusk and through the night, flying slowly back and forth over rough grass and hovering over likely spots, or watching from a fence post.

When they hear prey they drop onto it, driving their talons through grass or snow. In Britain some also hunt by day, especially after a wet or windy night. In damp temperate regions, small mammals make up more than 90% of the diet, mostly voles, mice and shrews. Small prey is swallowed whole, and the bones and fur are later coughed up as pellets, which scientists study to learn what the owls eat.

In hot, dry places they take more reptiles and birds; on the Cape Verde Islands, geckos are the staple. The barn owl never hoots: its call is a long, eerie, piercing screech, and both young and adults hiss like snakes at intruders.
family:
Pairs usually stay together for life, returning to the same nest site year after year. In Europe most nesting happens between March and June, and in good rodent years a pair may raise two broods.

The female lays about five chalky white eggs, sometimes as few as two or as many as nine, one every other day, on a carpet of her own shredded pellets. She incubates for about 30 days while the male brings food, so the chicks hatch days apart. The chicks are half their adult weight at 2 weeks and fledge at about 9 weeks, but rely on their parents until around 13 weeks old.

Wild barn owls are short-lived, averaging about four years, and only one young in three survives to breed, mostly because many starve in their first winter. A few wild birds have passed 18 years, and captive ones have lived beyond 25.
remarkable: A barn owl does not need to see its prey at all. Experiments show that its facial disc is part of the hearing system: with the ruff feathers removed, an owl can still tell where a sound comes from horizontally but can no longer judge its height.
outlook:
Globally the barn owl is listed as Least Concern, and as a prolific breeder it can bounce back from short-term crashes. But it has become scarcer in many places. A survey in 1995 to 1997 put Britain's population at 3,000 to 5,000 breeding pairs, out of roughly 150,000 pairs across Europe, where it is a Species of European Concern.

The main problems are the loss of hedgerows and rough grassland to modern farming, the demolition or sealing of old buildings, collisions with cars on road verges, and poisoning from pesticides and rat poisons. Nest boxes help a great deal, and in Israel and Jordan farmers have used barn owls instead of pesticides to control rodents, a scheme since copied in several other countries.
people:
The barn owl has collected an extraordinary list of names, including ghost owl, church owl, demon owl, hissing owl, monkey-faced owl and screech owl. Shakespeare's 'scritch-owl' in A Midsummer Night's Dream is this bird, and in Britain its scream was thought to foretell storms: hail in England, snow in Glamorgan, rain in Scotland.

Its reputation was often sinister. In parts of Europe barn owls were killed and nailed to barn doors to ward off curses and lightning, a custom that lasted in France and Switzerland into the 1960s. In Yorkshire, owl broth was once given to children with whooping cough, and a 1979 sighting of a human-like 'Owlman' in Cornwall may have been a barn owl.
relatives:
The species was named Strix alba by the Italian naturalist Giovanni Antonio Scopoli in 1769; alba is Latin for 'white', because it was far paler than any other owl he knew. It now sits in the genus Tyto with the other barn owls and masked owls, which are distinct from the 'true' owls; in the air, the square tail helps tell them apart. Until recently, barn owls around the world were treated as one species.

Genetic studies in 2016 to 2018 split them into four: the western barn owl, the American barn owl, the eastern barn owl and the Andaman masked owl. The western barn owl's lineage separated from the American barn owl's about 5 million years ago.
didYouKnow: Black, or melanistic, western barn owls are thought to occur in only about 1 in every 100,000 birds.

quiz.prompt: What sound does the western barn owl make?
choices: A soft two-note hoot repeated through the night
quiz.explanation: Barn owls never hoot; their call is a long, piercing screech.

quiz.prompt: What do barn owls cough up after eating?
choices: Undigested insect wings mixed with sand and grit
quiz.explanation: Small prey is swallowed whole, and the indigestible fur and bones come back up as pellets.

quiz.prompt: About how long does a wild barn owl live on average?
choices: Over 40 years, like many large birds
quiz.explanation: Wild barn owls average about four years, though captive birds can pass 25.

name: Serval
range: Wetlands, grasslands and moist savannas across sub-Saharan Africa
tagline: The long-legged African cat that hunts by ear
lede: With legs longer for its size than any other cat's and ears like radar dishes, the serval stalks tall African grass listening for rats it cannot see. When it locates one, it springs high into the air and comes down on its target with its front paws.
home:
Servals live across much of sub-Saharan Africa, from the Sahel to the far south, with a small population in Morocco and a reintroduced one in Tunisia; they are feared extinct in Algeria. They prefer places near water, such as wetlands and moist savanna, where reeds and tall grass give cover, and they also live in grassland, moorland and bamboo thickets up to 3,800 metres on Mount Kilimanjaro. They avoid rainforest and true desert.

Each serval keeps a home range of 10 to 32 square kilometres, spending most of its time in a few core areas, and the ranges of neighbours overlap widely.
anatomy:
The serval is a slender, medium-sized cat standing 54 to 62 centimetres at the shoulder and weighing about 8 to 18 kg, with females usually lighter.

Its head-and-body length is 67 to 100 centimetres, and its tail is short, around 30 centimetres, with a black tip. The golden-yellow to buff coat is covered in black spots and stripes, and the backs of its ears are black with a white band. Its exceptional leg length comes mainly from greatly lengthened bones in the feet, and its long toes are unusually mobile.

Its big, closely set ears can each swivel through 180 degrees independently. Servals look a little like caracals but lack their ear tufts and have a rounder skull. Black servals have been seen in the wild, mostly in Kenya.
life:
Servals are active by day and night, often peaking in early morning, at twilight and around midnight, and rest in shade through the midday heat. They walk 2 to 4 km each night, often along regular trails.

Rodents, especially vlei rats, make up 80 to 97% of the diet, and most prey weighs under 200 grams, though they also catch shrews, hares, frogs, insects, reptiles and birds as large as flamingos. A hunting serval may sit motionless for up to 15 minutes, then leap up to 4 metres and stun its prey with a blow from its forepaws before biting the head or neck.

They are skilled hunters: one study in Ngorongoro found that about half their attempts succeeded, and they averaged 15 to 16 kills a day. Servals are solitary and avoid fights, marking their ranges with urine, droppings and saliva. Like many cats they can purr, and they also chirp, hiss, cackle and growl.
family:
Females come into heat once or twice a year, and births tend to be timed just before local rodent populations boom. After a pregnancy of 2 to 3 months, the mother gives birth to 1 to 4 kittens in dense cover or an old aardvark or porcupine burrow.

Newborns weigh about 250 grams, are blind, and have soft greyish fur; their eyes open after 9 to 13 days. A mother with young kittens has to hunt almost twice as hard as other servals, and if disturbed she carries the kittens one by one to a safer spot.

At about six months the young get their permanent canines and begin hunting, and they leave their mother at around a year old. Servals live about 10 years in the wild and up to 20 in captivity.
remarkable: In a single bound a serval can rise more than 2 metres off the ground and cover up to 3.6 metres horizontally, enough to catch birds as they try to flee. Guided almost entirely by sound, this pounce from above lets it strike rodents hidden deep in grass.
outlook:
The serval is listed as Least Concern and occurs in many protected areas, and hunting it is banned or regulated in most countries where it lives. Its main threat is the loss and degradation of the wetlands and grasslands it depends on.

Pastoralists sometimes kill servals to protect their livestock, even though servals rarely take farm animals. The trade in serval skins, though declining, continues in countries such as Benin and Senegal, and in West Africa the animal is also used in traditional medicine.
people:
People have known servals for thousands of years: Ancient Egyptian art shows them as gifts or trade goods brought from Nubia. The name comes from the Portuguese lobo-cerval, meaning lynx, which the French naturalist Buffon applied in 1765 to a spotted cat kept in the royal menagerie at Versailles. Servals are sometimes kept as pets, though ownership is regulated in some countries because they remain wild animals.

In 1986 the first savannah cat was born from a male serval and a female domestic cat. The breed inherited some tameness from its mother, and it has since become a popular pet, known for its leaping, swimming and dog-like habit of following its owner around.
relatives:
The serval is the only member of the genus Leptailurus, from Greek words meaning 'delicate cat'. Its closest relatives are the caracal and the African golden cat, which together form one of the eight main lineages of the cat family.

This group arose about 8.5 million years ago, and its ancestor reached Africa between 8.5 and 5.6 million years ago. The serval was first described scientifically in 1776, and many supposed species were later named from individual skins. Today three subspecies are recognised: one in southern Africa, one in central and West Africa, and one in East Africa.
didYouKnow: One serval being chased by dogs escaped by climbing more than 9 metres up a tree, although servals climb only occasionally.

quiz.prompt: How does the serval mainly find its prey?
choices: By feeling ground vibrations through its long toes
quiz.explanation: Its large ears, which swivel independently, let it locate rodents hidden in grass.

quiz.prompt: What record does the serval hold among cats?
choices: Biggest ears of any wild cat relative to its tail length
quiz.explanation: Thanks to lengthened foot bones, it has the longest legs of any cat relative to body size.

quiz.prompt: Which domestic cat breed comes from servals?
choices: The Egyptian Mau, first bred in ancient Nubia
quiz.explanation: Savannah cats come from crossing servals with domestic cats; the first was born in 1986.

name: Short-beaked Echidna
range: Throughout Australia and in eastern New Guinea
tagline: A spiny, egg-laying mammal with a lightning tongue
lede: The short-beaked echidna is a mammal that lays eggs, has no true teeth, and catches ants with a sticky tongue that flicks in and out 100 times a minute. Covered in spines and built like a bulldozer, it is the most widespread native mammal in Australia.
home:
Short-beaked echidnas live throughout Australia, including Tasmania and Kangaroo Island, and in coastal and highland regions of eastern New Guinea. They can live almost anywhere with a good supply of ants and termites, from forests full of fallen, termite-riddled logs to scrub, grassland, arid inland country and the outer suburbs of cities. They have no fixed nest and do not defend territories.

Each roams a home range of typically 40 to 60 hectares, and neighbours can share ranges and even shelters without trouble. Little is known about their distribution in New Guinea.
anatomy:
Echidnas are typically 30 to 45 centimetres long and weigh 2 to 7 kg, with a 75 mm snout and no visible neck. Cream-coloured spines up to 5 centimetres long, which are modified hairs made of keratin, cover the back and sides, with honey-coloured to black fur between them.

The short, powerful limbs end in strong digging claws, and long, backward-curving claws on the hind feet are used to groom between the spines. The mouth opens no wider than 5 mm, but the tongue can reach 18 centimetres beyond the snout, stiffened by a rush of blood and coated in sticky mucus.

The leathery snout is packed with touch sensors and electroreceptors that can detect weak electric fields. A huge muscle under the skin lets it roll into a spiny ball, helped by one of the shortest spinal cords of any mammal.
life:
Echidnas use smell and their sensitive snouts to find food, tearing open nests and rotting logs with their claws. They eat mainly ants and termites, preferring termites when available because they carry less indigestible shell, and take beetle larvae and earthworms too.

A 3 kg echidna can eat 200 grams of termites in 10 minutes, swallowing soil along with them. They cannot sweat or pant, so in hot weather they become active at dusk or night; body temperatures above 34 °C are thought to be fatal.

In winter they hibernate, their body temperature falling as low as 4 °C and their heart slowing to four to seven beats a minute. When threatened, an echidna digs straight down or curls into a ball, and it can swim, using its snout as a snorkel.
family:
During the mating season, between May and September, a female may be followed by a 'train' of up to 10 males that trail her for as long as 4 weeks.

After mating she lays a single soft, leathery egg, 13 to 17 mm across, directly into a pouch on her belly, where it hatches after about 10 days. The tiny hatchling, called a puggle, weighs less than half a gram. Monotremes have no nipples, so the puggle sucks milk from special patches of skin; the milk is rich in iron, which turns it pink.

Once its spines grow, at two to three months, it is moved out of the pouch into a burrow, and it leaves for good at around six months. Echidnas live about 10 years in the wild on average, and one in a Philadelphia zoo reached 49.
remarkable: The short-beaked echidna has the largest prefrontal cortex relative to body size of any mammal, making up half its brain compared with 29% in humans. Its learning ability has been compared with that of a cat or a rat, and it can remember a solution for over a month.
outlook:
The short-beaked echidna is common and widespread and is not considered threatened. In Australia the biggest dangers are cars and habitat clearance: about a third of echidna deaths reported in Victoria over a decade were caused by vehicles, and fields cleared completely for crops such as wheat have lost their echidnas.

Drainage culverts under roads help them cross safely. Foxes, cats, dingoes, goannas and birds of prey take mostly young animals, and an introduced tapeworm caught at shared water holes can be fatal. In New Guinea, hunting with dogs has increased as old taboos fade, and echidnas seem to have vanished from highland areas.
people:
Echidnas appear in the art, stories and totems of Aboriginal Australians. One story tells of hunters who threw spears at a wombat in the dark; the wombat used the spears for its own defence and became an echidna. The Noongar people call it nyingarn, and in Pitjantjatjara its name, tjilkamata, can also mean 'slowpoke'.

Today it appears on Australia's 5-cent coin, and an echidna called Millie was a mascot of the 2000 Summer Olympics. Video gamers know Knuckles the Echidna, the superhumanly strong red echidna of the Sonic the Hedgehog games. Older books called it the spiny anteater, though it is only distantly related to true anteaters.
relatives:
Echidnas and the platypus are the monotremes, the only living mammals that lay eggs. The short-beaked echidna is the only member of its genus, Tachyglossus, meaning 'fast tongue', and shares its family with the larger long-beaked echidnas of New Guinea, which eat mostly worms and grubs.

Echidnas are thought to have split from the platypus around 66 million years ago. George Shaw first described the species in 1792, placing it in the same genus as the giant anteater, and its scientific name went through four revisions before settling. Five subspecies are recognised, differing in hairiness and spine length.
didYouKnow: A captive echidna once moved a refrigerator around a scientist's home, and another has been recorded shifting a 13.5 kg stone.

quiz.prompt: What is a baby echidna called?
choices: A spikelet, after its soft early spines
quiz.explanation: Young echidnas are known as puggles.

quiz.prompt: How many eggs does a female echidna lay each time she breeds?
choices: A clutch of about a dozen, buried in sand
quiz.explanation: Each mating produces a single egg, laid straight into her pouch.

quiz.prompt: Why is echidna milk pink?
choices: It mixes with red clay from the walls of the burrow
quiz.explanation: Its high iron content gives the milk a pink colour.
